quick_hits: Instead of trapping prey in a web, a spitting spider shoots a sticky mixture from its fangs that pins a small animal to the surface. The spider then moves in to bite.
The unusually high, rounded front of the body houses enlarged glands involved in producing the spider's sticky prey-catching fluid.
Spitting spiders have six eyes arranged in three pairs rather than the eight eyes found in many familiar spiders.
It is a slow hunter. Rather than chasing fast prey, it approaches within range and immobilizes the target before closing in.
A female carries her egg sac beneath her body, held in her mouthparts, rather than leaving it attached to a web.
species.range_and_origin: A tropical species now found widely around the world, often in and around buildings. It is introduced and established in Florida.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A small brown spider about a quarter-inch long, with long slender legs and a conspicuously high, rounded front body section.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Brown to chestnut overall, with darker mottling on the rounded front of the body and patterned markings across the abdomen.

blocks.label: Eyes
blocks.text: Six small eyes are arranged in three pairs. This can help confirm a spitting spider in a close photograph, but the eyes are difficult to see without magnification.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Other spitting spiders can look very similar. The high rounded front of the body and six-eye arrangement help identify the family, but confirming Scytodes fusca may require a close photograph or specialist examination.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a small mottled-brown spider with long thin legs and an unusually high, rounded front body section. During the day it may rest on a wall, beneath an overhang or in another sheltered spot. The six eyes are useful only in a close photograph.

species.diet: Small insects and other spiders. The sticky attack allows a relatively slow-moving spider to immobilize prey before approaching closely.
species.behavior: It hunts on foot rather than building a prey-catching web. Most activity occurs at night; by day it often rests in a sheltered place. The spider approaches prey slowly rather than chasing it.
species.ecological_role: A predator of small insects and other spiders in sheltered habitats. It in turn can be eaten by larger spiders, lizards and other small predators.
species.habitat: Strongly associated with warm, sheltered, low-humidity spaces: the interiors and exterior walls of buildings, covered walkways, greenhouses, garden sheds, and similar structures. Outdoors it favors surfaces beneath overhangs, inside hollow trees, under loose bark, and among dense ground debris. It is a synanthropic species — one that thrives alongside human habitation — and is rarely found far from some form of cover.
species.where_to_look: Check sheltered surfaces such as the undersides of benches, covered structures, exterior walls, beneath overhangs and under loose bark. During the day the spider may remain motionless in a protected corner; it hunts after dark.
species.when_to_see: Most active at night. During the day it may be found resting in sheltered places. Florida's warm climate allows activity through much of the year, but Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local seasonal pattern.

size.length: About a quarter-inch long, not counting the legs.

danger.people: Not considered medically significant to people. This small spider is not aggressive and normally retreats or remains still when disturbed. Avoid handling it.
danger.pets: No known meaningful risk to pets.

interaction.guidance: Observe without touching or handling. A resting spider can be photographed where it is without disturbing its shelter.

invasive.notes: Introduced and established in Florida. It is not currently treated as a major invasive species or management concern.

conservation.status: Widespread globally and not known to be of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Established in Florida and potentially present year-round in sheltered habitat. Palma Sola records are too limited to estimate local frequency or seasonality.

quick_hits: Adult paper wasps drink nectar, but their larvae are fed animal prey. Workers hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects, chew them up and carry the food back to the nest.
Paper wasps scrape fibers from weathered wood and dead plant stems, chew them into pulp and use the material to build their nest.
Unlike a hornet or yellowjacket nest, a paper-wasp nest has no enclosing paper shell. The open cells remain visible, usually facing downward beneath a sheltered attachment point.
A female can begin a nest herself. After the first workers mature, they take over much of the foraging, nest building and defense.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, including Florida and the Gulf Coast.
more_information: The cells near the outer edge of a growing nest may be more rounded, while cells packed among neighbors become more nearly hexagonal.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A slender wasp about three-quarters of an inch long, with a narrow waist, long legs and long wings folded along the body at rest. The legs often trail below the body in flight.

blocks.label: Coloration
blocks.text: Southern Paper Wasps have extensive yellow markings along with darker reddish-brown or black areas. Color and pattern vary, and several other Florida paper wasps can look similar.

blocks.label: The nest
blocks.text: The nest is a single exposed comb of papery cells, usually hanging with the openings facing downward. There is no outer paper covering. Nests may be attached to vegetation or sheltered parts of structures.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Several paper-wasp species occur in Florida and can be difficult to separate without a close view. Red Paper Wasps are much more reddish overall. Yellowjackets are more compact, with shorter-looking legs and a heavier body. Honey bees are hairier and lack the extremely narrow wasp waist.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a slender wasp with long legs and a narrow waist. Paper wasps often trail their legs in flight. Their exposed, downward-facing paper comb is even easier to recognize, but do not approach a nest for a closer look.

species.diet: Adults feed mainly on nectar and other sugary liquids. Larvae are fed chewed caterpillars and other insects captured by the workers.
species.behavior: A female may begin a nest alone or with other females. Once workers emerge, they perform much of the foraging, nest building and defense while reproduction becomes concentrated in the dominant egg-laying female.
species.ecological_role: Paper wasps prey on caterpillars and other insects, including species that feed on garden plants. Adults also visit flowers for nectar and may carry pollen between blooms. The wasps themselves are eaten by birds, spiders and other predators.
species.habitat: Open and semi-open habitats with a mix of woody vegetation and sheltered structures nearby. In Florida that means forest edges, shrubby wetland margins, gardens, park borders, and any built structure offering a protected overhang for nesting. The species nests low in vegetation in natural settings — on Baccharis, yaupon holly (Ilex vomitoria), and blackberry stems have all been documented — and readily uses fence rails, eaves, and porch ceilings in human-modified landscapes.
species.where_to_look: Watch flowering plants for adults drinking nectar or searching foliage for caterpillars. Nests may be attached beneath sheltered overhangs or among woody vegetation. If you notice a nest, watch from a distance rather than moving closer.
species.when_to_see: Most easily seen during warm weather, when adults forage by day on flowers and vegetation. Nest activity changes through the year, and sheltered adults may survive periods when active colonies are less conspicuous.

size.length: About three-quarters of an inch long.

danger.people: Paper wasps can sting repeatedly when defending a nest. Stings are painful, and some people can have a severe allergic reaction. Give nests plenty of space and never touch, shake or spray one. A wasp feeding away from its nest is much less defensive, but it can still sting if handled or trapped against the skin.
danger.pets: Keep pets away from nests. Dogs or cats that investigate a colony can receive multiple stings, often around the face. Multiple stings or a sting inside the mouth warrants veterinary advice.

interaction.guidance: Watch foraging wasps without touching or swatting at them. Give any nest plenty of space and do not approach it for photographs or identification. Report nests in high-traffic areas to park staff rather than disturbing them.

conservation.status: Native and not considered a species of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Most visible during warm months when colonies are active and adults are foraging. Seasonal timing varies with climate and colony history.

blocks.text: A relatively large hoverfly, about half to three-quarters of an inch long.

blocks.text: Black and yellow, with a wasp-like banded abdomen and yellow markings on the dark thorax.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: As a true fly, it has one functional pair of wings rather than the two pairs found in wasps and bees.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look on flowers for a large black-and-yellow fly that resembles a wasp. Hovering in place, large fly-like eyes and a single functional pair of wings help reveal what it really is.

species.diet: Adults feed on nectar and pollen. Larvae feed in wet, decaying organic material.
species.behavior: Adults visit flowers for nectar and pollen and can hover almost motionless before shifting position. The larval stage develops in wet, decaying organic material, including water-filled cavities in trees.
species.ecological_role: Adults can carry pollen between flowers while feeding. Larvae consume organic material in wet tree cavities, while adults and larvae also become food for other animals.
species.habitat: Forest edges, open woodland, and areas with a mix of mature trees and flowering plants. Larvae specifically require trees with water-filled rot cavities, making older trees and standing dead wood important habitat components. Adults range more widely, visiting open sunny areas where flowers are available.
species.where_to_look: Check flowering plants in sunny openings and along woodland edges. Adults are usually encountered singly, either visiting flowers, hovering nearby or resting on sunlit foliage.
species.when_to_see: Look during warm weather when adults are active around flowers. Palma Sola has too few records to define a local seasonal pattern.

size.length: About half to three-quarters of an inch long.

danger.people: Harmless to people. This is a fly and has no stinger.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling. A feeding adult may return repeatedly to the same patch of flowers if left undisturbed.

invasive.notes: A native species across the eastern United States, including Florida. Not invasive.

Florida's Mabel Orchard Orbweaver was long treated as the same species as the Orchard Orbweaver farther north. Modern research separated the two, so older references may call Florida spiders Leucauge venusta.

species.range_and_origin: Native to Florida and the American tropics, ranging through the Caribbean and Central and South America.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A small, slender spider with a long abdomen and thin legs. Females are about a quarter-inch long; males are smaller.

blocks.label: Top of the abdomen
blocks.text: The top of the elongated abdomen is silvery-white with darker longitudinal markings.

blocks.label: Underside
blocks.text: The underside has silvery, greenish and yellow markings with orange-red near the rear. That red-orange can cause momentary confusion with a black widow, but the body shape and the web are very different.

blocks.label: Legs and body
blocks.text: The long slender legs are greenish with darker joints. The front part of the body is pale greenish to yellow-brown.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: The closely related Leucauge argyra also occurs in Florida and can look very similar. Orange-red abdominal markings help distinguish Mabel Orchard Orbweaver, but close photographs may be needed for a confident identification.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a small silver-bodied spider beneath a tilted orb web stretched between low branches and stems. The abdomen is elongated, the legs are slender and greenish, and orange-red markings occur underneath. The web is often built fairly low in shrubby vegetation.

species.diet: Small flying insects caught in the web, including gnats, mosquitoes and flies.
species.behavior: The female waits beneath the center of her web and detects trapped prey through vibrations in the silk, then moves to the struggling insect, bites it and wraps it in silk. Males wander in search of females rather than maintaining prey-catching webs.
species.ecological_role: Mabel Orchard Orbweavers catch small flying insects and are themselves prey for birds, lizards and predatory or parasitic insects.
species.habitat: Shrubby meadows, woodland edges, orchards, and gardens with moderate moisture and dappled light — anywhere low, branchy vegetation provides anchoring points for a tilted orb web at roughly knee-to-waist height. Also common in wooded suburban settings, along hedgerows, and beneath overhanging eaves. One of the most abundant spiders in Florida citrus groves.
species.where_to_look: Look among low, branchy vegetation along garden edges, shrubby paths and lightly wooded areas. The tilted orb web is often built from knee to waist height and becomes easiest to see when sunlight or dew catches the silk.
species.when_to_see: Look during warm, humid weather when webs are conspicuous among low vegetation. The species is common in Florida, but there are not enough Palma Sola observations to define a local seasonal peak.

size.length: Females about a quarter-inch long; males smaller.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to people. The spider uses venom to subdue small prey but is not considered medically significant and normally retreats when disturbed.
danger.pets: No known meaningful risk to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch without touching the spider or web. If disturbed, the spider may drop on a silk line and hide below. An accidentally damaged web can be repaired or rebuilt.

conservation.status: Common in Florida and not considered a species of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Common in Florida during warm weather. Local seasonal timing at Palma Sola is not yet well established.

species.teaser: The orange-red marking on its underside sometimes causes confusion with a black widow, but this small spider has a completely different body shape and web.

how_it_lives.text: The female waits beneath the center of her web and detects trapped prey through vibrations in the silk. She moves to the struggling insect, bites it and wraps it in silk.
The web catches small flying insects such as gnats, mosquitoes and flies.
Males wander in search of females rather than maintaining prey-catching webs. A male approaching a female may signal through vibrations in her silk.

how_to_know_it.label: Size and shape
how_to_know_it.text: A small, slender spider with a long abdomen and thin legs. Females are about a quarter-inch long; males are smaller.

how_to_know_it.label: Top of the abdomen
how_to_know_it.text: The top of the elongated abdomen is silvery-white with darker longitudinal markings.

how_to_know_it.label: Underside
how_to_know_it.text: The underside has silvery, greenish and yellow markings with orange-red near the rear. That red-orange can cause momentary confusion with a black widow, but the body shape and the web are very different.

how_to_know_it.label: Legs and body
how_to_know_it.text: The long slender legs are greenish with darker joints. The front part of the body is pale greenish to yellow-brown.

how_to_know_it.label: Similar species
how_to_know_it.text: The closely related Leucauge argyra also occurs in Florida and can look very similar. Orange-red abdominal markings help distinguish Mabel Orchard Orbweaver, but close photographs may be needed for a confident identification.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Females about a quarter-inch long; males smaller.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a small silver-bodied spider beneath a tilted orb web stretched between low branches and stems. The abdomen is elongated, the legs are slender and greenish, and orange-red markings occur underneath. The web is often built fairly low in shrubby vegetation.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look among low, branchy vegetation along garden edges, shrubby paths and lightly wooded areas. The tilted orb web is often built from knee to waist height and becomes easiest to see when sunlight or dew catches the silk.
Look during warm, humid weather when webs are conspicuous among low vegetation. The species is common in Florida, but there are not enough Palma Sola observations to define a local seasonal peak.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: Common in Florida during warm weather. Local seasonal timing at Palma Sola is not yet well established.

what_it_does_here.text: Shrubs and low tree branches provide the framework for the web. The spider stretches its supporting threads between stems and leaves, so dense, branchy vegetation creates many possible web sites. Orchard orbweavers are especially common in moist gardens, woodland edges and Florida citrus groves.

at_a_glance.text: Its orb web is usually tilted close to horizontal rather than standing vertically. The spider hangs beneath the center with its belly facing upward.
When disturbed, the spider may drop from its web on a silk safety line and hide in the vegetation or leaf litter below.

Florida's Mabel Orchard Orbweaver was long treated as the same species as the Orchard Orbweaver farther north. Modern research separated the two, so older references may call Florida spiders Leucauge venusta.
A spider does not need to see an insect hit its web. Vibrations traveling through the silk tell it where struggling prey has landed.

quick_hits: A Bobolink may travel about 12,500 miles in a year, migrating between northern North America and southern South America. Over a long life, its migration can add up to several trips around the circumference of the Earth.

Breeding males are black below with a pale back, white shoulders and a buff-colored nape. Before fall migration they molt into streaky brown plumage much like the female, so the Bobolinks passing through Florida in late summer look completely different from spring males.

Florida lies on a major Bobolink migration route. Many birds traveling between eastern North America and South America pass through Florida and the West Indies rather than following the mainland through Mexico and Central America.
Bobolinks replace all of their feathers twice each year. One complete molt follows the breeding season, and another occurs on the South American wintering grounds before they head north again.
species.range_and_origin: Bobolinks breed in grasslands across southern Canada and the northern United States and spend the northern winter in southern South America, especially Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina. Their annual migration links grasslands separated by thousands of miles.
more_information: The scientific name oryzivorus means roughly 'rice eater.' Migrating Bobolinks once descended on southern rice fields in such numbers that they became known as Ricebirds and were treated as agricultural pests.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: Larger than most sparrows but smaller than a Red-winged Blackbird, with a compact body, short pointed bill and fairly short tail.

blocks.label: Breeding male
blocks.text: In spring, the male is mostly black below with a pale back, white shoulders and a buff-colored patch on the back of the head. The unusual dark-below, pale-above pattern makes breeding males easy to recognize.

blocks.label: Female and nonbreeding male
blocks.text: Buffy brown with dark streaks on the back and sides, a dark line through the eye and a pale stripe along the crown. The nape is relatively plain and the bill is pale pinkish.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Migrating Bobolinks often travel in loose flocks. Listen for the short metallic pink call, which may reveal birds overhead before you see them.

identification.what_to_look_for: In spring, look for males that are black below with a pale back and buff nape. Fall birds are streaky brown and much easier to overlook. Migrating flocks often give a short metallic pink call, so listening can be as useful as looking.

species.diet: Their diet changes with the season. During breeding they eat mostly insects and feed insects to their young. During migration and winter they rely much more heavily on seeds and grain.
species.behavior: Outside the breeding season, Bobolinks often travel in flocks. They migrate largely at night and stop in fields and marshy grasslands during the day to feed and rest.
species.sounds: Migrating Bobolinks often give a short metallic call usually written as pink or bink. A flock may be heard overhead before it is seen. On the breeding grounds, males sing a much longer bubbling, tumbling flight song.
species.ecological_role: During the breeding season Bobolinks consume large numbers of insects, while migrants and wintering birds feed heavily on grass and crop seeds. They are also prey for hawks and other predators during their long migrations.
species.habitat: On their breeding grounds, Bobolinks require tall, dense grasslands with mixed herbaceous cover — damp meadows, native prairies, and hayfields with few woody plants. During migration through Florida, habitat requirements are looser: flocks stop in open fields, wet meadows, flooded agricultural land, marsh edges, and overgrown grassy areas. They tend to favor interior grassland patches over narrow strips and avoid areas with dense shrub or tree cover.
species.where_to_look: Look in open grassy areas, wet meadows and weedy edges rather than wooded parts of the park. Migrating flocks often feed low among grasses and seed heads and can disappear into the vegetation until they fly. Listen for the metallic pink call from birds overhead or moving between feeding areas.
species.when_to_see: Bobolinks pass through Florida during spring and fall migration rather than living here year-round. Look mainly from late April into May and again from August into October. Because many migrate at night, birds may stop to feed in open grassy areas during the day.

size.length: About six to seven inches long, with a wingspan close to a foot.

interaction.guidance: Watch from paths and avoid walking into grassy areas where migrants may be feeding or resting. Long-distance migrants depend on stopover habitat to rebuild energy during their journey.

invasive.notes: Native to North America and a natural migrant through Florida.

conservation.status: Bobolinks remain widespread, but their population has declined substantially. The 2025 State of the Birds report places the species in its Orange-Alert Tipping Point category, reflecting long-term losses and more recent decline. Loss and alteration of grassland habitat are major concerns.

seasonality.note: A passage migrant in Florida, mainly in spring and fall. Spring birds may include males in breeding plumage; fall birds are usually streaky brown.

species.teaser: Florida is not a destination for most Bobolinks. It is a crossing point on their migration between northern grasslands and southern South America.

how_it_lives.text: Outside the breeding season, Bobolinks often travel in flocks. They migrate largely at night and stop in fields and marshy grasslands during the day to feed and rest.
Their diet changes with the season. During breeding they eat mostly insects and feed insects to their young. During migration and winter they rely much more heavily on seeds and grain.

how_to_know_it.label: Size and shape
how_to_know_it.text: Bigger than a sparrow, smaller than a Red-winged Blackbird. Compact, fairly short-tailed, with a stubby pointed bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Spring male
how_to_know_it.text: Black below with a pale back, white shoulders and a buff patch on the back of the head. Dark underneath and pale on top is an unusual combination, and it makes spring males unmistakable.

how_to_know_it.label: Female and fall male
how_to_know_it.text: Buffy brown with dark streaking, a dark line through the eye and a pale stripe along the crown. The bill is pale pink.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A short metallic pink, often from birds passing overhead.
In fall the streaky brown birds are easy to walk straight past. Listening does more than looking.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Open grassy areas, wet meadows and weedy edges — not the wooded parts of the park. Feeding flocks drop low among grasses and seed heads and can disappear into the vegetation until something puts them up.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: A passage migrant only. Look from late April into May, and again from August into October. Many travel at night and come down to feed during the day.

what_it_does_here.text: Bobolinks are not here to stay. Florida is a crossing point on a route between northern grasslands and southern South America, and a bird in the park is refuelling between legs of that trip.

Grass carries them at every stage — insects while they are breeding, then the seeds of grasses and sedges through migration and winter. On the northern breeding grounds the female hides her nest on the ground beneath dense cover.
The scientific name oryzivorus means roughly rice eater. Migrating flocks once came down on southern rice fields in such numbers that the birds were known as Ricebirds and treated as pests.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Bobolinks are still widespread, but the population has fallen substantially and the 2025 State of the Birds report places them in its Orange-Alert Tipping Point category. Loss of grassland is the main concern. Stopover habitat matters for a bird making a trip this long, so keeping to the paths and out of grass where migrants may be feeding is worth doing.

at_a_glance.text: A Bobolink may fly about 12,500 miles in a year, between grasslands in northern North America and southern South America.
Spring males are black below with a pale back and a buff nape. By fall they have molted into streaky brown and look much like the females.
Florida sits on a major Bobolink route — birds cross here rather than following the mainland down through Mexico.
They replace every feather twice a year: once after breeding, and again in South America before heading north.

species.plant_connections: Bobolinks depend on open, grassy vegetation throughout their lives. During migration they feed among grasses, sedges and other seed-producing plants in fields and wet meadows. On their northern breeding grounds, females hide their nests on the ground beneath dense grasses.

quick_hits: On hot days, a perched Scarlet Skimmer may point its abdomen almost straight at the sun. Aiming the tip skyward reduces the amount of its body exposed to direct sunlight.
Mature males become vivid red, while females and young males are yellowish to olive-brown. A young male can therefore look more like a female than like the red adult he will become.
Scarlet Skimmers are native to Asia, not Florida. They were first recorded in the Miami area in the 1970s and are now established across much of the Florida peninsula.
Both sexes have amber-orange coloring at the bases of the wings. It is especially useful when identifying the yellow-brown females and immature males.
Before becoming an aerial hunter, a dragonfly lives underwater as a nymph. Scarlet Skimmer nymphs prey on small aquatic animals before climbing out of the water for their final molt.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Asia and introduced to Florida, where it was first recorded in the Miami area in the 1970s. It is now established through much of the Florida peninsula and readily uses ponds, canals and other human-made waters.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A medium-sized dragonfly about an inch and a half long, with a sturdy body and broad, clear wings.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Mature males are bright red across most of the body, with reddish eyes and a thin dark line along the top of the abdomen. The wing bases are washed with amber-orange.

blocks.label: Female and immature male
blocks.text: Females and immature males are yellowish to olive-brown rather than red. Look for the dark line along the abdomen and amber-orange coloring near the wing bases.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Roseate Skimmer males are pink-purple rather than scarlet red. Needham's Skimmers are generally more orange. Females and immature Scarlet Skimmers are harder to identify than mature males, so the wing-base color and abdominal markings are useful.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look around sunny pond edges for a medium-sized dragonfly repeatedly returning to a low perch. Mature males are bright red; females and young males are yellow-brown. Amber-orange coloring at the wing bases is useful in both sexes.

species.diet: Adults catch small flying insects in the air. The aquatic nymphs prey on insect larvae and other small animals in the water.
species.behavior: Males defend stretches of shoreline from low perches, making short patrol flights and often returning to the same stem. Females come to the water to lay, touching the tip of the abdomen to the surface as they fly.
species.ecological_role: Scarlet Skimmers are predators at both stages of life. Adults catch flying insects; aquatic nymphs eat small animals underwater. In turn, dragonflies and their nymphs are eaten by fish, birds and other predators.
species.habitat: Open freshwater wetlands — ponds, marshes, slow streams, drainage ditches, and canals — with emergent or shoreline vegetation for perching. The species tolerates disturbed and human-modified water bodies readily, which accounts for much of its success as an introduced species in Florida. Manatee County's mix of retention ponds, canal-side vegetation, and park wetlands suits it well.
species.where_to_look: Look around sunny ponds, drainage areas and other still or slow-moving freshwater. Males often choose a low stem near the shoreline, make short flights over the water and return to the same perch.
species.when_to_see: Most active on warm, sunny days. Florida's long warm season allows adults to be seen through much of the year, but local seasonal timing at Palma Sola is not yet well established.

size.length: About an inch and a half long.

danger.people: Harmless to people. Dragonflies do not sting and do not seek out people to bite.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the shoreline or path. A male often returns to the same perch after a short flight, making it possible to observe without following or handling it.

invasive.notes: Introduced and established in Florida. It is not currently a major management target or listed among Florida's principal invasive species.

conservation.status: Globally widespread and not considered threatened.

seasonality.note: Most likely on warm, sunny days. There are not yet enough local observations to define a reliable seasonal peak at Palma Sola.

species.teaser: On hot days, a perched Scarlet Skimmer may point its abdomen almost straight at the sun, reducing the amount of its body exposed to direct sunlight.

how_it_lives.text: Males defend stretches of shoreline from low perches, making short patrol flights and often returning to the same stem.
Adults catch small flying insects in the air, using their spiny legs to help trap prey. The aquatic nymphs hunt small animals among submerged vegetation.
Females lay eggs at the water, touching the tip of the abdomen to the surface as they fly.

quick_hits: S-banded Tiger Beetles have turned up on offshore platforms far out in the Gulf of Mexico, evidence that these small beetles can be carried remarkable distances over open water.
A pale, winding band across each wing cover forms the S-shaped marking that gives this species its name.
Adults hunt on foot, sprinting across open ground after ants, flies and other small invertebrates and seizing them with large curved jaws.
This is a beetle of open ground, not dense vegetation. It uses bare or sparsely vegetated mud and soil along coastal and brackish wetland edges.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Florida and other coastal areas around the Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic coast, Caribbean and parts of the American tropics. In Florida it is associated especially with open, moist ground near saline and brackish wetlands.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A small, long-legged beetle about half an inch long, with large eyes and prominent curved jaws.

blocks.label: Wing covers
blocks.text: The dark brown to reddish-brown wing covers have pale markings, including a winding band across the middle that forms the S-shape behind the common name.

blocks.label: Head and legs
blocks.text: The head is large, with prominent eyes and curved jaws. Long legs hold the body above the ground and are built for rapid running.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Several tiger beetles occur in Florida's coastal wetlands. The Saltmarsh Tiger Beetle and Margined Tiger Beetle can occur in similar habitat, but their pale wing-cover markings differ. A clear photograph of the back is useful for confirming the species.

identification.what_to_look_for: Watch open, damp ground for a small beetle running in quick bursts. When it stops, look for the pale S-shaped marking across the dark wing covers. Large eyes, long legs and prominent jaws give it the characteristic tiger-beetle build.

species.diet: Adults hunt ants, flies, small beetles and other small invertebrates on open ground. Larvae capture small animals that pass their burrow entrances.
species.behavior: Adults hunt across open ground in short, rapid runs. When approached they may run or fly a short distance and land again. Females place eggs in suitable soil, and each larva then builds its own burrow and remains there while it grows.
species.ecological_role: Both adults and larvae are predators of small invertebrates. Tiger beetles in turn are eaten by larger insects, birds and other predators, linking the small animals of bare wetland surfaces to the larger food web.
species.habitat: Moist, open, sparsely vegetated substrates in coastal and near-coastal settings — principally mudflats, tidal margins, brackish and saltmarsh edges, and the exposed banks of tidal creeks. The species requires bare or nearly bare ground for running and for larval burrow construction; dense vegetation excludes it. It tolerates saline and brackish soils that most insects avoid.
species.where_to_look: Look for patches of open, damp ground near wetland edges. Tiger beetles need bare or sparsely vegetated surfaces where they can run after prey, so they are less likely in dense groundcover.
species.when_to_see: Look during warm daylight hours, when adults hunt on exposed ground. Species-specific seasonal timing at Palma Sola is not yet well established.

size.length: About half an inch long.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to people. Tiger beetles have strong jaws for catching small prey but should simply be observed rather than handled.

interaction.guidance: Watch without chasing or handling. Repeated approaches may cause the beetle to run or fly away. Avoid trampling bare wetland-edge soil, where larvae may live in burrows.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and the broader Gulf and Atlantic coastal zone. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Native and not currently considered a species of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Recorded at Palma Sola, but there are not enough local observations to define a reliable seasonal peak.

species.teaser: The larva spends most of its life inside a vertical burrow, waiting at the entrance to grab insects that pass within reach.

how_it_lives.text: Adults hunt across open ground in short, rapid runs. When approached they may run or fly a short distance and land again.
Adults chase ants, flies, small beetles and other invertebrates across open ground, catching them with large curved jaws.

how_it_lives.label: The larva's burrow
how_it_lives.text: Females place eggs in suitable soil. After hatching, each larva constructs its own burrow and remains there while it grows.

species.behavior: Adults perch on vegetation between flights and visit flowers for nectar. Males may use lookout perches and fly out rapidly toward other insects entering their area.

conservation.status: Widespread and established in Florida and the Caribbean; not known to be of conservation concern.

danger.people: Harmless to people. It does not sting or bite.

species.diet: Caterpillars feed on palm leaves. Adults drink flower nectar.
species.ecological_role: Caterpillars consume palm foliage and are prey for predators and parasitoids. Adults feed at flowers and may carry pollen between blooms.
species.habitat: Subtropical woodland edges, hammocks, coastal scrub, pinelands, salt marsh edges, and suburban gardens and parks — essentially any landscape that supports palms, native or ornamental. The species has adapted readily to human-modified environments wherever palms are planted.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: A large skipper with a wingspan around two inches.

blocks.label: Upperside
blocks.text: Dark brown to nearly black above, with females generally somewhat paler.

blocks.label: Underside
blocks.text: The underside is rich chestnut brown, while bluish-gray hairs can show on the head and body.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large, dark skipper around palms and flowering garden plants. When perched, the rich chestnut underside and bluish-gray scaling on the body help separate it from smaller brown skippers.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling. If one is resting on a palm or flower, leave it in place and observe from the path.

invasive.notes: Introduced and established in Florida. It is not currently treated as a major invasive species or management concern.

species.plant_connections: Palms are the center of the Monk Skipper's life cycle. Females lay eggs on palm foliage, and the caterpillars both eat the leaves and use them to build silk-bound shelters. Native saw palmetto and cabbage palm are hosts, along with several ornamental palms. Adults leave the palms to feed at flowers nearby.
quick_hits: This is a large, dark skipper with rich chestnut coloring underneath the wings and bluish-gray scaling on the body.
A caterpillar folds or binds part of a palm frond into a shelter, resting inside and feeding on the surrounding leaf.
Its caterpillars feed on palms, including native saw palmetto and cabbage palm as well as several ornamental palms.
Native to Cuba and nearby Caribbean islands, the Monk Skipper became established in Florida by the late 1940s and is now widespread through the peninsula.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Cuba, the Bahamas and neighboring Caribbean areas. The Monk Skipper became established in Florida in the mid-twentieth century and now occurs through much of peninsular Florida.

seasonality.presence: much of the year in central Florida
seasonality.note: Recorded from March through December in central Florida. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a local pattern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Several skippers in Florida are brown and easily confused. The Monk Skipper is notably large, with a mostly dark upperside and a rich chestnut underside; most look-alikes are smaller and differently marked below.

size.length: Wingspan about two inches.

species.when_to_see: In central Florida, adults are recorded through much of the year, especially from spring through late fall. Palma Sola currently has too few records to say how regularly the species occurs here.
species.where_to_look: Look around palm plantings and nearby flowering beds. Adults visit flowers, while eggs and caterpillars occur on palm fronds. Saw palmetto and cabbage palm are among the documented host plants.
species.teaser: Monk Skipper caterpillars feed on palms and build shelters from the fronds, so landscapes rich in palms provide both food and shelter for the young.

how_it_lives.text: Adults perch on vegetation between flights and visit flowers for nectar. Males may use lookout perches and fly out rapidly toward other insects entering their area.

how_it_lives.label: A shelter made of palm
how_it_lives.text: A caterpillar folds and binds palm leaf tissue with silk to make a shelter, then feeds on the surrounding frond.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: A large skipper with a wingspan around two inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Upperside
how_to_know_it.text: Dark brown to nearly black above, with females generally somewhat paler.

how_to_know_it.label: Underside
how_to_know_it.text: The underside is rich chestnut brown, while bluish-gray hairs can show on the head and body.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a large, dark skipper around palms and flowering garden plants. When perched, the rich chestnut underside and bluish-gray scaling on the body help separate it from smaller brown skippers.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look around palm plantings and nearby flowering beds. Adults visit flowers, while eggs and caterpillars occur on palm fronds. Saw palmetto and cabbage palm are among the documented host plants.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: Recorded from March through December in central Florida. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a local pattern.

what_it_does_here.text: The Monk Skipper is a Caribbean butterfly, native to Cuba, the Bahamas and neighbouring islands, that became established in Florida during the mid-twentieth century.

Palms are the center of the Monk Skipper's life cycle. Females lay eggs on palm foliage, and the caterpillars both eat the leaves and use them to build silk-bound shelters. Native saw palmetto and cabbage palm are hosts, along with several ornamental palms. Adults leave the palms to feed at flowers nearby.

at_a_glance.text: This is a large, dark skipper with rich chestnut coloring underneath the wings and bluish-gray scaling on the body.
A caterpillar folds or binds part of a palm frond into a shelter, resting inside and feeding on the surrounding leaf.
Its caterpillars feed on palms, including native saw palmetto and cabbage palm as well as several ornamental palms.
Native to Cuba and nearby Caribbean islands, the Monk Skipper became established in Florida by the late 1940s and is now widespread through the peninsula.

quick_hits: It drills orderly rows of sapwells and returns to keep them open, drinking the sap and eating insects attracted to it.
Sapsucker wells also feed other wildlife. Hummingbirds and other birds, insects and sometimes mammals drink sap from holes they could not open themselves.
Yellow-bellied Sapsuckers breed far to the north and spend the winter in Florida, making them a seasonal woodpecker here rather than a year-round resident.
The yellow belly can be surprisingly faint. A bold white stripe along the folded wing is often a more reliable field mark.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Yellow-bellied Sapsuckers breed mainly in northern forests and migrate south for winter, when they occur throughout Florida and farther into the Caribbean, Mexico and Central America.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A medium-sized black-and-white woodpecker with a red forehead and a bold white stripe along the folded wing. Males have a red throat; females have a white throat. The pale belly may show only a faint yellow wash.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: The white wing stripe flashes prominently in flight. Like other woodpeckers, it flies in an undulating series of flaps and glides.

blocks.label: Look for the holes
blocks.text: Even without the bird, neat horizontal rows of small holes in bark can reveal a sapsucker's presence.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look first for the bold white stripe along the folded wing and red on the forehead. Males also have a red throat. On trees, watch for orderly rows of small sapwells.

species.diet: Tree sap is an important food, along with insects, spiders, fruit and berries. Insects caught around sticky sapwells may also be eaten.
species.behavior: It drills rows of small holes through bark and returns repeatedly to keep them open. Sap collects at the wells, providing food for the bird and attracting insects.
species.sounds: Calls include a nasal, catlike mew. Drumming is irregular and stuttering rather than an even roll, and birds sometimes drum on resonant metal surfaces.
species.ecological_role: Sapsucker wells create a food source used by many other animals, including hummingbirds and insects. The bird also excavates nesting cavities on its breeding grounds that can later be used by other cavity-nesting animals.
species.plant_connections: Few birds alter living plants as visibly as a sapsucker. It drills and maintains sapwells in the bark of many kinds of trees, returning repeatedly to drink the flowing sap. Trees differ in how readily their sap flows, and individual birds may favor particular trees. The rows of old and active wells can remain visible long after the bird has moved on.

size.length: About eight inches long, with a wingspan around fifteen inches.

species.habitat: In winter, uses a broad range of wooded habitats — deciduous forests, mixed woodlands, parks, suburban trees, orchards, and even palm groves. Less selective than on its boreal breeding grounds; found in any setting with mature trees large enough to support sapwells.
species.where_to_look: Scan trunks of mature trees for neat horizontal rows of small holes. Once you find active sapwells, watch quietly from a distance; a sapsucker may return to feed or maintain them.
species.when_to_see: A winter visitor to Florida, generally present from fall into spring. Palma Sola currently has only one documented observation, so local peak timing and regularity are not yet known.

seasonality.note: Winter visitor to Florida. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a local peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch without approaching closely or touching active sapwells. If you find a tree with fresh wells, leave the bark undisturbed so the bird can continue using them.

invasive.notes: A native North American species and a natural winter visitor to Florida. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened. Like other native migratory birds, it is protected under federal law.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Red-bellied Woodpeckers are year-round Florida residents and are larger, with barred black-and-white backs and no long white stripe along the folded wing.
Downy Woodpeckers are smaller and lack the sapsucker's bold wing stripe and its rows of sapwells.

Hummingbirds, insects and other animals drink at sapwells the sapsucker drills and keeps open, so one bird's feeding habit quietly supplies several others. The nest cavities it cuts on the northern breeding grounds get the same second life, taken over by animals that cannot excavate their own.

quick_hits: A large flycatcher with an olive back, lemon-yellow belly and rusty tail, usually high in the canopy.
Listen before you look. A sharp rising WHEEP carrying through the treetops is usually this bird.
It nests in tree cavities and often works shed snakeskin into the lining — or plastic and cellophane where snakeskin is not available.
It is a summer bird here, present spring through late summer and gone by autumn.
species.range_and_origin: Breeds across the eastern United States and southern Canada and winters in the Caribbean, Mexico, and South America. In our area it is a summer breeding resident - present spring through late summer and gone by fall.
more_information: The Great Crested Flycatcher is a cavity nester, raising its young inside holes in trees (and readily using nest boxes). It is famous for lining the nest with a shed snakeskin - and scientists think this is deliberate intimidation: the snakeskin may help scare off mice, squirrels, and other small raiders eyeing the eggs. When no snakeskin is available, these birds improvise with crinkly substitutes that mimic it: plastic wrappers, onion skins, and cellophane have all turned up in their nests.

It is a true flycatcher, hunting on the wing. From a still perch it watches for flying insects, then launches into a quick aerial chase, snapping the prey out of the air with an audible clack of the bill before looping back - pure canopy acrobatics.

blocks.label: Plumage
blocks.text: Olive-brown above with a gray throat and breast and a bright lemon-yellow belly. The tail and wings flash rufous (rusty) - a good field mark.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: A large, big-headed flycatcher with a slight bushy crest and an upright posture when perched.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look up. This is a canopy and mid-story bird that rarely comes to the ground - scan the treetops for a flash of yellow belly and a rusty tail, and let the loud rising "WHEEP!" lead your eyes to it.

species.diet: A true flycatcher with a varied appetite. It hunts beetles, crickets, caterpillars, moths, and bees, and readily supplements its diet with wild fruit such as elderberries and blackberries. It feeds mostly by hawking - perching still, spotting a flying insect, then launching out to snap it from the air with an audible clack of the bill before looping back to its perch.
species.behavior: An active canopy hunter that catches insects in flight (hawking) and gleans them from foliage. Vocal and conspicuous by sound, though often hidden in the leaves. A cavity nester that defends its nest hole vigorously.
species.sounds: Loud and vocal. The signature call is a sharp, rising "WHEEP!" that carries through the treetops, along with a rolling "prrrreet." If you hear a bossy, far-carrying shout from high in the canopy, this is often the bird making it.
species.ecological_role: A canopy insect predator that helps keep beetle, moth, and other insect populations in check, and a seed disperser for the fruiting plants it feeds on. As a cavity nester it depends on older trees and dead snags with suitable holes.

size.length: about 7 to 8 inches (a large flycatcher)
size.lifespan: commonly several years; can exceed 10 years in the wild.

species.habitat: Woodlands, parks, and gardens during migration and winter.
species.where_to_look: High in the canopy and mid-story of woodland edges, hammocks, and shaded park trees - rarely on or near the ground.
species.when_to_see: Spring through late summer, when breeding birds are most vocal and active (roughly March to September). They leave by early fall and are absent in winter, so don't look for them on a January walk. Listen for the loud "WHEEP!" to locate one.

seasonality.note: A summer resident in our area - arrives around March or April to breed and departs by early fall for the Caribbean and South America. Absent in winter.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Eastern Phoebes are smaller and plain gray-brown, wag their tails constantly and hunt from low perches. Great Crested Flycatchers are larger, yellow-bellied, rusty-tailed and stay high in the canopy.

species.teaser: It weaves shed snakeskin into the lining of its nest — and where snakeskin is scarce, will use cellophane or plastic instead.

how_it_lives.text: Hunts from a perch in the canopy, darting out to take insects in flight and gleaning others from foliage. Beetles, crickets, caterpillars, moths and bees are all taken, along with wild fruit.

how_it_lives.label: Snakeskin in the nest
how_it_lives.text: It nests in tree cavities and often includes shed snakeskin in the lining. Birds have also been recorded using cellophane, plastic and other similar materials. Why Great Crested Flycatchers choose them is not settled.

how_to_know_it.label: Plumage
how_to_know_it.text: Olive-brown above with a gray throat and breast and a bright lemon-yellow belly. The tail and wings flash rusty.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: A large, big-headed flycatcher with a slight crest, about seven or eight inches long.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A loud rising WHEEP that carries through the treetops, plus a rolling prrrreet.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Scan the canopy and mid-story of shaded trees and woodland edges. This bird is rarely near the ground, and is usually heard before it is seen.

where_to_find_it_here.text: High in the canopy and mid-story of woodland edges, hammocks and shaded park trees — rarely on or near the ground.
A summer breeding resident, present roughly spring through late summer. Do not look for one on a January walk.

what_it_does_here.label: It cannot dig its own hole
what_it_does_here.text: This flycatcher nests in cavities but cannot excavate one. It depends on holes made by woodpeckers or opened by decay, so mature trees and standing dead wood are what allow it to breed here at all.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Leave dead limbs and cavity trees standing wherever it is safe to keep them. This bird nests in tree holes it cannot excavate itself, so standing dead wood is its housing supply.

at_a_glance.text: It nests in tree cavities and often works shed snakeskin into the lining — or plastic and cellophane where snakeskin is not available.
A large flycatcher with an olive back, lemon-yellow belly and rusty tail, usually high in the canopy.
Listen before you look. A sharp rising WHEEP carrying through the treetops is usually this bird.
It is a summer bird here, present spring through late summer and gone by autumn.

quick_hits: Adults have bold black-and-white crown stripes, a plain gray breast and a pinkish or yellowish bill.
White-crowned Sparrows breed far to the north and west and occur in Florida only during the nonbreeding season.
On the ground, they often use a two-footed backward hop to kick aside leaves and expose seeds and other food.
Their songs are learned rather than entirely innate. Regional populations develop recognizable song dialects, and birds living where two dialects meet may learn both.
species.range_and_origin: Breeds across the far north - Alaska, northern Canada, and high western mountains - and winters across much of the United States and Mexico. In Southwest Florida it's an uncommon winter visitor; you usually have to look for it, here from roughly October to April before it heads back north.
more_information: While many sparrows look like little brown streaks of camouflage, the adult White-crowned Sparrow stands out like it's wearing a tiny cycling helmet. It brings a bit of northern flair down to Florida for the colder months and makes itself right at home in our thickets and brushy edges.

It's a ground forager with a signature move: the "double-scratch," a quick two-footed hop backward that kicks leaf litter aside to uncover seeds. Even in winter, when it isn't nesting, you'll hear it practicing its song or trading sharp chink call notes with others from deep in the bushes.

And consider the trip it made to get here: some White-crowned Sparrows fly more than 2,500 miles from the Alaskan tundra to their wintering grounds - an astonishing haul for a bird that weighs about as much as a few quarters.

blocks.label: The crown
blocks.text: Adults wear unmistakable high-contrast black-and-white head stripes. A bird with brown-and-tan stripes instead isn't a different species - it's a youngster on its first trip south.

blocks.label: Posture
blocks.text: Sits noticeably upright when alert, showing off a sleek, pearly-grey breast.

blocks.label: The double-scratch
blocks.text: On the ground it feeds with the "double-scratch" - a quick two-footed backward hop that kicks leaves away to reveal hidden seeds. It's an inherited, instinctive move: even birds raised without leaf litter do it automatically.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look low, not high. Scan brushy borders, overgrown fence lines, and low shrubbery near open grassy areas for an upright, boldly striped sparrow scratching in the leaf litter.

species.diet: Mainly a seed-eater, especially here in winter: weed seeds, grass seeds, berries, and the odd bit of spilled birdseed. It does take insects too, mostly up north in the breeding season.
species.behavior: A ground-foraging edge bird that scratches through leaf litter with a two-footed backward hop. Spends most of its time low in brush and along weedy borders, rarely up in the canopy.
species.sounds: A sweet, clear whistled song that opens with one or two long notes and ends in a buzzy trill. Even in winter you'll hear it practicing, along with a sharp chink call note from the bushes as birds keep track of one another.
species.ecological_role: A winter seed-eater that helps disperse the seeds of weeds and grasses, and part of the seasonal influx of northern songbirds that pass the colder months in Florida.
species.plant_connections: Forages along brushy edges and weedy ground, feeding on the seeds of grasses, weeds, and low shrubs.

size.length: about 6.5 to 7 inches (a fairly large, long-tailed sparrow)
size.lifespan: commonly several years; banded birds have exceeded 13 years.

species.habitat: Brushy edges, thickets, weedy fields, and shrubby borders near open ground - anywhere with low cover to dive into and open soil to scratch for seeds.
species.where_to_look: Look low, not high. Brushy borders, overgrown fence lines, and the low shrubbery near open grassy areas - classic edge habitat, not the canopy.
species.when_to_see: An uncommon winter visitor, generally here from about October to April. Early morning is best, scanning the brushy edges. Don't expect a guaranteed sighting - finding one is a small birding win. Gone by late spring.

seasonality.note: A nonbreeding visitor to Florida. Palma Sola records are too limited to define a local peak or exact arrival and departure dates.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Because they spend so much time on the ground, give them a little room so they don't feel cornered against a bush. Stay still and they'll usually carry on foraging while you watch.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Also has bold head stripes, but shows a bright white throat patch and yellow between the eye and bill. White-crowned Sparrows have a plain gray throat and no yellow facial spot.

species.teaser: Adult White-crowned Sparrows have bold black-and-white crown stripes. Young birds make their first southward migration wearing the same pattern in brown and tan.

how_it_lives.text: In winter, White-crowned Sparrows spend much of the day on or near the ground, moving between open feeding patches and nearby shrubs where they can quickly take cover. Outside the breeding season they often occur in loose flocks.
Seeds make up much of the winter diet, including seeds of grasses and other low plants. Insects become more important during the breeding season.
It forages on the ground with one signature move — the double-scratch, a quick two-footed hop backward that kicks the leaf litter aside and uncovers seeds.

how_to_know_it.label: The crown
how_to_know_it.text: Adults have bold black-and-white crown stripes. Immature birds have the same striped pattern in brown and tan.

how_to_know_it.label: Build
how_to_know_it.text: Fairly large for a sparrow, with an upright posture and plain gray breast.

how_to_know_it.label: The double-scratch
how_to_know_it.text: On the ground it often hops backward with both feet to move leaves aside, then moves forward to pick up exposed food.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The song begins with clear whistles and ends with buzzes or trills. White-crowned Sparrows have regional song dialects. Calls include a sharp chink.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About seven inches long — a fairly large sparrow.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look low along brushy borders, weedy ground and thickets. Adults have bold black-and-white crown stripes; immature birds have brown-and-tan stripes. Watch for birds scratching backward through leaf litter.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Brushy edges, low thickets, weedy ground and leaf litter near open grassy areas.
A winter visitor to Florida. Palma Sola sightings are occasional, so do not expect to find one on every visit.

what_it_does_here.text: A ground-feeding seed and insect consumer that becomes part of Florida's winter songbird community.

what_it_does_here.label: Low cover, low food
what_it_does_here.text: Low vegetation provides both food and cover. White-crowned Sparrows feed on seeds from grasses and other weedy plants, scratch through leaf litter beneath shrubs, and retreat into dense thickets when disturbed.
Some White-crowned Sparrows fly more than 2,500 miles from the Alaskan tundra to reach their wintering grounds. That is a long haul for a bird weighing about as much as a few quarters.

quick_hits: A Blue-gray Gnatcatcher is almost constantly moving, flicking its long black-and-white tail as it searches the outer branches of trees for small prey.
Despite the name, gnats are not an important part of its known diet. It eats small insects and spiders picked from foliage or caught in short flights.
Both parents build a small cup nest from plant fibers, bark and grasses, bind it with spider silk, and cover the outside with bits of lichen and bark.
A pair may build as many as seven nests in one breeding season, often recycling material from an earlier nest after a nesting attempt fails.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Blue-gray Gnatcatchers breed across much of the United States and southern Canada, with many moving south toward the southern United States, Mexico and the Caribbean outside the breeding season. Florida supports birds through much of the year.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: A tiny, slender songbird about four inches long, with a tail that looks unusually long for its body.

blocks.label: Plumage
blocks.text: Blue-gray above and whitish below, with a thin white eye ring and a long black tail edged with white. Breeding males develop a narrow black line across the forehead; females and nonbreeding males lack it.

blocks.label: Behavior
blocks.text: Usually in motion, hopping and sidling through outer foliage while repeatedly cocking or flicking the long tail.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a very small gray-and-white bird moving quickly through the outer foliage of trees. The long black-and-white tail is often cocked or flicked from side to side. A thin nasal call may reveal the bird before you see it.

species.diet: Small insects and spiders, including leafhoppers, beetles, caterpillars, flies and small wasps. Prey is picked from foliage or caught during short flights.
species.behavior: It searches the outer foliage of trees and shrubs, hopping along branches, hovering briefly and making short flights after prey. The long tail is frequently cocked or flicked as it forages, and flashing the white outer tail feathers may help startle insects into moving.
species.sounds: The call is a thin, nasal note often given repeatedly while the bird forages. The breeding song is a soft series of wheezy notes and may include imitations of other birds.
species.ecological_role: A small predator of insects and spiders in tree and shrub foliage. Gnatcatchers in turn become prey for larger birds, snakes and other predators.
species.plant_connections: Trees and shrubs provide both hunting habitat and nesting material. Gnatcatchers search leaves and outer branches for prey, while breeding pairs build their nests from bark, grasses and other plant fibers. Lichen camouflages the outside, and spider silk binds the structure together.

size.length: About four inches long, with a wingspan around six inches.

species.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodlands, pine flatwoods with oak understory, hardwood swamps, riparian edges, and wooded suburban areas. In Florida, birds make use of a wide range of wooded habitats year-round — from sandhills and scrub oak to residential parks with sufficient tree cover. Prefers habitat edges and areas with openings in the canopy.
species.where_to_look: Look along wooded edges and wherever trees have open outer branches. Blue-gray Gnatcatchers usually search the foliage rather than the trunk, moving quickly from branch to branch. Listen for the thin nasal call and then follow the movement.
species.when_to_see: Blue-gray Gnatcatchers occur in Florida through much of the year, with both resident and migratory birds contributing to the state's population. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a reliable local seasonal pattern.

seasonality.note: The species occurs in Florida in multiple seasons, but Palma Sola currently has too few records to establish local abundance or migration peaks.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path without following a bird closely through the vegetation, especially if it is carrying nesting material or food.

conservation.status: Common and widespread; not considered threatened.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Ruby-crowned Kinglets are similarly tiny and active but have shorter tails and no white outer tail feathers.

species.teaser: Its tiny nest is covered with lichen and held together with spider silk, making it look remarkably like a knot on a tree branch.

how_it_lives.text: It searches the outer foliage of trees and shrubs, hopping along branches, hovering briefly and making short flights after prey. The long tail is frequently cocked or flicked as it forages, and flashing the white outer tail feathers may help startle insects into moving.

how_it_lives.label: The nest
how_it_lives.text: Pairs build with plant fibers, bark and grasses, bind the nest with spider silk and cover it with lichen. After a nest fails, they may dismantle it and reuse the material elsewhere.

how_to_know_it.text: A tiny, slender songbird about four inches long, with a tail that looks unusually long for its body.

how_to_know_it.label: Plumage
how_to_know_it.text: Blue-gray above and whitish below, with a thin white eye ring and a long black tail edged with white. Breeding males develop a narrow black line across the forehead; females and nonbreeding males lack it.

how_to_know_it.label: Behavior
how_to_know_it.text: Usually in motion, hopping and sidling through outer foliage while repeatedly cocking or flicking the long tail.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The call is a thin, nasal note often given repeatedly while the bird forages. The breeding song is a soft series of wheezy notes and may include imitations of other birds.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a very small gray-and-white bird moving quickly through the outer foliage of trees. The long black-and-white tail is often cocked or flicked from side to side. A thin nasal call may reveal the bird before you see it.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look along wooded edges and wherever trees have open outer branches. Blue-gray Gnatcatchers usually search the foliage rather than the trunk, moving quickly from branch to branch. Listen for the thin nasal call and then follow the movement.

Blue-gray Gnatcatchers occur in Florida through much of the year, with both resident and migratory birds contributing to the state's population. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a reliable local seasonal pattern.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: The species occurs in Florida in multiple seasons, but Palma Sola currently has too few records to establish local abundance or migration peaks.

what_it_does_here.text: Trees and shrubs provide both hunting habitat and nesting material. Gnatcatchers search leaves and outer branches for prey, while breeding pairs build their nests from bark, grasses and other plant fibers. Lichen camouflages the outside, and spider silk binds the structure together.

at_a_glance.text: A Blue-gray Gnatcatcher is almost constantly moving, flicking its long black-and-white tail as it searches the outer branches of trees for small prey.
Despite the name, gnats are not an important part of its known diet. It eats small insects and spiders picked from foliage or caught in short flights.
Both parents build a small cup nest from plant fibers, bark and grasses, bind it with spider silk, and cover the outside with bits of lichen and bark.
A pair may build as many as seven nests in one breeding season, often recycling material from an earlier nest after a nesting attempt fails.

quick_hits: A Yellow-throated Vireo combines a bright yellow throat and yellow eye markings with an olive back, gray wings and two white wing bars.
This is a migrant through Florida rather than a breeding bird at Palma Sola. It passes through the state on its journeys between northern breeding grounds and tropical wintering areas.
Behavior helps separate it from similarly colored warblers. Yellow-throated Vireos move methodically through branches, often pausing to inspect a perch before continuing.
The song is a slow series of burry, two- or three-part phrases separated by noticeable pauses.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. Yellow-throated Vireos breed across much of the eastern United States and southern Canada and winter in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. Florida lies along the migration route.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A sturdy songbird with a thick, slightly hooked bill, bright yellow throat and breast, yellow markings around the eyes, olive-green upperparts and two white wing bars. The belly is white.

blocks.label: Confusion species
blocks.text: Pine Warblers can show similar yellow-and-white colors, but their bills are thinner and their movements are usually quicker. Yellow-throated Vireos have a heavier, slightly hooked bill and bold yellow around the eyes.

identification.what_to_look_for: Search the middle and upper parts of mature trees for a yellow-throated bird moving slowly through branches. Look for the yellow eye markings, two white wing bars and thick, slightly hooked bill. Its deliberate pace is often as useful as its color.

species.diet: Mostly insects and other small invertebrates, including caterpillars and beetles. It also eats berries, especially outside the breeding season.
species.behavior: It searches branches and foliage slowly, pausing often to inspect leaves, twigs and bark for prey. Like many small migratory songbirds, it travels mostly at night.
species.sounds: The song is a slow series of short, burry phrases with clear pauses between them. The call is harsher and less musical.
species.ecological_role: A canopy predator of insects and other small invertebrates. Fruit eaten during migration may also move seeds away from the parent plant.
species.plant_connections: Trees provide nearly everything this bird needs during a migration stop: branches and leaves hold the insects it hunts, and fruiting shrubs and trees can provide additional food. During the breeding season farther north, pairs suspend a cup-shaped nest from a fork in a small branch using plant fibers and spider silk.

size.length: About five to six inches long, with a wingspan around nine inches.

species.habitat: Open deciduous forests and forest edges with tall trees, ideally with an open understory and proximity to water. During migration in Florida, uses a variety of wooded habitats including parks, riparian corridors, and mature shade trees in gardens. Avoids dense closed-canopy forest and pure conifer stands.
species.where_to_look: Look in mature trees along woodland edges, gardens and other open wooded areas. Yellow-throated Vireos usually forage in the middle and upper canopy, where their slow movements can make them surprisingly easy to overlook.
species.when_to_see: A spring and fall migrant through Florida. Palma Sola has only a few records, all from one spring date, so the park does not yet have enough observations to define a reliable local migration peak.

seasonality.note: Spring and fall migrant through Florida. Palma Sola records are currently too limited to define local peak dates.

interaction.guidance: Watch from established paths and avoid following a bird closely through the vegetation during a migration stop.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Pine Warblers can show similar yellow-and-white plumage, but Yellow-throated Vireos have a heavier, slightly hooked bill and bold yellow markings around the eyes.

Like many small migratory songbirds, it travels mostly at night.

quick_hits: Unlike most warblers, Black-and-white Warblers forage directly on tree trunks and large branches, moving up, down and sideways while searching bark for insects.
Its feet are well suited to gripping bark, including a long hind toe and claw that help it cling while moving over trunks and branches.
The song is a thin repeated wee-see, wee-see, wee-see, often compared to a squeaky wheel.
Despite spending so much time on trunks and large limbs, Black-and-white Warblers build their nests on the ground beside roots, logs or rocks.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. Black-and-white Warblers breed across much of eastern and central North America and winter in Florida, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America and northern South America.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A small black-and-white striped warbler with a slightly downcurved bill. Its habit of creeping directly over tree trunks and large limbs is often the easiest way to recognize it.

blocks.label: Male and female
blocks.text: Adult males have a black throat and darker cheek. Females and immature birds are paler, with a whitish or buff throat.

blocks.label: Possible confusion
blocks.text: Other black-and-white warblers work among leaves and twigs. Behavior separates them more reliably than plumage does.

identification.what_to_look_for: Scan trunks and heavy branches rather than just the leaves. Look for a small striped bird creeping directly over the bark, sometimes moving downward or sideways as well as upward.

species.diet: Mostly insects and spiders taken from bark, including caterpillars, beetles, ants and other small arthropods.
species.behavior: It forages on bark rather than leaf tips, probing crevices and working under loose flakes for prey that leaf-gleaning birds do not reach.
species.sounds: The song is a very high series of repeated wee-see phrases, often compared to a squeaky wheel. Calls are short, sharp notes.
species.ecological_role: A predator of insects and spiders living on and beneath tree bark. Its bark-foraging style lets it exploit food that many foliage-feeding warblers overlook.
species.plant_connections: Mature trees are the feeding surface. Black-and-white Warblers search rough bark, trunk crevices and large limbs for insects and spiders. Farther north on the breeding grounds, fallen leaves, roots, logs and other material on the forest floor help conceal the ground nest.

size.length: About five inches long, with a wingspan around eight inches.

species.habitat: Mature and second-growth deciduous or mixed woodland; also found in parks, riparian corridors, and suburban areas with large trees during migration and winter. In Florida's winter, it uses a wide range of wooded habitats including mangroves, oak hammocks, and tree-lined parks.
species.where_to_look: Check trunks and large branches of mature trees. The bird often forages much lower than other warblers, so scan at eye level as well as overhead.
species.when_to_see: A migrant and winter visitor in Florida. Palma Sola has only a few records, so local peak timing is not yet established.

seasonality.note: Occurs in Florida during migration and winter. Palma Sola records are too limited to define a local peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and let the bird continue working along the trunk rather than following it from tree to tree.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Blackpoll Warblers can also be strongly black and white in breeding plumage, but they forage through foliage rather than creeping directly over trunks. Black-and-white Warblers are usually recognized first by behavior.

how_it_lives.text: Bark holds prey that leaf-gleaning birds never reach — insect eggs and larvae wedged in crevices, spiders under loose flakes. It works a trunk methodically, probing as it goes and often circling to the far side out of view.
It eats insects, spiders and other small arthropods taken from bark and crevices.

how_it_lives.label: A nest on the ground
how_it_lives.text: During the breeding season farther north, the nest is placed on the ground, often beside a tree, stump, rock or fallen log.
