quick_hits: Northern Parulas are tiny blue-gray and yellow warblers, often easier to hear in the canopy than to follow with your eyes.
In the southern United States, females often build inside hanging Spanish moss, hollowing a small chamber within the strands and lining it with finer material.
They search the outer foliage for insects, sometimes hanging beneath leaves or twig tips to reach prey on the underside.
The song rises as a buzzy trill and ends abruptly with a sharp final note, a pattern that can reveal the bird high overhead before you see it.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. Northern Parulas breed across much of eastern North America, including parts of Florida, and winter mainly in southern Florida, the Caribbean and Central America.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A very small warbler with blue-gray upperparts, a greenish patch on the back, yellow throat and breast, two white wing bars and broken white crescents around the eyes. Adult males also show a dark and chestnut band across the breast.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look high in mature trees for a tiny blue-gray and yellow bird working the outer leaves and branch tips. Broken white eye crescents and two white wing bars are useful clues. Listen for the rising buzzy song when birds are vocal.

species.diet: Mostly insects and spiders taken from leaves and branch tips. Small amounts of fruit, seeds or nectar may be taken outside the breeding season.
species.behavior: It moves through outer foliage, picking insects from leaves and sometimes hovering or hanging underneath branch tips to reach prey.
species.sounds: The song is a rising buzzy trill that accelerates and ends abruptly with a sharper final note. Calls are short chips.
species.ecological_role: A small canopy predator of insects and spiders. Parulas in turn become prey for larger birds and other predators.
species.plant_connections: Spanish moss is nesting habitat, not decoration, for Northern Parulas in the southern part of their breeding range. The female hollows a chamber inside a hanging clump and lines it with finer material. Spanish moss is an epiphyte rather than a true moss and takes support — not food — from the tree, so a mature tree draped with healthy Spanish moss can provide nesting structure without being harmed by it.

size.length: About four and a half inches long, with a wingspan around seven inches.

species.habitat: During the breeding season, mature moist woodland draped with Spanish moss or beard lichens, often near water. Outside the breeding season it becomes a habitat generalist, turning up in nearly any wooded setting — parks, shade trees, scrubby edges, and overgrown gardens — during migration and winter.
species.where_to_look: Look in mature trees and wooded edges, scanning the middle and upper canopy. During migration and winter, Northern Parulas use a wide variety of wooded habitats, including parks and gardens.
species.when_to_see: Northern Parulas occur in Florida during migration and winter, and they breed in parts of the state. Palma Sola currently has only one observation event, in March, so local seasonal timing is not yet established.

seasonality.note: Recorded at Palma Sola during spring migration. Local observations are too limited to define a reliable seasonal pattern.

interaction.guidance: Watch from established paths and avoid following a feeding bird closely through the vegetation.

conservation.status: Widespread and currently considered a species of low conservation concern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Yellow-throated Warblers are larger, with a longer bill, black facial markings and no broken white eye crescents. Northern Parulas are much smaller and more compact.

quick_hits: Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest the waxy fruits of bayberries and wax myrtles, foods many other birds cannot use efficiently. That extra winter food helps them remain farther north than most other warblers.
Unlike many warblers that search mainly for insects in foliage, Yellow-rumped Warblers also catch insects in flight, forage on the ground and switch heavily to fruit during winter.
The birds seen in Florida are usually the white-throated 'Myrtle' form. Farther west, the 'Audubon's' form has a yellow throat.
The birds at Palma Sola are winter visitors. They breed far to the north and leave Florida again in spring.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Yellow-rumped Warblers breed mainly across Canada, Alaska and parts of the northern United States, then move south for winter. Florida is wintering habitat rather than breeding habitat.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: A sturdy warbler about five and a half inches long, with a fairly large head and a narrow tail.

blocks.label: Winter plumage
blocks.text: Winter birds are gray-brown above and pale below, with streaking on the breast and sides. Look for the bright yellow rump, small yellow patches along the sides, a white throat and two pale wing bars.

blocks.label: Spring males
blocks.text: By spring, males can become much more strongly patterned in gray, black and white, while retaining the yellow rump and side patches.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Palm Warblers are also common Florida winter visitors but usually forage lower and repeatedly bob or wag the tail.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look first for the yellow rump, often easiest to see when the bird flies. Winter birds also show a white throat, yellow patches along the sides and two pale wing bars. Listen for a short, flat check call from shrubs and trees.

species.diet: Insects and other small arthropods are important during the breeding season. In winter, fruit becomes a major food source, including wax myrtle, bayberry, poison ivy, grapes and other berries.
species.behavior: Yellow-rumped Warblers forage at several heights, searching foliage and bark, catching insects in short flights and sometimes feeding on the ground. They migrate at night.
species.sounds: The most useful sound in Florida is a short, flat check call, often given while the bird is foraging or flying. The male's breeding song is a soft series of whistled notes, but visitors here are much more likely to hear the call.
species.ecological_role: Yellow-rumped Warblers eat insects during much of the year and consume large quantities of fruit in winter. Seeds from some fruits can pass through the bird and be carried away from the parent plant.
species.plant_connections: Wax myrtle is especially important winter food. Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest its wax-coated fruits, helping them survive when insects are scarce. They also eat fruits from poison ivy, grapes and other woody plants, making fruiting shrubs and vines important winter habitat.

size.length: About five and a half inches long.

species.habitat: Breeds in mature coniferous and mixed coniferous-deciduous forests in the far north. In winter — the only time it occurs in Florida — it occupies a wide range of open habitats: woodland edges, shrubby thickets, coastal vegetation, parks, residential areas, dunes with bayberry or wax myrtle, and even open beaches. One of the most habitat-flexible warblers in North America.
species.where_to_look: Check fruiting wax myrtles and other shrubs, especially during winter. Birds also forage through tree canopies and along woodland edges, sometimes flying out from a branch to catch an insect. Listen for the short check call when a flock is moving through.
species.when_to_see: A winter visitor to Florida, generally present from fall into spring. Palma Sola records are still too few to define a local peak.

seasonality.note: Winter visitor to Florida. Recorded at Palma Sola, but local observations are too few to establish how regularly it occurs in the park.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and avoid disturbing birds feeding in fruiting shrubs.

invasive.notes: Native North American species and a natural seasonal visitor to Florida. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

quick_hits: It forages more like a creeper than many warblers, moving along branches and probing bark crevices, pine cones and clusters of needles with its unusually long bill.
In Florida, Yellow-throated Warblers often work through palm crowns, creeping among the fronds and probing for insects hidden between them.
Early naturalist Mark Catesby called it the Yellow-throated Creeper, a name that describes its methodical branch-crawling behavior better than its modern name does.
The bill is longer than on most warblers, helping it reach insects hidden in bark cracks, pine cones and tightly packed foliage.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States and neighboring parts of the Americas. Yellow-throated Warblers breed across much of the Southeast and winter farther south, including Florida, Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. Some Florida populations are resident.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A gray-and-white warbler with a bright yellow throat, black face markings, a long white eyebrow and two white wing bars. Black streaks run along the sides of the white underparts.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: The bill is noticeably long and pointed for a warbler, an especially useful clue when the bird is probing bark or foliage.

blocks.label: Sexes and ages
blocks.text: Females and young birds resemble adult males but are usually somewhat duller.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Blackburnian Warblers can also show a bright throat, but their back and facial pattern are different. Black-and-white Warblers creep along branches in a similar way but are entirely black and white.

identification.what_to_look_for: Scan high branches and palm crowns for a gray-and-white bird moving deliberately along limbs and probing into bark or foliage. Look for the bright yellow throat, black face pattern, long white eyebrow and unusually long bill.

species.diet: Insects and spiders, including beetles, caterpillars, flies and scale insects. The bird probes bark, pine cones, needles and other tight spaces where prey hides.
species.behavior: It moves methodically along branches, probing bark cracks, pine cones and clusters of needles with its long bill. It also makes short flights to catch insects.
species.sounds: The song is a clear series of descending whistles that speeds up before rising at the end. Males often sing from high in the canopy. The call is a sharp chip.
species.ecological_role: A canopy predator of insects and spiders, including prey hidden in bark crevices and clusters of foliage.
species.plant_connections: Trees are both hunting habitat and, during the breeding season, nest sites. Yellow-throated Warblers probe bark, pine cones, needle clusters and palm fronds for insects. During the nonbreeding season they also forage around flowers such as agave and coconut palm, where insects gather. In places with Spanish moss, nests may be tucked into hanging strands high in trees.

size.length: About five and a half inches long, with a wingspan around eight inches.

species.habitat: Pine forests with open understories, bald cypress swamps, live-oak woodlands draped in Spanish moss, and riverine bottomlands with large sycamores. In Florida winters, also found in palm groves and mixed woodlands in parks and gardens.
species.where_to_look: Look high in pines, live oaks and palms. In Florida, Yellow-throated Warblers often search palm crowns, creeping among the fronds and probing for insects. They also work bark, pine cones and clusters of needles in the upper branches of trees.
species.when_to_see: Yellow-throated Warblers occur in Florida during winter and migration, with resident populations in parts of the state. Palma Sola currently has too few observations to establish how regularly they occur here.

seasonality.presence: winter resident; year-round in parts of north/north-central Florida
seasonality.note: Occurs in Florida during winter and migration, with resident populations elsewhere in the state. Palma Sola records are too limited to define a local seasonal peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch from established paths. These birds usually forage high overhead, so stop in a safe place before following one through the canopy with binoculars.

conservation.status: Widespread and currently considered a species of low conservation concern, although mature forest habitat remains important.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Black-and-white Warblers also creep along trunks and branches but lack the yellow throat. Blackburnian Warblers can show yellow or orange on the throat but have a different facial and back pattern.

how_to_know_it.text: A gray-and-white warbler with a bright yellow throat, black face markings, a long white eyebrow and two white wing bars. Black streaks run along the sides of the white underparts.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: The bill is noticeably long and pointed for a warbler, an especially useful clue when the bird is probing bark or foliage.

how_to_know_it.label: Sexes and ages
how_to_know_it.text: Females and young birds resemble adult males but are usually somewhat duller.

at_a_glance.text: It forages more like a creeper than many warblers, moving along branches and probing bark crevices, pine cones and clusters of needles with its unusually long bill.
In Florida, Yellow-throated Warblers often work through palm crowns, creeping among the fronds and probing for insects hidden between them.
Early naturalist Mark Catesby called it the Yellow-throated Creeper, a name that describes its methodical branch-crawling behavior better than its modern name does.
The bill is longer than on most warblers, helping it reach insects hidden in bark cracks, pine cones and tightly packed foliage.

species.teaser: In Florida, this warbler often searches palm crowns, probing between fronds with a long bill for insects hidden from view.

quick_hits: The Cape May Warbler has an unusually shaped, semitubular tongue that helps it drink nectar from flowers and juice from fruit.
The scientific name tigrina refers to the dark streaks across the male's yellow breast.
On its northern breeding grounds, Cape May Warbler numbers rise when spruce budworms become abundant. In years with abundant food, females can lay unusually large clutches for a warbler.
Florida is mostly a stop along the journey. Most Cape May Warblers continue across the Caribbean to their wintering grounds.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America and the Caribbean region. Cape May Warblers breed in boreal forests across Canada and the northern United States, migrate through Florida, and winter mainly in the Caribbean.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Breeding males have yellow underparts heavily streaked with black, a chestnut cheek patch, dark eyestripe and a large white patch in the wing.

blocks.label: Female and nonbreeding
blocks.text: Females and immature birds are much duller, usually gray-olive above and pale yellowish below with fine streaking. A yellowish rump, short tail and slightly downcurved bill can help with identification.

blocks.label: Confusion species
blocks.text: Dull birds can resemble other migrating warblers. Cape May Warblers have a relatively short tail, fine streaking across the breast and sides, and a slender bill that curves slightly downward. Palm Warblers repeatedly pump the tail; Yellow-rumped Warblers show a brighter yellow rump.

identification.what_to_look_for: In spring, look for a yellow bird with heavy dark breast streaking and a chestnut cheek patch. Duller birds are harder: look for the short tail, streaked underparts and slightly downcurved bill. Cape May Warblers often forage high in trees, so a clear view may take patience.

species.diet: Insects dominate on the breeding grounds, especially spruce budworm caterpillars when they are abundant. During migration and winter, Cape May Warblers also drink flower nectar and fruit juice.
species.behavior: Cape May Warblers usually forage high in trees, picking insects from foliage and branch tips and sometimes flying out to catch insects in the air. Migration occurs mostly at night. Outside the breeding season they also visit flowers for nectar and may defend productive flowering plants from other nectar feeders.
species.sounds: The song is a very high, thin series of repeated notes. The call is a soft, high sip. The song can be difficult to hear for people who have lost sensitivity to high frequencies.
species.ecological_role: Cape May Warblers are important predators of spruce budworm caterpillars on their northern breeding grounds. During migration and winter they also feed at flowers, putting them in direct contact with pollen as they drink nectar.
species.plant_connections: This warbler changes its relationship with plants through the year. In northern spruce forests it searches needles and branch tips for spruce budworm caterpillars. During migration and winter it also visits flowers for nectar and punctures fruit for juice. Flowering trees and shrubs can therefore be good places to look for one in Florida.

size.length: About five inches long, with a wingspan around eight inches.

species.habitat: Breeds in mature boreal spruce-fir forest, typically stands 25 to 75 years old with trees exceeding 35 feet. During migration it uses a wide variety of wooded and shrubby habitats — conifers are preferred but deciduous trees, thickets, and even palm trees are used. In Florida and the Caribbean it turns up in parks, gardens, coffee plantations, scrub, and mangrove edges.
species.where_to_look: Scan the upper parts of trees during migration, especially branch tips where birds search for insects. Also check flowering trees and shrubs: Cape May Warblers sometimes come lower to drink nectar. The weeping bottlebrush in the park is the kind of nectar-rich flowering tree worth checking.
species.when_to_see: Primarily a migrant through Florida, especially during spring and fall, with some birds wintering in southern Florida. Palma Sola has recorded the species in spring, but there are too few park observations to establish a local seasonal pattern.

seasonality.note: Passage migrant through Florida and occasional winter visitor. Palma Sola records are currently too limited to define a local peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and avoid following a feeding bird from tree to tree. If one is visiting flowers, staying back may let it return repeatedly to the same plant.

conservation.status: Globally classified as Least Concern, but long-term monitoring has documented substantial population declines. Its numbers also fluctuate with outbreaks of spruce budworm on the breeding grounds.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Palm Warblers characteristically bob the tail. Cape May Warblers have a short tail, streaked breast and slightly downcurved bill.
Yellow-rumped Warblers show a brighter yellow rump. A dull Cape May shows finer streaking below and a slimmer, slightly downcurved bill.

quick_hits: Palm Warblers spend unusual amounts of time on the ground, walking rather than hopping and bobbing the tail almost constantly. That tail movement is often the quickest way to recognize one.
The name is misleading. The species was named from early specimens collected on Hispaniola, where palms were part of the landscape; Palm Warblers themselves are not especially tied to palms.
Two forms occur in Florida. 'Yellow' Palm Warblers are brighter yellow below and winter mainly along the Gulf Coast; the duller western form has a whitish belly. The two overlap in the Southeast.
Unlike most warblers, Palm Warblers are often easiest to find in open grass, weedy edges and low shrubs rather than high in trees.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Palm Warblers breed mainly in boreal bogs and open conifer country across Canada, then winter in the southeastern United States, Caribbean and parts of Central America.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A small brownish warbler with yellow under the tail, a pale eyebrow and a habit of walking on the ground while repeatedly bobbing its tail.

blocks.label: Breeding plumage
blocks.text: Spring birds develop a rusty cap and stronger breast streaking. The Yellow form is extensively yellow below; the western form has a paler belly.

blocks.label: Winter plumage
blocks.text: Winter birds are duller brown and less strongly streaked, but yellow under the tail and the repeated tail bob remain useful clues.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look low. A Palm Warbler often walks across grass, bare ground or low vegetation while repeatedly bobbing its tail. Yellow under the tail, a pale eyebrow and brownish streaking help confirm the identification.

species.diet: Mostly insects and spiders, with fruit and seeds added during winter. Palm Warblers forage mainly on the ground and in low vegetation.
species.behavior: It spends much of its time walking on the ground and through low vegetation, repeatedly bobbing its tail as it searches for prey.
species.sounds: The song is a thin, buzzy trill. Calls are short, sharp notes often given in flight.
species.ecological_role: Palm Warblers eat small insects and spiders and are themselves prey for larger animals. Winter fruit feeding may also move some seeds.
species.plant_connections: The Palm Warbler's name overstates its relationship with palms. At Palma Sola, low vegetation, weedy ground and leaf litter are more important because that is where it searches for insects. Fruiting shrubs such as bayberry and sea grape can also provide winter food.

size.length: About five inches long, with a wingspan around eight inches.

species.habitat: Winters in open, scrubby, and edge habitats: weedy fields, forest edges, coastal scrub, marshes, mangroves, parks, and gardens. Avoids dense closed-canopy forest. Breeds in sphagnum bogs with scattered spruce, tamarack, and cedar in the boreal forest far to the north.
species.where_to_look: Look in open grassy and weedy areas, along woodland edges, in low shrubs and around leaf litter. Palm Warblers spend much more time near the ground than most warblers and may forage with sparrows and Yellow-rumped Warblers.
species.when_to_see: A winter visitor to Florida, also seen during migration. Palma Sola has only a few records, so local abundance and peak timing are not yet established.

seasonality.note: A winter visitor and migrant in Florida. Palma Sola records are currently too limited to define a local peak.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and let the bird continue feeding rather than following it closely across open ground.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Yellow-rumped Warblers usually forage more in shrubs and trees and show a bright yellow rump. Palm Warblers spend more time walking on the ground and repeatedly bob the tail.

quick_hits: A plain, grayish-brown bird that sits upright on an exposed perch, wags its tail, and darts out to catch a flying insect — that is an eastern phoebe.
The tail-wagging is almost constant and is the quickest way to recognize it — few other small birds pump their tail so persistently.
It calls its own name: a burry, two-note 'fee-bee' that it repeats from a favorite perch.
A winter visitor to Florida, it breeds farther north and returns each fall.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. Breeds across the eastern U.S. and southern Canada; winters in the southeastern U.S. and Mexico. A winter visitor in the Bradenton area.
more_information: The Eastern Phoebe was the first bird ever banded in North America. In 1804 John James Audubon tied silver thread to the legs of nestlings to see whether the same birds returned the following year. They did.

blocks.text: Small and dark — a flycatcher bill.

identification.what_to_look_for: A plain gray-brown bird on an exposed perch, wagging its tail and darting out after insects.

species.diet: Flying insects — caught by sallying from a perch. Some berries in winter.
species.behavior: Sits on exposed perches, pumps tail, darts out to catch insects. Returns to the same perch. Solitary.
species.sounds: A burry, emphatic 'fee-bee' — says its name.
species.ecological_role: A predator of flying insects, taken on short sallies from a perch. Phoebes are in turn prey for small hawks and other predators.
species.plant_connections: Trees and shrubs matter to a phoebe as furniture rather than food. It hunts from an exposed twig with clear air in front of it, so open branch tips at the edge of a planting are more useful to it than dense cover. In winter it also takes small fruits when insects are scarce.

size.length: About six inches long, with a wingspan around ten inches.

species.habitat: Open areas with perches — forest edges, fences, buildings, park structures.
species.where_to_look: Watch exposed perches at the edge of open ground — fence lines, low branches, the corners of buildings. A phoebe returns to the same perch after each sally, so once you find one it tends to stay findable.
species.when_to_see: A winter visitor to Florida, generally present from autumn into early spring.

seasonality.note: Breeds to the north; winters in Florida.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path. A phoebe will usually keep hunting from the same perch if you stay still rather than following it.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Great Crested Flycatchers are larger and show a yellow belly and rusty tail. The phoebe is plain gray-brown and wags its tail almost constantly.

how_it_lives.text: It picks an exposed perch, pumps its tail, darts out to take an insect in the air, and comes back to the same spot. Then does it again.
Flying insects almost entirely, with some small fruits in winter when insects are scarce. Usually alone.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: An upright, medium-sized flycatcher, plain gray-brown above and pale below, with a small dark bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Tail
how_to_know_it.text: Wags almost constantly. This is the best field mark on the bird.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A burry, emphatic fee-bee, repeated from a perch.
Plain is the point. There is no wing bar, no eye ring and no color to fix on, so posture and the tail do the work.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Watch exposed perches at the edge of open ground — fence lines, low branches, the corners of buildings. A phoebe comes back to the same perch after each sally, so once you have found one it stays findable.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: A winter visitor, generally present from autumn into early spring.

what_it_does_here.text: Open branch tips matter to a phoebe because they give an unobstructed launch over open air. Dense foliage can hold plenty of insects, but the bird needs somewhere to watch from and room to fly out after them.

In 1804 John James Audubon tied silver threads to the legs of young Eastern Phoebes to see whether they would return the following year. Some did. The experiment is generally regarded as the first bird-banding experiment in North America.
what_it_does_here.label: An experiment in 1804

at_a_glance.text: An Eastern Phoebe hunts from a perch, darting out after a flying insect and often returning to exactly the same branch.
The tail-wagging is nearly constant, and it is the quickest way to know one — few small birds pump their tail so persistently.
It says its own name: a burry two-note fee-bee, repeated from a favorite perch.
A winter visitor here. It breeds farther north and comes back each fall.

species.teaser: It says its own name. A burry two-note fee-bee from an exposed perch, over and over, is usually the bird itself telling you what it is.

quick_hits: The American Robin is a winter visitor in Florida, not a year-round resident. Birds arrive in flocks and leave again before the breeding season.
Brick-red breast, dark gray-brown back and a yellow bill.
In winter it feeds mainly on fruit rather than worms, which is why flocks turn up wherever berries are ripe.
The head-tilting pause on a lawn is a bird locating prey — it uses sight and hearing rather than smell.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Breeds across the U.S. and Canada; winters in the southern U.S. including Florida. A seasonal visitor here.
more_information: The American robin is arguably the most familiar bird in North America — but in Florida it is a seasonal guest, arriving in flocks from late fall and departing by spring.
In winter it shifts from its summer diet of earthworms and insects to one dominated by berries and fruit, and large flocks can strip a fruiting tree in hours.
Its presence on a Florida lawn is a good seasonal marker: if you see robins, it is probably winter.

identification.what_to_look_for: A plump, upright bird with a red breast hopping across a lawn. In Florida, a winter visitor in flocks.

species.diet: Earthworms and insects (summer); berries and fruit (winter).
species.behavior: Runs across open ground, tilts head to listen for worms. Forms large flocks in winter. Feeds heavily on fruit.
species.sounds: A rich, caroling song ('cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio') — but mostly heard on the breeding grounds, not in Florida.
species.ecological_role: Berry disperser in winter; earthworm and insect predator in summer.
species.plant_connections: Heavy berry consumer in winter — disperses many native and ornamental fruit species.

size.lifespan: commonly a few years.

species.where_to_look: Open lawns and under fruiting trees in winter.

seasonality.note: A winter visitor to Florida, arriving in flocks and departing before the breeding season.

danger.people: Harmless.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a flock rather than a single bird, either working a lawn or stripping fruit from a tree.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Open lawns and beneath fruiting trees and shrubs. In winter the fruit matters more than the grass, so check anything in berry.
A winter visitor, generally present from late autumn into early spring.

what_it_does_here.label: Fruit in, seeds out
what_it_does_here.text: Winter robins swallow whole fruits and pass the seeds intact, so a flock working a berry-laden shrub carries those seeds well away from the parent plant. This is one of the few bird-and-plant relationships here that is genuinely seed dispersal rather than seed eating.

at_a_glance.text: The American Robin is a winter visitor in Florida, not a year-round resident. Birds arrive in flocks and leave again before the breeding season.
Brick-red breast, dark gray-brown back and a yellow bill.
In winter it feeds mainly on fruit rather than worms, which is why flocks turn up wherever berries are ripe.
The familiar head-tilting pause on a lawn helps a robin locate prey in the soil. Sight matters most, and research suggests hearing may help as well.

species.teaser: In most of the country the robin means spring. In Florida it means winter — they arrive in flocks to eat fruit and leave before the singing starts.

quick_hits: A small, fast butterfly checkered in gray, white and dark charcoal, darting low over open ground and landing flat to bask.
Males carry a dusting of blue-gray hairs on the body and wing bases that gives them a frosty look.
Its caterpillars feed on mallows — fanpetals and wireweed — plants that grow as common weeds in open ground.
Skippers hold their wings differently from other butterflies, often basking with them spread flat against the ground.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern U.S., Caribbean, and tropical Americas. Year-round resident in southern Florida.
more_information: The tropical checkered-skipper is one of the more recognizable skippers thanks to its bold checkered wing pattern of gray, white, and dark marks. Males get an additional dusting of blue-gray hairs that gives them a distinctive frosty appearance.

It belongs to the spread-winged skippers (subfamily Pyrginae). When basking, these butterflies lay their wings completely flat — a quick field clue that instantly separates them from grass skippers, which angle their wings upward like a tent.

It is a butterfly of disturbed, open ground — roadsides, gardens, weedy lots, and park edges — where its caterpillar host plants grow. Look for fanpetals and wireweed (Sida species) in sunny weedy patches; what looks like a nuisance weed is a nursery for this skipper.

blocks.label: Flight

Adults sip nectar from small flowers, particularly Sida species, Frogfruit (Phyla nodiflora), and Spanish Needles (Bidens alba).
species.behavior: Fast, darting flight close to the ground. Basks with wings open. Males patrol low over open ground.
species.ecological_role: Pollinator of low flowers including Frogfruit and Spanish Needles; caterpillars feed on mallow-family plants (Sida species and relatives), making roadside 'weeds' an essential part of its life cycle.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillar host plants are mallows (Malvaceae). Adults nectar at many low flowers.

size.length: wingspan about 1 to 1.5 inches
size.lifespan: adult lifespan not specifically documented for this species; typical of short-lived skippers

what_it_does_here.text: The caterpillars eat mallow-family plants — fanpetals and wireweed — which most gardens treat as weeds. A patch of scruffy open ground left alone is what keeps this butterfly present.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Leaving some low weedy ground unmown is the most useful thing for this butterfly. That is where its host plants grow.

quick_hits: A dragonfly with orange-and-brown banded wings — like a tiny Halloween decoration perched on a plant stem near the pond.
It perches at the very tip of a stem and flutters in the breeze like a flag, which is unusual for a dragonfly — most prefer rigid, still perches.
Males patrol territories over open water, but they spend long stretches resting on stem tips between patrols.
The wing pattern makes it one of the easiest dragonflies to identify at a glance.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the eastern United States. Common in Florida near ponds and wetlands.
more_information: Dragonflies spend most of their lives underwater. The nymph hunts small aquatic animals for months before climbing out on a stem, splitting its skin and emerging as the winged adult that lives only a few weeks.

blocks.label: Wings

blocks.label: Perch

blocks.label: Size

identification.what_to_look_for: A dragonfly with boldly banded orange-and-brown wings perched at the tip of a stem near water.

species.diet: Small flying insects, caught in the air.
species.behavior: Perches on flexible stem tips and flutters in the wind. Males patrol open water. Aerial hunter.
species.ecological_role: An aerial predator of small flying insects, and prey in turn for birds, frogs and larger dragonflies. The aquatic young hunt small animals underwater before emerging as adults.
species.plant_connections: This dragonfly needs standing plants more than most. It hunts from the tips of emergent stems — grasses, sedges and other plants rooted in shallow water — and prefers a flexible stalk it can ride rather than a rigid twig. Where wetland plants are cleared back to open water, the perches go with them.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks.

species.habitat: Ponds, marshes, and wetland edges.
species.where_to_look: Check stem tips around the ponds and wet margins, especially where grasses and sedges stand above open water. Look for the stalk that is swaying differently from the ones around it — that is usually the dragonfly, not the breeze.
species.when_to_see: A warm-season dragonfly, most common spring through fall.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Eastern Amberwings are much smaller with plain amber wings. The Halloween Pennant is larger and its wings carry bold dark bands rather than an even wash of color.

how_it_lives.text: It perches on the flexible tip of a stem and lets the wind move it, wings held out. That is the easiest way to find one: look for the stalk that is swaying differently from everything around it.
Males patrol stretches of open water and return to a favored perch between flights. The hunting happens in the air — small flying insects taken on the wing.

how_it_lives.label: Before the wings
how_it_lives.text: The young live underwater as nymphs, hunting small aquatic animals among submerged plants. When ready they climb a stem into the air and emerge as adults, leaving the split skin behind on the stalk.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings and body
how_to_know_it.text: Orange-amber wings crossed by dark brown bands, over a yellowish to orange body.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: A medium dragonfly, wingspan about three inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Perch
how_to_know_it.text: Sits at the tip of a flexible stem and sways with it.
Look for the stalk that is moving differently from the ones around it. That is usually the dragonfly rather than the breeze.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Check stem tips around the ponds and wet margins, especially where grasses and sedges stand above open water. Males patrol the open water, but they spend long stretches resting between patrols.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: A warm-season dragonfly, most common from spring through fall.

what_it_does_here.text: It takes small flying insects in the air, and it needs standing plants more than most dragonflies do — emergent grasses and sedges rooted in shallow water, and preferably a flexible stalk it can ride. Where wetland plants are cleared back to open water, the perches go with them.

Most of the animal's life happens underwater and out of sight. The nymph hunts small aquatic animals for months, then climbs out on a stem, splits its skin and emerges as the winged adult, which lives only a few weeks.

at_a_glance.text: A dragonfly with orange-and-brown banded wings, like a small Halloween decoration on a stem beside the pond.
It perches at the very tip of a flexible stem and rides the breeze like a flag. Most dragonflies choose something rigid.
The wing pattern makes it one of the easiest dragonflies here to name at a glance.

species.teaser: It perches on the very tip of a flexible stem and lets the wind swing it, like a small flag. Most dragonflies choose something rigid.

quick_hits: One of Florida's largest grasshoppers, an adult Eastern Lubber can reach about three inches long.
The wings are too small for sustained flight. Adults mostly walk and climb, with only short hops when disturbed.
The black, yellow, orange or red coloration is a warning. Lubbers contain defensive chemicals and can release a foul-smelling froth when threatened.
Lubbers eat many kinds of plants. In gardens, a large group can cause conspicuous damage even though the insect itself is native to Florida.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States and common throughout Florida.
more_information: Loggerhead Shrikes are among the few predators known to handle chemically defended lubbers. A shrike may impale prey on a thorn or barbed wire before eating it.

blocks.text: Very large and heavy-bodied. Adults are usually black with yellow, orange or red markings, though coloration varies.

blocks.label: Nymph

blocks.label: Wings

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a very large, slow-moving grasshopper walking through low vegetation or across paths. Adults are brightly patterned; young lubbers are mostly black with a colored stripe down the back.

species.diet: Leaves and other plant tissue from many species, including both native vegetation and garden plants. Members of the amaryllis family are among the documented favorites.
species.behavior: Lubbers cannot fly well and move mainly by walking and climbing through vegetation. When threatened they rely more on chemical defense than escape: a disturbed lubber may hiss, spread its short wings and release a foul-smelling secretion.
species.ecological_role: A large native herbivore. Lubbers convert plant material into animal biomass, although their chemical defenses make them poor prey for many predators.
species.plant_connections: Plants are its food. Eastern Lubbers feed on a wide variety of leaves and move readily between wild vegetation and cultivated beds. Members of the amaryllis family are documented favorites, and the park grows several — crinum and amaryllis among them. A few insects usually cause limited damage; large concentrations can defoliate individual plants.

size.length: Adults can reach about three inches long; females are larger than males.

species.habitat: Gardens, roadsides, fields, and open woodland — common in disturbed habitats.
species.where_to_look: Look in sunny planting beds, weedy edges and low vegetation. Lubbers feed on a wide range of plants and are often easiest to notice walking across paths between feeding sites.
species.when_to_see: Most visible from spring through warm weather as nymphs grow into large adults. Local Palma Sola records are too limited to define a precise peak.

seasonality.note: Nymphs appear in spring and grow into adults through the warm months. Palma Sola records are too limited to define a local peak.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when left alone. Do not handle or eat lubbers; a disturbed insect can release irritating, foul-smelling defensive secretions. Wash your hands if you come into contact with one.
danger.pets: Do not encourage pets to eat lubbers. Their chemical defenses can make them unpalatable and potentially cause illness.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling. If lubbers are damaging park plants, leave control to park staff rather than crushing, spraying or moving them.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida. Not invasive. Eastern Lubbers can nevertheless become serious garden pests when local numbers are high.

conservation.status: Common native species and not a conservation concern.

quick_hits: A Marsh Rabbit is smaller and darker than an Eastern Cottontail, with shorter ears and a small, inconspicuous brownish tail.
Marsh Rabbits are strong swimmers and usually stay close to water, using wetlands as both feeding habitat and escape cover.
They feed on grasses, sedges and other vegetation growing in and around wetlands.
Most activity occurs around dusk, dawn and at night, so a rabbit seen crossing a path may disappear into dense vegetation quickly.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States from Virginia to Florida. Year-round resident in Florida's wetlands.
more_information: The marsh rabbit is the rabbit of Florida's damp places — swamps, pond edges, marshes, and dense wet thickets. It is smaller and darker than the eastern cottontail, with proportionally shorter ears and a dingy brown tail instead of the cottontail's white powder puff.

Its willingness to swim sets it apart from most rabbits. When threatened, it may plunge into water and swim with only its nose above the surface, or sit motionless in shallow water among emergent vegetation.
It is most active at dawn and dusk, feeding on grasses, sedges, and aquatic plants.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small, dark rabbit near water with short ears and no white tail. If it runs toward water instead of away, it is a marsh rabbit.

species.diet: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, and other low vegetation — a strict herbivore.
species.behavior: Crepuscular — most active at dawn and dusk. Swims readily. Freezes when threatened before bolting.
species.ecological_role: Herbivore and prey animal — a food source for hawks, owls, bobcats, and snakes.
species.plant_connections: Feeds on grasses, sedges, and wetland plants.

size.lifespan: commonly 1 to 4 years in the wild.

species.habitat: Marshes, wet thickets, pond edges, and dense vegetation near water.
species.where_to_look: Along pond edges and in dense low vegetation, especially at dawn or dusk.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, most visible at dawn and dusk.

seasonality.note: Crepuscular; rarely seen in midday.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: Unlike the familiar cottontail of open fields, the Marsh Rabbit is closely tied to wet ground and dense vegetation. It moves through grasses and thickets and can swim strongly when crossing water or escaping danger.
Its food is vegetation growing in and around wetlands, including grasses, sedges and other green plant material.

how_it_lives.label: Nesting on the ground
how_it_lives.text: Females place shallow nests on the ground in dense cover, lining them with grass and fur.

It swims, which almost no other rabbit does. A Marsh Rabbit under threat may go straight into the water and swim with only its nose above the surface, or sit motionless in the shallows among the stems until whatever worried it has gone.

how_to_know_it.label: Size and shape
how_to_know_it.text: Small and compact, about fourteen to sixteen inches long, with noticeably shorter ears than an Eastern Cottontail.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Dark brown to blackish-brown, generally darker than a cottontail.

how_to_know_it.label: Tail
how_to_know_it.text: Small and inconspicuous, gray-brown rather than the cottontail's obvious white puff.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look near dense vegetation around wet areas for a small, dark rabbit with short ears and no conspicuous white cottontail. Marsh Rabbits may also walk rather than making the long bounding hops associated with many rabbits.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look along dense, damp vegetation near pond margins, wet swales and other low areas. Marsh Rabbits usually remain close to thick plant cover and water rather than feeding far out on an exposed lawn.
Present year-round in Florida but most active around dusk, dawn and at night. Daytime sightings are possible, especially where dense vegetation provides nearby cover.

what_it_does_here.text: A native wetland herbivore and an important prey animal for owls, foxes, bobcats, alligators and other predators.

what_it_does_here.label: Cover and food are the same plants
what_it_does_here.text: Wetland plants provide both food and shelter. Marsh Rabbits eat grasses, sedges and other green vegetation and stay close to dense plant growth where they can feed while remaining near cover. Maintaining thick, low vegetation around wet areas preserves the structure this rabbit depends on.

Marsh Rabbits are strong swimmers and usually stay close to water, using wetlands as both feeding habitat and escape cover.
They feed on grasses, sedges and other vegetation growing in and around wetlands.

species.teaser: A Marsh Rabbit will readily enter the water, swimming across wetland channels to escape danger or move between feeding areas.

quick_hits: Ruby-throated Hummingbirds can hover almost motionless at a flower while beating their wings about 53 times each second.
A male's throat can flash brilliant red and then look nearly black when the viewing angle changes. The color comes from microscopic feather structure interacting with light.
Some migrants cross the Gulf of Mexico in a single over-water flight, while others follow the Gulf Coast around it.
It weighs about as much as a penny but may chase much larger birds away from a productive flower patch.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. Breeds across the eastern U.S. and southern Canada; winters in Central America. Present in Florida mainly during migration and winter, though some breed in the northern part of the state.
more_information: The ruby-throated hummingbird is the default hummingbird of the eastern United States — the only species that regularly breeds east of the Mississippi. Its tiny size, hovering flight, and iridescent plumage make it one of the most charismatic visitors to any garden.

To fuel its metabolism, it visits hundreds of flowers per day and also eats tiny insects and spiders for protein. Its heart beats over 1,200 times per minute in flight, and it enters a torpor-like state overnight to conserve energy.
In the Bradenton area it is most likely during fall and spring migration, with some wintering birds.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Tiny — about 3 inches long, weighing roughly a tenth of an ounce.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Iridescent green above, white below, with a brilliant ruby-red throat (gorget) that can look black.

blocks.label: Female
blocks.text: Green above, white below, no red throat.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Hovers in place, wings beating so fast they blur.

identification.what_to_look_for: A tiny hovering bird at flowers or feeders. Males flash a ruby-red throat in the right light. Listen for the humming of the wings.

species.diet: Nectar from flowers and feeders; tiny insects and spiders for protein.
species.behavior: Hovers to feed. Fiercely territorial — chases other hummingbirds and larger birds from flower patches. Incredibly fast and agile.
species.sounds: A rapid, chittering series of notes; the hum of the wings is often the first clue.
species.ecological_role: Pollinator of tubular flowers; insect predator. A key player in the pollination of many native wildflowers.
species.plant_connections: Visits many native and garden flowers, especially tubular red, orange, and pink blooms.

size.length: 3 to 3.5 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 3 to 5 years, occasionally much longer.

species.habitat: Gardens, woodland edges, and flowery areas during migration.
species.where_to_look: Around the flower beds, especially tubular blooms. Listen for the wing hum.
species.when_to_see: Most likely during fall and spring migration; some winter here. A seasonal visitor.

seasonality.note: Arrives in March as spring migration moves north; passes through again August through October heading south. A small number may linger into winter in sheltered coastal spots, but reliable presence for Manatee County is March through October.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: Nectar supplies much of the bird's energy, but Ruby-throated Hummingbirds also catch tiny insects and spiders, sometimes taking insects directly from spider webs.
Feeds while hovering and frequently returns to favored flowers. Individuals may defend productive feeding areas by chasing other hummingbirds and larger birds.

how_it_lives.label: A nest built with spider silk
how_it_lives.text: The female builds a tiny nest on a slender tree branch using plant down held together with spider silk. The silk lets the nest stretch as the young grow.

The metabolism sets the whole schedule. It visits hundreds of flowers a day and takes small insects and spiders for protein, its heart runs past 1,200 beats a minute in flight, and it drops into a torpid state overnight to avoid starving before morning.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Tiny — only about three inches long, with a wingspan around four inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Male
how_to_know_it.text: Green above and pale below, with an iridescent red throat that can look black when the light is wrong.

how_to_know_it.label: Female
how_to_know_it.text: Green above and whitish below, without the male's red throat; the outer tail feathers show white tips.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Can hover in place, stop abruptly and fly backward.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Calls are rapid, high chips and chatters. At close range, the wing hum may reveal a bird before you see it.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Watch flowering beds for a tiny green bird hovering at tubular flowers, then darting to a nearby perch. Adult males show the red throat only when the light strikes it correctly.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Watch flower beds and woodland edges, especially where tubular blooms are producing nectar. A feeding bird often returns repeatedly to a productive patch and perches nearby between visits.
Most likely during spring and autumn migration. Ruby-throated Hummingbirds can also occur along the Gulf Coast outside the main migration periods, so an individual outside those windows is possible.

what_it_does_here.text: Carries pollen between flowers while feeding on nectar, and also consumes tiny insects and spiders.

what_it_does_here.label: Flowers, trees and spider silk
what_it_does_here.text: Flowers provide the high-energy nectar that fuels hummingbird flight. Tubular red, orange and pink blooms are frequently used, but hummingbirds visit flowers of other colors as well. Trees provide resting places and, on the breeding grounds, slender branches for the female's spider-silk-bound nest.
This is the only hummingbird that regularly breeds east of the Mississippi, so in this half of the country it is simply the hummingbird.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Flowering plants supply everything this bird needs. Watch without crowding one that is feeding.

at_a_glance.text: Ruby-throated Hummingbirds can hover almost motionless at a flower while beating their wings about 53 times each second.
A male's throat can flash brilliant red and then look nearly black when the viewing angle changes. The color comes from microscopic feather structure interacting with light.
Some migrants cross the Gulf of Mexico in a single over-water flight, while others follow the Gulf Coast around it.
It weighs about as much as a penny but may chase much larger birds away from a productive flower patch.

species.teaser: A Ruby-throated Hummingbird passing through Florida may continue around the Gulf Coast or launch directly across the Gulf of Mexico toward Central America.

quick_hits: Brown Pelicans hunt by plunging headfirst from the air after fish. American White Pelicans feed mainly from the surface instead.
DDT once caused severe breeding failures in Brown Pelicans. Populations recovered strongly after the pesticide was banned.
The throat pouch acts as a scoop. After a dive, the pelican drains the water before swallowing the fish.
Brown Pelicans often fly just above the water in lines, alternating wingbeats with long glides.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the coasts of the Americas. In Florida it is a year-round resident of bays, estuaries, beaches and nearshore waters.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Gray-brown body with a pale head and long gray bill. Breeding adults develop richer yellow and chestnut colors on the head and neck.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Often flies low over the water in lines, alternating flaps and glides.

blocks.label: Feeding
blocks.text: Plunge-dives headfirst from the air.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large brown-gray pelican flying low over nearby water or plunging headfirst after fish. American White Pelicans are much whiter and usually feed from the water's surface rather than diving.

species.diet: Mostly fish caught by plunge-diving.
species.behavior: Plunge-dives for fish, rests on pilings and other exposed structures, and often travels low over the water in loose lines.
species.ecological_role: A predator of schooling fish in coastal and estuarine waters.
species.plant_connections: Brown Pelicans nest colonially on coastal islands, using mangroves, shrubs or low trees where available, as well as the ground on suitable islands. Coastal vegetation provides nest structure and helps isolate colonies from disturbance and land predators.

size.length: Wingspan about six to seven feet.

species.habitat: Coastal waters, bays, estuaries, and nearshore areas.
species.where_to_look: Look overhead for birds moving between nearby coastal waters. Brown Pelicans are primarily birds of bays, estuaries and the coast, so Palma Sola sightings are more likely to be flyovers than birds using the park ponds.
species.when_to_see: Present year-round around the Bradenton coast. Palma Sola has only one recorded sighting, so park appearances should be considered rare.

seasonality.note: Year-round coastal resident; Palma Sola currently has only one documented sighting.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Never offer fish by hand, and keep discarded fishing line and hooks out of the water and shoreline.

conservation.status: A major U.S. conservation recovery. DDT caused widespread reproductive failure by thinning eggshells. After DDT was banned in 1972, populations recovered; the southeastern population, including Florida, was federally delisted in 1985, and the remaining listed populations were removed in 2009. Brown Pelicans remain protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much larger and almost entirely white, with black flight feathers. White Pelicans usually scoop fish from the surface; Brown Pelicans characteristically plunge-dive.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: A hunting bird spots fish from above, folds its wings and plunges into the water. The throat pouch scoops fish and water; the water is drained before the catch is swallowed.
Between feeding bouts, Brown Pelicans rest on pilings, docks, sandbars and other open sites or travel low over coastal water.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: A heavy coastal bird with a wingspan of six to seven feet.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Gray-brown body with a pale head and a long gray bill. Breeding adults develop richer yellow and chestnut tones on the head and neck.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Travels low over the water in loose lines, alternating a few wingbeats with a long glide.

how_to_know_it.label: Feeding
how_to_know_it.text: Plunge-dives headfirst from the air. No other large waterbird here feeds that way.
Look overhead rather than along the shoreline — a park sighting is almost always a bird crossing between coastal waters.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Brown Pelicans belong to the bay and the beach, not to park ponds. The realistic sighting at Palma Sola is a bird passing overhead, so this is one to catch by looking up.
They are present along the Bradenton coast all year, but the park has a single documented record. Seeing one here is luck rather than timing.

what_it_does_here.text: Brown Pelicans hunt schooling fish in bays and nearshore water. The throat pouch works as a scoop: after a dive the bird drains the water out over the edge of the bill before swallowing.

They nest in colonies on coastal islands, building in mangroves, shrubs and low trees where those exist and on open ground where they do not. Coastal vegetation gives the nests structure and keeps the colony separated from disturbance and from land predators.

The species is also one of the clearest conservation recoveries in the country. DDT thinned pelican eggshells badly enough to cause widespread breeding failure; after the pesticide was banned in 1972 numbers climbed back, and Florida's population was removed from the federal endangered list in 1985.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Never offer fish by hand, and keep discarded fishing line and hooks out of the water and off the shoreline. Line and tackle are among the most serious hazards pelicans face.

at_a_glance.text: Brown Pelicans hunt by plunging headfirst from the air after fish. American White Pelicans feed mainly from the surface instead.
DDT once caused severe breeding failures in Brown Pelicans. Populations recovered strongly after the pesticide was banned.
The throat pouch acts as a scoop. After a dive, the pelican drains the water before swallowing the fish.
Brown Pelicans often fly just above the water in lines, alternating wingbeats with long glides.

species.teaser: Brown Pelicans hunt from the air, folding their wings and plunging headfirst into the water after fish.

quick_hits: A compact white egret standing on dry grass rather than at the water's edge is usually a Cattle Egret.
It feeds by following something larger. Cattle, a mower or a tractor pushes insects out of the grass ahead of it, and the egret walks behind picking them off.
Cattle Egrets reached the Americas without human help. The species spread from Africa to South America in the late 1800s and had reached Florida by the middle of the twentieth century.
Breeding adults develop orange-buff patches on the crown, back and breast, and the bill and legs brighten.
species.range_and_origin: Originally an Old World species. It crossed to South America in the late 1800s and spread north, reaching Florida by the mid-twentieth century. Now a common year-round resident.
more_information: The spread across the Atlantic appears to have happened without human transport. Birds are thought to have crossed from Africa to South America under their own power in the late 1800s, then expanded north through the Americas over the following decades.

blocks.label: Where it stands
blocks.text: Dry fields and lawns rather than shallow water. That alone separates it from the park's other white waders most of the time.

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Compact and stocky, with a shorter, thicker neck than a Snowy or Great Egret.

blocks.label: Bill and legs
blocks.text: Short, stout and yellow to orange. Not the long black bill of a Snowy Egret.

blocks.label: Breeding adults
blocks.text: Orange-buff patches appear on the crown, back and breast.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a small, thick-necked white bird walking on open grass with a short yellow bill. If it is following a mower or a large animal, that is the bird.

species.diet: Grasshoppers, crickets, flies and other insects flushed from grass, with small vertebrates taken occasionally.
species.behavior: Feeds on foot in open grass, following livestock, mowers or other disturbance that flushes insects. Gregarious, usually in loose groups, and colonial when nesting.
species.ecological_role: A predator of insects in open grassland and pasture rather than in water.
species.plant_connections: This egret separates its two lives between very different plants. It feeds on open mown or grazed grass, where short turf lets it walk and see what is flushed out, but it nests colonially in trees and shrubs near water, often alongside other wading birds. Neither habitat works without the other.

size.length: About twenty inches tall, with a wingspan around three feet.

species.habitat: Fields, lawns, pastures, and open ground — near livestock or mowers.
species.where_to_look: Check open grassy areas rather than the pond edges — especially anywhere the grass is being cut or disturbed. Cattle Egrets often feed in loose groups.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola has only a single record, so treat it as an occasional visitor rather than a bird to expect.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local pattern.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. If the bird changes its behavior or moves away as you approach, give it more room.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Snowy Egrets are slimmer with a long black bill, black legs and yellow feet, and they feed in shallow water. Cattle Egrets are stocky, short-billed and usually on dry grass.
Great Egrets are much larger and taller with a long yellow bill and black legs. A Cattle Egret is roughly half the height and thick-necked.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: It hunts by following something bigger. Cattle, a tractor, a mower — anything that walks through grass and flushes insects out ahead of it. The egret walks behind and picks off what jumps.
Grasshoppers, crickets and flies make up most of the diet. Usually in loose groups, and colonial when nesting.

It feeds on open mown or grazed grass, where short turf lets it walk and see what is flushed out, but it nests colonially in trees and shrubs near water, often alongside other wading birds. Neither habitat works without the other.

This egret arrived under its own power. An Old World species, it crossed the Atlantic to South America in the late 1800s, spread north, and reached Florida by the middle of the twentieth century — one of very few birds to colonize a new continent without human help.

at_a_glance.text: A compact white egret standing on dry grass rather than at the water's edge is usually a Cattle Egret.
It feeds by following something larger. Cattle, a mower or a tractor pushes insects out of the grass ahead of it, and the egret walks behind picking them off.
Cattle Egrets reached the Americas without human help. The species spread from Africa to South America in the late 1800s and had reached Florida by the middle of the twentieth century.
Breeding adults develop orange-buff patches on the crown, back and breast, and the bill and legs brighten.

species.teaser: The one egret you are more likely to see on a mown lawn than at the water's edge. It follows whatever is flushing insects out of the grass.

quick_hits: A medium white egret with a black bill, black legs, and bright yellow feet — as if it is wearing golden slippers.
The bright yellow feet are a feeding tool: it shuffles them through the water to stir up small fish and shrimp, then strikes.
A century ago it was nearly wiped out for its lacy breeding plumes, just like the great egret — and its recovery helped fuel the early Audubon movement.
Smaller and more active than the great egret, it dashes and darts through the shallows rather than standing still.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. Year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The plume trade nearly ended this species. Breeding birds grow fine recurved feathers that were worth more than their weight in gold to the hat trade in the late 1800s, and the campaign to stop the killing became one of the founding causes of the Audubon movement.

blocks.label: Feet
blocks.text: Bright yellow — the 'golden slippers.' The single best field mark.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Black and slender.

blocks.label: Legs
blocks.text: Black.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Medium — about 24 inches, smaller than the great egret.

identification.what_to_look_for: A medium white egret actively running through shallows. Check the feet: if they are yellow, it is a snowy egret.

species.diet: Small fish, shrimp, crabs, insects, and aquatic invertebrates — often flushed with foot-shuffling.
species.behavior: Active, energetic hunter — runs, shuffles feet, and strikes rapidly. More animated than other egrets.
species.sounds: Generally quiet; some harsh squawks at the colony.
species.ecological_role: A predator of small fish, shrimp and aquatic insects in shallow water. Its nesting colonies concentrate many birds in a few trees, which in turn attracts predators and scavengers.
species.plant_connections: Wetland plants matter at both ends of the day. The egret hunts along the vegetated shallows where small fish and shrimp shelter among stems and roots, and it nests colonially in trees and shrubs standing over or beside water, where the nests are hard for ground predators to reach.

size.length: 22 to 26 inches
size.lifespan: commonly up to 17 years.

species.habitat: Wetlands, ponds, marshes, tidal flats — any shallow water.
species.where_to_look: Work the shallow edges — pond margins, wet flats, anywhere the water is only a few inches deep. Look for the egret that will not stand still. If the feet are yellow, it is this one.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Great Egrets are considerably larger, with a yellow bill and black feet, and they hunt by standing still. The Snowy Egret has a black bill, yellow feet and rarely stops moving.
Young Little Blue Herons are also white but have dull greenish legs and a pale bill with a dark tip, and they feed slowly rather than dashing about.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: The busiest of the egrets. Where a Great Egret stands still and waits, this one runs, stops, stirs the bottom with a bright yellow foot to flush something out, and stabs at whatever moves.
Small fish, shrimp, crabs and insects. The foot-shuffling is the giveaway — no other white heron here feeds like that.

how_to_know_it.label: Feet
how_to_know_it.text: Bright yellow — the golden slippers, and the single best field mark.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill and legs
how_to_know_it.text: Both black, the bill slender and sharp.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Medium, around two feet tall — noticeably smaller than a Great Egret.
The other giveaway is temperament. This is the white egret that will not stand still.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Work the shallow edges — pond margins and wet flats where the water is only a few inches deep.
Present year-round, turning up occasionally rather than on every visit.

what_it_does_here.text: The yellow feet are a tool, not decoration. The egret shuffles one foot through the silt to panic small fish and shrimp out of cover, then strikes at whatever breaks. It works the vegetated shallows for the same reason — stems and roots are where the prey is hiding.

It nests in colonies in trees and shrubs standing over or beside water, out of reach of anything hunting from the ground. A colony packs many birds into a few trees, which draws its own crowd of predators and scavengers.

A century ago the species was nearly finished. Breeding birds grow fine recurved plumes that were worth more than their weight in gold to the hat trade of the late 1800s, and the campaign to stop the killing became one of the founding causes of the Audubon movement.

at_a_glance.text: A medium white egret with a black bill, black legs and bright yellow feet — as if it were wearing golden slippers.
The yellow feet are a hunting tool: it shuffles them through the shallows to stir prey into moving.
Smaller and far more active than a Great Egret, dashing through the shallows rather than standing still.

species.teaser: It stirs the bottom with one bright yellow foot to panic small fish into moving, then strikes at whatever breaks cover.

quick_hits: Adult Little Blue Herons are dark slate-blue with a purplish head and neck, and they usually hunt with slow, deliberate movements in shallow water.
Young Little Blue Herons are white. As they acquire adult plumage, blue feathers replace the white in patches, creating a distinctive blue-and-white 'calico' stage.
White juveniles are more readily tolerated among feeding Snowy Egrets than dark adults are, and young Little Blues can feed more successfully while accompanying those flocks.
Little Blue Herons are State-designated Threatened in Florida. Loss and degradation of wetland feeding and nesting habitat remain concerns.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. In Florida, Little Blue Herons occur year-round in freshwater, brackish and saltwater wetlands.

blocks.label: Adult
blocks.text: Dark slate-blue body with a purple-maroon head and neck. The bill is pale blue-gray at the base and dark at the tip.

blocks.label: Juvenile
blocks.text: White overall, with greenish legs and a two-toned gray-and-dark bill.

blocks.label: Molting immature
blocks.text: Blue and white in irregular patches. These transitional birds are often called calico Little Blue Herons.

identification.what_to_look_for: Adults are small dark-blue herons with a purple-toned head and a two-colored bill. White juveniles can resemble Snowy Egrets, but Little Blues have greenish legs and a thicker bill that is pale at the base and dark at the tip. Their feeding movements are also usually slower and more deliberate.

species.diet: Small fish, amphibians, crayfish, shrimp, crabs and aquatic insects.
species.behavior: Little Blue Herons usually forage slowly and deliberately, wading through shallow water or pausing to watch for prey. They take small fish, amphibians, crustaceans and insects.
species.ecological_role: A predator of small fish, amphibians, crustaceans and insects in shallow wetlands.
species.plant_connections: Little Blue Herons nest in colonies in low trees and shrubs, often on islands or over flooded ground where water helps limit access by land predators. The birds gather sticks and greener plant material for the nest. Around feeding areas, emergent vegetation provides cover for the small fish and invertebrates they hunt.

size.length: About two feet tall, with a wingspan a little over three feet.

species.habitat: Freshwater and saltwater wetlands, pond edges, marshes.
species.where_to_look: Look in shallow water along pond edges and wetland margins. Little Blue Herons usually move slowly, watching the water with the bill angled downward before making a short strike.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola has only a few records, so it should be considered an occasional park visitor rather than something to expect on every visit.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola has too few observations to define a local seasonal pattern.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Give feeding or roosting birds enough room to continue what they are doing without moving away from you.

conservation.status: State-designated Threatened in Florida and globally classified as Least Concern. FWC identifies habitat degradation, disturbance, reduced prey availability and other wetland pressures among potential threats.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: A juvenile Little Blue Heron is white like a Snowy Egret, but has greenish legs and a thicker two-toned bill. Snowy Egrets have black legs with bright yellow feet and usually forage more actively.
Adult Tricolored Herons are also blue-gray but have a bright white belly and a white stripe down the front of the neck. Adult Little Blues are dark below as well as above.

quick_hits: Look below a regular owl roost for compact pellets of fur and bone. Owls swallow much of their prey whole and later cough up the parts they cannot digest.
The deep series of hoots heard after dark is one of the easiest ways to detect a Great Horned Owl.
Its diet is exceptionally broad for a raptor, ranging from mice and rabbits to skunks, waterbirds and other birds of prey.
Great Horned Owls begin nesting unusually early. In Florida, nesting can start in December, often in an old nest originally built by a hawk, crow, heron or squirrel.
species.range_and_origin: Native across the Americas. Year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The great horned owl is the apex nocturnal predator of Florida's woodlands. It is large, powerful, and unfussy about what it eats — mammals, birds, reptiles, and even other raptors are on the menu.
It does not build its own nest. Instead it takes over the nests of hawks, herons, or squirrels, which is one reason it nests so early — it needs to claim a nest before the original builder returns.
The deep hooting call is one of the signature sounds of the natural night. Pairs often duet, with the female's voice pitched higher than the male's.

Its January nesting is the reason for a small local ritual: most winters, photographers appear along the park's northern edge with long lenses, waiting on a nest nearby. Nearly every great horned owl record from around Palma Sola falls between December and February.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Large — about 22 inches tall with a 4-foot wingspan.

blocks.label: Ear tufts
blocks.text: Prominent feathered 'horns' on the head.

blocks.label: Eyes
blocks.text: Large, forward-facing, bright yellow.

blocks.label: Sound
blocks.text: Deep, resonant 'hoo-hoo-hoooo hoo-hoo' — the classic owl hoot.

identification.what_to_look_for: A large, bulky owl with ear tufts, most often detected by its deep hooting at dusk or dawn. Daytime sightings are rare — look for a large shape pressed against a tree trunk.

species.diet: Mammals, birds, reptiles — including skunks, rabbits, hawks, and other owls. One of the least picky predators.
species.behavior: Nocturnal hunter, perch-and-pounce. Roosts during the day pressed against tree trunks. Nests very early (January–February in Florida).
species.sounds: A deep, resonant hooting: 'hoo-hoo-hoooo hoo-hoo.' Also hisses and bill-clacks when disturbed.
species.ecological_role: Apex nocturnal predator — controls populations of rodents, rabbits, and other prey.

size.length: 18 to 25 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 13 years or more in the wild.

species.habitat: Woodlands, swamps, and suburban areas with large trees.
species.where_to_look: Listen at dusk for the hooting. Scan large tree trunks for a roosting shape during the day.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, but nocturnal — most likely heard at dusk or early morning.

seasonality.note: Great Horned Owls nest early in Florida, but Palma Sola currently has too few formal observations to define a local seasonal peak.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Also has ear tufts and yellow eyes but is dramatically smaller — only about eight or nine inches tall. Great Horned Owls are large, heavy-bodied birds with wingspans around four feet.
