how_it_lives.text: Usually hunts from a perch at night, flying down or out after prey. Mostly mammals and birds, including rabbits, rodents, skunks and waterbirds, with reptiles, amphibians and other prey also taken.

how_it_lives.label: A borrowed nest
how_it_lives.text: Great Horned Owls usually take over an existing nest rather than building one. An old stick nest made by a hawk, crow, heron or squirrel may be occupied, and tree cavities and broken snags are also used.

It builds nothing of its own. A Great Horned Owl takes over the old nest of a hawk, heron or squirrel, and that is much of why it nests so early — the nest has to be claimed before whoever built it comes back for it.
Pairs often duet through the winter nights, and it is the female whose voice is pitched higher.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: A large, bulky owl with a wingspan around four feet.

how_to_know_it.label: Ear tufts
how_to_know_it.text: Two prominent feather tufts on the head. They are not ears.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Mottled brown and gray, with a pale throat, a broad facial disc and bright yellow eyes.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A deep series of resonant hoots. Pairs may call back and forth, with the female's voice usually higher than the male's.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a large, bulky owl with prominent ear tufts and yellow eyes. By day it may roost against a trunk or inside dense foliage; after dark, listen for deep hooting.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Listen around large trees at dusk and after dark. By day, scan substantial trunks, dense crowns and old nest structures for a resting bird.
A year-round Florida resident, but mainly nocturnal, so most detections are by voice. Palma Sola currently has too few formal observations to define a local seasonal peak.

Nearly every Great Horned Owl record from around Palma Sola falls between December and February. Most winters, photographers appear along the park's northern edge with long lenses, waiting on a nest nearby — if you see the tripods, someone has already found the owl.

what_it_does_here.text: A large nighttime predator that takes mammals, birds, reptiles and other animals across a wide range of habitats.

what_it_does_here.label: Big trees, old nests
what_it_does_here.text: Large trees provide both daytime roosts and nest support. Because the owl rarely builds its own nest, the presence of old stick nests, cavities and broken snags matters as much as the trees themselves.

take_care.label: The risk
take_care.text: Do not approach a nest or try to handle an owl. Adults defend themselves and their young with powerful talons.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Keep your distance, especially near a nest, and do not gather beneath a roost for photographs. If an owl becomes alert to you or leaves its perch, you are too close.

take_care.label: Rodent poison
take_care.text: An owl that eats poisoned rodents is poisoned in turn. Rodent bait is one of the main hazards to owls living near people.

at_a_glance.text: Look below a regular owl roost for compact pellets of fur and bone. Owls swallow much of their prey whole and later cough up the parts they cannot digest.
The deep series of hoots heard after dark is one of the easiest ways to detect a Great Horned Owl.
Its diet is exceptionally broad for a raptor, ranging from mice and rabbits to skunks, waterbirds and other birds of prey.
Great Horned Owls begin nesting unusually early. In Florida, nesting can start in December, often in an old nest originally built by a hawk, crow, heron or squirrel.

species.teaser: Sometimes the first sign of a Great Horned Owl is on the ground: compact pellets of fur and bone beneath a daytime roost.

quick_hits: A medium-sized hawk built for speed in tight spaces — long tail, short rounded wings, and the agility to chase songbirds through dense trees.
If the birds at a feeder suddenly vanish, a Cooper's hawk is often the reason.
Adults have a blue-gray back and rusty-barred chest; immatures are brown and streaky — a different look entirely.
It has adapted well to suburban life, and backyard bird feeders are effectively hawk feeders from its perspective.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Present year-round in Florida, with additional birds arriving in winter from the north.
more_information: Flying at speed through branches is dangerous work. Studies of Cooper's Hawk skeletons have found a high rate of healed fractures in the chest, evidence of collisions survived during pursuit.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: Long tail with a rounded tip, short rounded wings — built for agility.

blocks.label: Adult
blocks.text: Blue-gray above, rusty-barred chest, dark cap.

blocks.label: Immature
blocks.text: Brown above, white below with brown streaks.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Fast, agile, with quick wingbeats and glides through trees.

identification.what_to_look_for: A sleek hawk with a long tail gliding through trees or perched quietly near a bird feeder. Adults are blue-gray and rusty; immatures are brown and streaky.

species.diet: Mostly birds — doves, robins, jays, starlings, and smaller songbirds. Also takes squirrels and chipmunks.
species.behavior: Ambush hunter, using cover to approach prey. Fast, agile flight through dense trees. Often perches quietly near feeders.
species.sounds: A sharp, rapid 'kak-kak-kak' — most vocal near the nest in spring.
species.ecological_role: A predator of birds and small mammals in wooded and suburban areas. Its hunting shapes the behavior of smaller birds, which fall silent and freeze when one is nearby.
species.plant_connections: Trees are what make this hawk possible. Short wings and a long tail are built for flying fast through branches rather than over open ground, so wooded edges and dense canopy are hunting habitat, not obstacles. Cooper's Hawks also build their stick nests high in trees, usually against the trunk.

size.length: About fifteen to twenty inches long, with a wingspan around two and a half feet. Females are noticeably larger than males.

species.habitat: Woodlands, parks, and suburban areas with trees and prey.
species.where_to_look: Scan canopy edges and quiet perches near where small birds gather. The sudden silence of a noisy garden is often the first clue, before you see the hawk at all.
species.when_to_see: Year-round, with more birds present in winter.

seasonality.note: Northern migrants supplement residents in winter.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance. A hunting hawk that notices you will usually leave, and it may have been waiting a long time for that chance.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Red-shouldered Hawks are broader-winged, soar in the open and call loudly overhead. A Cooper's Hawk has short rounded wings and a long tail, and usually hunts from cover rather than soaring.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: An ambush hunter that uses cover to get close, then comes fast. It flies through dense trees at speed, which most hawks its size will not attempt.
Mostly other birds — doves, robins, jays, starlings, smaller songbirds — plus squirrels and chipmunks. If one is perched quietly near your feeder, that is why.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: A long tail with a rounded tip and short rounded wings — the build of a bird that flies through branches rather than over them.

how_to_know_it.label: Adult
how_to_know_it.text: Blue-gray above, rusty barring across the chest, dark cap.

how_to_know_it.label: Immature
how_to_know_it.text: Brown above, white below with brown streaks.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A sharp, rapid kak-kak-kak, mostly near the nest in spring.
Females are noticeably larger than males — enough that a big female and a small male can look like two different birds.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Scan canopy edges and quiet perches near wherever small birds are gathering. A sudden burst of alarm calls, or small birds abruptly dropping into cover, can be the clue that a hawk has arrived.
Present year-round, with more birds around in winter when northern migrants add to the residents.

what_it_does_here.text: Trees are what make the hawk possible. Short wings and a long tail are built for flying hard through branches, so wooded edges and dense canopy are hunting ground rather than obstacles, and the stick nest goes high in a tree against the trunk.
Flying at speed through branches is dangerous work. Studies of Cooper's Hawk skeletons have found a high rate of healed fractures in the chest — collisions the birds survived.

at_a_glance.text: A medium-sized hawk built for speed in tight spaces — long tail, short rounded wings, and the agility to chase songbirds through dense trees.
If every bird at a feeder vanishes at once and the garden goes quiet, a Cooper's Hawk is often the reason.
Adults are blue-gray above with a rusty-barred chest. Immatures are brown and streaky, and look like a different bird entirely.

species.teaser: If every bird at a feeder vanishes at once and the garden goes quiet, look up. A Cooper's Hawk is often the reason.

quick_hits: A repeated, descending kee-aah is the Red-shouldered Hawk's familiar call and is often the first clue that one is nearby.
It is strongly associated with wooded habitats near water, often hunting from a perch beneath or within the canopy.
Adults show reddish barring across the chest and translucent crescent-shaped panels near the wingtips in flight.
Blue Jays frequently imitate the Red-shouldered Hawk's call, so a convincing kee-aah does not always belong to a hawk.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. A common year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The red-shouldered hawk is the hawk of Florida's neighborhoods and wooded parks. It is more tied to trees and water than the open-country red-tailed hawk, so it turns up regularly in suburban landscapes with mature canopy.
It hunts from low perches, dropping onto lizards, frogs, snakes, crayfish, and small mammals — prey it spots by watching the ground from a branch.
Its loud, carrying call is one of the most commonly heard raptor sounds in Florida, and blue jays mimic it often enough that the call alone is not a guarantee.

blocks.label: Chest
blocks.text: Reddish-orange barring across the breast.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Translucent crescent-shaped panel near the wingtips; banded tail.

blocks.label: Sound
blocks.text: Loud, repeated 'kee-ahh' — carrying and distinctive.

blocks.label: Habitat
blocks.text: Perches in wooded areas near water, not typically soaring high over open fields.

identification.what_to_look_for: A medium hawk perched in a tree near water, with a barred reddish chest. The loud 'kee-ahh' call is often the first clue.

species.diet: Lizards, frogs, snakes, crayfish, small mammals, and insects — hunted from a perch.
species.behavior: Perch-hunts from mid-canopy, dropping onto prey below. Very vocal. Pairs often call back and forth.
species.sounds: A loud, descending 'kee-ahh, kee-ahh' — one of the most recognizable hawk calls in the eastern U.S.
species.ecological_role: Top predator of small vertebrates in wooded habitats; helps control lizard and rodent populations.
species.plant_connections: Nests in large trees; hunts from canopy perches.

size.length: 17 to 24 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 15 to 20 years.

species.habitat: Wooded areas near water — swamps, riparian corridors, suburban neighborhoods with mature trees.
species.where_to_look: Listen for the 'kee-ahh' call in the canopy near the ponds.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, vocal and visible in every season.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident. Current Palma Sola records come from one observer and are too limited to define local frequency.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Longer-tailed and more slender, built for chasing birds through trees. Red-shouldered Hawks are broader-winged and show reddish barring plus pale wing crescents.
Usually more associated with open areas, with broader, paler underwings and no translucent wing crescents. Adults often show a reddish tail.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: From a perch inside the canopy, a Red-shouldered Hawk watches the ground and shallow water for frogs, lizards, snakes, crayfish, rodents and other prey, then drops down to capture it.
Pairs are highly vocal and may call back and forth across a territory.
It hunts from low perches, watching the ground from a branch and dropping onto lizards, frogs, snakes, crayfish and small mammals.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: Medium-sized, broad-winged hawk with a fairly long, banded tail.

how_to_know_it.label: Chest
how_to_know_it.text: Adults have reddish-orange barring across the breast.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Translucent crescent-shaped panels near the wingtips and a strongly banded tail.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A loud, descending kee-aah, often repeated several times. Blue Jays can imitate it closely.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a medium-sized hawk perched inside mature trees, especially near ponds or other wet areas. Adults have reddish barring below; in flight, look for the pale crescents near the wingtips and strongly banded tail. The repeated kee-aah often reveals the bird first.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The loud, carrying call is one of the most familiar raptor sounds in Florida — but Blue Jays imitate it well and often, so the call on its own is not proof.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in mature trees around ponds, wooded edges and other damp areas. Red-shouldered Hawks often watch the ground from a mid-level perch rather than sitting conspicuously in completely open country.
A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola has several records, but all of them come from one observer, so the dataset is not strong enough to call the species reliably present.

what_it_does_here.label: Trees and water together
what_it_does_here.text: Large trees provide both nest sites and hunting perches. Red-shouldered Hawks are strongly associated with mature wooded habitat near water, where branches give them elevated views of prey moving through the ground layer and wetland edge.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Keep back from an active nest. If the adults repeatedly call or circle because you are there, move away.

at_a_glance.text: A repeated, descending kee-aah is the Red-shouldered Hawk's familiar call and is often the first clue that one is nearby.
It is strongly associated with wooded habitats near water, often hunting from a perch beneath or within the canopy.
Adults show reddish barring across the chest and translucent crescent-shaped panels near the wingtips in flight.
Blue Jays frequently imitate the Red-shouldered Hawk's call, so a convincing kee-aah does not always belong to a hawk.

species.teaser: If you hear a loud kee-aah from the trees, look for a Red-shouldered Hawk — but keep Blue Jay mimicry in mind.

quick_hits: A stocky blackbird with a glossy brown head (male) and a drab gray-brown body (female) — smaller and chunkier than a grackle.
It is North America's most notorious brood parasite: it lays its eggs in the nests of other birds and leaves them to do all the work.
Over 200 species have been documented raising cowbird young, often at the expense of their own chicks.
The strategy evolved on the Great Plains, where cowbirds followed bison herds and could not stay in one place long enough to raise their own young.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Year-round resident in much of the southeastern U.S. including Florida.
more_information: Some host species have learned to answer. Yellow Warblers will build a new nest floor over a cowbird egg and start again, occasionally producing a stack of several storeys.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Glossy black body with a rich chocolate-brown head.

blocks.label: Female
blocks.text: Plain gray-brown all over — easy to overlook.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: Stocky, short-tailed, with a thick conical bill.

blocks.label: Behavior
blocks.text: Often on the ground near livestock or in mixed blackbird flocks.

identification.what_to_look_for: A stocky blackbird with a brown head (male) or a plain gray-brown bird (female), often feeding on the ground in open areas.

species.diet: Seeds, grain, and insects — forages on the ground, often near livestock.
species.behavior: Feeds on the ground. Males display with a gurgling song and a bow. Females scout nests of other species.
species.sounds: Male gives a liquid, gurgling 'glug-glug-gleee.' Female makes a dry chatter.
species.ecological_role: A seed and insect eater, and a brood parasite whose eggs are raised by other species. Where host songbirds are already under pressure, that parasitism can add to it.
species.plant_connections: Cowbirds feed mainly on the seeds of grasses and weeds, so open, seeding ground is their habitat rather than dense planting. The birds they parasitize are mostly shrub- and tree-nesting songbirds, which means the edge between open ground and woody cover is where the two meet.

size.length: About seven to eight inches long, with a wingspan around a foot.

species.habitat: Open ground, fields, lawns, edges, and anywhere near livestock or feeders.
species.where_to_look: Look on open lawns and short grass, often walking rather than hopping, and often mixed in with grackles and other blackbirds.
species.when_to_see: Present in Florida year-round, though numbers rise and fall through the seasons.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path without feeding. Cowbirds gather readily where seed is put out.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Grackles are larger and longer-tailed with pale eyes. Cowbirds are stocky and short-tailed, and the male's chocolate-brown head is unlike anything on a grackle.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: It feeds on the ground, often around livestock, taking seeds, grain and insects. Males display with a bow and a strange liquid gurgle of a song.

how_it_lives.label: What the females are doing
how_it_lives.text: Watching other birds. A cowbird builds no nest of her own — she finds the nest of another species, lays an egg in it and leaves. The host incubates it and raises the chick alongside its own, or in place of them.

how_to_know_it.label: Male
how_to_know_it.text: Glossy black with a rich chocolate-brown head.

how_to_know_it.label: Female
how_to_know_it.text: Plain gray-brown all over, and easy to overlook.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: Stocky and short-tailed, with a thick conical bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The male gives a liquid, gurgling glug-glug-gleee. The female answers with a dry chatter.
Usually on the ground in the open, walking rather than hopping, and often mixed in with grackles.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Open lawns and short grass, often among other blackbirds.
Present year-round, though numbers rise and fall through the seasons.

what_it_does_here.text: Cowbirds historically followed roaming bison herds across open country. Laying in another bird's nest allowed them to reproduce without staying in one place while the herds moved on.
Some hosts have an answer. Yellow Warblers will build a new nest floor straight over a cowbird egg and start again, occasionally ending up with a nest several storeys tall.
Here they feed mostly on grass and weed seeds out in the open, while the songbirds they parasitize nest in shrubs and trees. The edge between open ground and woody cover is where the two meet.

at_a_glance.text: A stocky blackbird — the male glossy black with a chocolate-brown head, the female plain gray-brown.
It builds no nest. The female lays her eggs in other birds' nests and leaves them to raise her young.
More than 200 bird species have been documented receiving cowbird eggs.

species.teaser: A cowbird builds no nest. The female lays her eggs in other birds' nests and leaves them to raise her young.

quick_hits: A lanky blackbird with pale yellow eyes and a long tail that it folds into a keel or V shape in flight.
The black is structural, not pigment. In direct light the head and body show bronze, purple or green.
It walks rather than hops, striding across open lawns in loose flocks.
The call is a short, harsh creak, often compared to a rusty hinge.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. Year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The common grackle is one of those birds people either love or tolerate. It is smart, bold, and everywhere — striding across lawns, raiding feeders, and gathering in noisy flocks in parking lots and trees.
The iridescence is real and striking in good light: the Florida form typically shows a bronze or greenish sheen on the body and a purplish head.
Grackles are among the most adaptable birds in North America, thriving in cities, suburbs, farms, and parks.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: All black with iridescent bronze, purple, or green sheen in sunlight. Pale yellow eyes.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Long and keel-shaped — folded into a V in flight.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: About 12 inches, larger than a robin.

blocks.label: Sound
blocks.text: A loud, squeaky, rusty-hinge call.

identification.what_to_look_for: A sleek black bird with yellow eyes and a long, V-shaped tail, walking boldly across open ground. The squeaky call clinches it.

species.diet: Insects, seeds, grain, fruit, small fish, and scraps — eats almost anything.
species.behavior: Walks on the ground, forages in flocks, visits feeders. Roosts in large communal groups.
species.sounds: A loud, squeaky, creaking call — like a rusty hinge.
species.ecological_role: Seed disperser and insect consumer; also a nest predator.
species.plant_connections: Feeds on seeds and berries from many plants.

size.length: 11 to 13 inches
size.lifespan: commonly several years.

species.habitat: Lawns, parks, parking lots, wetland edges — almost everywhere.
species.where_to_look: Open lawns, pond edges, and parking areas. Hard to miss.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Cowbirds are stocky and short-tailed with a dark eye; the male has a chocolate-brown head. Grackles are larger and longer-tailed with a pale yellow eye.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: Walks on the ground and forages in flocks, taking insects, seeds, grain, fruit and whatever else is available. It will also take eggs and nestlings from other birds' nests.
Outside the breeding season grackles roost communally, sometimes in very large numbers.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: All black at a glance, with pale yellow eyes. In good light the sheen resolves into a bronze or greenish body and a purplish head; in flat light it simply looks black.

how_to_know_it.label: Tail
how_to_know_it.text: Long and keel-shaped, folded into a V in flight.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About a foot long, with a wingspan around seventeen inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A loud, squeaky creak, like a rusty hinge.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: On a lawn, look for a long-tailed blackbird walking rather than hopping, with a pale eye that stands out against the dark head.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Open lawns, pond edges and parking areas, usually in loose flocks rather than singly.
A year-round Florida resident.

what_it_does_here.label: Lawn and seed
what_it_does_here.text: Grackles use the boundary between mown grass and seeding plants: short turf to walk and hunt insects on, and grasses, weeds and fruiting shrubs nearby for seed and fruit. They are among the birds most at home in a landscape that is partly cultivated.

at_a_glance.text: A lanky blackbird with pale yellow eyes and a long tail that it folds into a keel or V shape in flight.
The bronze, purple and green sheen comes from feather structure catching the light. In flat light the same bird looks almost black.
It walks rather than hops, striding across open lawns in loose flocks.
The call is a short, harsh creak, often compared to a rusty hinge.

species.teaser: Black until the light hits it. In sun the head turns bronze, purple or green, depending on the angle you are standing at.

quick_hits: A large dark bird circling overhead with its wings held in a shallow V, rocking side to side and rarely flapping, is almost certainly a Turkey Vulture.
It locates carrion largely by smell, an unusual ability among birds, and can find carcasses concealed beneath foliage.
The bare red head is not decorative. A featherless head stays cleaner when feeding inside a carcass.
It eats only carrion and does not kill live prey.
species.range_and_origin: Native across the Americas, from southern Canada to South America. A common year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The turkey vulture is one of the most recognizable silhouettes in the Florida sky. It soars for hours on thermals with almost no flapping, tilting and rocking in a distinctive wobbly flight that experienced birders can identify at great distance.

Unlike most birds, it relies heavily on smell — a rare trait. Gas-pipeline crews have historically watched for circling vultures to find leaks, because the odorant added to natural gas mimics the smell of decay.
It is harmless to live animals and pets. Despite its intimidating size and association with death, it feeds exclusively on carrion.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Large dark bird soaring with wings in a shallow V (dihedral), rocking side to side. Rarely flaps.

blocks.label: Underwing
blocks.text: Two-toned: dark leading edge, silvery-gray flight feathers.

blocks.label: Head
blocks.text: Small, bare, red (adult) — visible at close range.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Wingspan about 6 feet.

identification.what_to_look_for: A large dark bird soaring in circles with wings held in a V and a distinctive side-to-side rocking. Up close, the small bare red head is unmistakable.

species.diet: Carrion exclusively. Does not kill live prey.
species.behavior: Soars on thermals for hours. Roosts communally, often in dead trees or on buildings. Spreads wings to sun-dry in the morning.
species.sounds: Essentially voiceless — lacks the vocal anatomy of most birds. Hisses and grunts when disturbed.
species.ecological_role: Nature's cleanup crew — removes carrion that would otherwise breed disease. A keystone scavenger.

size.length: 25 to 32 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 15 to 20 years.

species.habitat: Open country, roadsides, and anywhere thermals form. Roosts in trees, on buildings, and on communication towers.
species.where_to_look: Look up — almost any time you see a large bird circling overhead without flapping, it is a turkey vulture.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, visible overhead on any warm day.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Bald Eagles hold their broad wings flat and fly steadily, with a large head projecting forward. Turkey Vultures have a tiny head, hold their wings in a shallow V and rock from side to side.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: Soars for hours on rising warm air, covering ground with almost no effort while searching for the smell of carrion below.
It roosts communally, often in dead trees or on structures, and spreads its wings in the morning sun to dry and warm.

It finds carrion by smell, which few birds can do. The sense is sharp enough that gas-pipeline crews have historically watched for circling vultures to locate leaks — the odorant added to natural gas smells like decay.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Large and dark, soaring with the wings held in a shallow V and rocking from side to side. It rarely flaps.

how_to_know_it.label: Underwing
how_to_know_it.text: Two-toned — dark leading edge, silvery-gray flight feathers behind.

how_to_know_it.label: Head
how_to_know_it.text: Small and bare, red in adults.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan around six feet.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Judge it by the shallow V and the rocking. A Bald Eagle holds its wings flat and steady; a vulture teeters.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look up. Almost any large bird circling overhead without flapping is this one.
A year-round Florida resident, visible overhead on any warm day once thermals begin to rise.

what_it_does_here.text: A scavenger that removes carrion which would otherwise decay in the open, reducing what is left to spread disease.

what_it_does_here.label: Dead trees as roosts
what_it_does_here.text: Vultures gather at communal roosts, and bare dead trees are favored because open branches give easy take-off and room to spread wings in the sun. A standing snag is worth more to them than a dense living canopy.

at_a_glance.text: A large dark bird circling overhead with its wings held in a shallow V, rocking side to side and rarely flapping, is almost certainly a Turkey Vulture.
It locates carrion largely by smell, an unusual ability among birds, and can find carcasses concealed beneath foliage.
The bare red head is not decorative. A featherless head stays cleaner when feeding inside a carcass.
It eats only carrion and does not kill live prey.

species.teaser: It finds its food by smell — one of very few birds that can — and can detect a carcass hidden under a forest canopy.

quick_hits: Slate-gray all over, with a black cap and a rusty patch under the tail that shows only when it lifts.
The cat-like mewing call is the surest way to find one, because the bird itself stays inside dense cover.
Like the mockingbird it borrows phrases from other birds, but it rarely repeats a phrase, so the song rambles rather than cycling.
In the Bradenton area it is mainly a winter visitor and migrant rather than a breeding bird.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Breeds across the eastern and central U.S. and southern Canada; winters in the southeastern U.S., Caribbean, and Central America. Present in the Bradenton area mainly as a winter visitor.
more_information: The gray catbird is a member of the Mimidae — the same mimic family as the mockingbird and brown thrasher. Its song is a long, wandering string of notes and phrases, many borrowed from other birds, but unlike the mockingbird it rarely repeats a phrase, so the song sounds more improvised.
The cat-like mewing call is distinctive and often the first clue that a catbird is hiding in the bushes nearby.
Despite its drab color, the rusty undertail coverts are a reliable field mark if you catch the bird flicking its tail.

what_it_does_here.label: Thickets are the habitat
what_it_does_here.text: This bird needs density, not variety. Hedgerows, tangled shrubs and unpruned garden edges give it both feeding cover and song perches, and the berries those same shrubs produce carry it through winter. A tidied-up border removes both at once.

It belongs to the same mimic family as the mockingbird and the brown thrasher, but sings very differently. A mockingbird repeats a phrase several times before switching; a catbird usually moves on after a phrase or two, producing a long stream of whistles, squeaks and borrowed sounds that seldom circles back.

Its small size lets it forage on thinner branches and weed stems that larger woodpeckers cannot use.

more_information: The cavities matter after the woodpecker leaves. Small birds that cannot excavate their own holes depend on old woodpecker nests, so a dead limb left standing keeps working for years.

species.ecological_role: A predator of insects on small branches and in plant stems. The nest cavities it excavates in dead wood are later used by chickadees, wrens and other small birds that cannot dig their own.
species.plant_connections: Its size is the whole story. A Downy Woodpecker is light enough to cling to twigs, dead flower stalks and goldenrod stems where larger woodpeckers cannot balance, so it reaches insects wintering inside plant stems. It also needs dead wood: nest cavities are chiselled into standing dead limbs and snags, and those holes are later used by other small birds.

size.lifespan: commonly several years.

how_it_lives.text: A quiet, methodical worker. It moves along thin branches and weed stems, tapping lightly rather than hammering, probing for insects and larvae. It will take seeds and suet too.
In winter it joins mixed flocks — chickadees, titmice, warblers — moving through the trees together. Several pairs of eyes find more food and spot more danger than one.

how_it_lives.label: Dead wood is the nest
how_it_lives.text: It chisels a cavity into a standing dead limb, and when the pair has finished with it, smaller birds that cannot dig their own take it over.

how_to_know_it.text: About six inches — the smallest woodpecker in North America.

how_to_know_it.text: A high, sharp pik, and a whinnying rattle that falls away at the end.
It taps lightly rather than hammering, and works thin branches and dead stems as often as trunks.

what_it_does_here.text: Being small is the whole strategy. A Downy is light enough to cling to twigs, dead flower stalks and goldenrod stems, which puts the insects wintering inside plant stems within reach — food that heavier woodpeckers cannot get at.

It also needs dead wood. Nest cavities are chiselled into standing dead limbs and snags, and those holes keep working long after the woodpecker has moved on: chickadees, wrens and other small birds cannot dig their own and take over old ones. A dead limb left standing is still doing a job.

In cooler months it travels with mixed flocks of chickadees, titmice and nuthatches.

quick_hits: The name misleads. The red belly is a faint wash that is rarely visible; the obvious red runs over the crown and nape.
Males carry red from the bill right back over the crown; females show red only on the nape.
It wedges food into bark crevices to hold it steady while feeding, and stores seeds and nuts the same way.
The cavities it excavates are later used by screech-owls, squirrels and small birds that cannot dig their own.
species.range_and_origin: Native throughout the eastern United States. A year-round resident in Florida, common in woodlands, suburbs, and parks.
more_information: The red-bellied woodpecker is one of those birds whose name sends people looking for the wrong field mark. The belly has a faint pinkish wash, but it is the bold red stripe on the head that identifies this bird — running from the bill to the nape on males, limited to the nape on females.
It is an adaptable, opportunistic feeder: insects, spiders, nuts, seeds, fruit, and occasionally tree frogs or small lizards. That flexibility is part of why it thrives in suburban Florida.
Its undulating flight — a few quick wingbeats, then a fold and a dip — is typical of woodpeckers and easy to spot crossing an open space.

quick_hits: A tiny pale-blue butterfly barely bigger than a thumbnail, flickering low over flower beds.
Males shine pale blue above; females are duller, with more dusky gray and brown.
The underside is white with fine gray bands and one or two small black-and-orange eyespots beside slender tails.
Plumbago is one of its caterpillar host plants, which keeps this butterfly close to garden plantings.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, the Caribbean, and south into the American tropics. In Florida it is a common, year-round resident of gardens, parks, and weedy open ground.
more_information: The cassius blue is a member of the gossamer-wing family — small, fragile butterflies often no bigger than a fingernail. Males are a soft, pale blue above; females wear more gray and brown, so the two can look like different butterflies at a glance.

Turn one over and the underside tells the real story: a fine pattern of gray-and-white bands and a couple of small black-and-orange eyespots near the rear edge of the hindwing. Combined with tiny tails that the resting butterfly slowly wiggles, those spots mimic a head and antennae at the wrong end of the body. A bird aiming for the "head" gets a harmless beakful of wingtip, and the butterfly escapes.

It is an easy butterfly to host. Its caterpillars feed on the buds and flowers of legumes and on plumbago, both common in Florida landscaping, which is part of why the cassius blue is such a constant presence in gardens.

species.plant_connections: Caterpillar host plants include legumes (such as peas and wild beans) and plumbago (leadwort) — common garden plants, which keeps this butterfly close to home.

quick_hits: A swimming crab with sapphire-blue claws turning up in a park pond is the Atlantic Blue Crab, and its presence indicates the water carries some salt.
Its scientific name means roughly 'savory beautiful swimmer' — a rare case of a name describing both the animal and the appetite for it.
The rear pair of legs are flattened into paddles, so unlike most crabs it genuinely swims rather than only walking.
Mature females can be told by red-tipped claws; males have blue ones.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the western Atlantic, from the U.S. East Coast through the Gulf of Mexico. It lives in estuaries and coastal waters and ranges into brackish and even fresh water, which is how it reaches inland ponds with a tidal or saltwater connection.
more_information: The blue crab is an estuary animal, built for the in-between waters where rivers meet the sea. Its Latin name, Callinectes sapidus, translates neatly as "savory beautiful swimmer" — a nod to its blue-tinged beauty, its swimming ability, and its long history as prized seafood along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

What sets it apart from a typical crab is the back pair of legs, flattened into broad paddles. With them the blue crab can truly swim, sculling sideways through open water rather than only scuttling along the bottom.

That tolerance for a wide range of saltiness is why it shows up where you might not expect a crab. Finding one in a park pond usually means the water is brackish or connected to tidal flow — the crab itself reading as a living water-quality clue. Sex is easy once you know the trick: mature females have red-tipped claws, like painted nails, while males' claws stay all blue.

identification.what_to_look_for: A broad crab with blue-tinged claws and paddle-shaped back legs in or near the water. Red-tipped "painted" claws mark a female; all-blue claws mark a male.

species.behavior: Active in and around the water, swimming with its paddle legs and foraging on the bottom. Defends itself readily with strong pincers when cornered. Burrows into mud to overwinter and to molt.
species.ecological_role: A wide-ranging omnivore and scavenger that helps clean and recycle material in estuarine and brackish waters, and an important link in coastal food webs.
species.plant_connections: Forages among submerged and shoreline vegetation, eating plant material and detritus along with animal prey.

danger.pets: Best kept away from pets — a curious dog that mouths a blue crab can get a painful pinch.

interaction.guidance: Look, do not touch. Give it room at the water's edge and do not handle it; those claws mean business.

conservation.status: Not a conservation concern in its native range, though it is a heavily fished species whose stocks are managed.

quick_hits: A small dark ladybird beetle with a rusty-orange head and tail, working over a plant looking for mealybugs.
The larva is covered in white waxy filaments and closely resembles the mealybugs it hunts, letting it feed among them.
It was brought from Australia in 1891 to control mealybugs and is now one of the oldest successes in biological pest control.
Both the larva and the adult eat the same prey — mealybugs, soft scales and their eggs.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Australia, introduced into the United States in 1891 as a biological control agent and now established in warm regions including Florida, where it lives wherever mealybugs and soft scales occur.
more_information: The mealybug destroyer is one of the early success stories of biological control. A ladybird beetle from Australia, it was imported in 1891 to fight citrus mealybugs in California and has since become a standard ally in greenhouses, groves, and gardens across the warm parts of the country.

Both the adult and the larva are predators of mealybugs, soft scales, and their eggs. The larva is the strange one: it grows a coat of white waxy filaments that makes it look uncannily like an oversized mealybug, a disguise that lets it feed right inside a colony of its prey.

Unlike many introduced insects, this one is considered beneficial rather than invasive. It specializes on soft-bodied scale pests, does not damage plants, and does not displace native wildlife in any notable way, which is why growers still release it deliberately.

species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States and the American tropics. In Florida it is found in open, sunny places where its rattlebox host plants grow.
more_information: The bella moth breaks the usual moth rules. It flies in daylight and wears a riot of pink, orange, yellow, and white — colors that function as a billboard rather than camouflage. The message is honest: this insect is chemically defended and tastes terrible.

The defense is borrowed from plants. Its caterpillars feed on rattlebox (Crotalaria) and related legumes, which are loaded with toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids, and the moth carries those compounds from caterpillar into adulthood. Birds quickly learn to leave the bright moth alone.

The chemistry even shapes its love life. A male advertises his alkaloid load to a female during courtship and transfers a dose to her when they mate; she folds that gift into her eggs, giving the next generation a head start on being unpalatable. Few small insects carry such a tidy story of plants, poison, and parenting.

quick_hits: A dragonfly with a vivid rose-pink to purple body cruising the pond edge is a mature male Roseate Skimmer.
The color belongs to mature males only. Females and young males are brown and tan, so the same species can look like two different insects.
Males hold territories along the shoreline, patrolling low over the water and returning to a favored perch.
Before flight, the young live underwater as nymphs, hunting mosquito larvae and other small aquatic animals.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southern United States and south into the American tropics. In Florida it is a common warm-season dragonfly of ponds, ditches, and other still waters.
more_information: The roseate skimmer stands out for a color most dragonflies never wear. Mature males develop a rosy-pink to red-violet abdomen and thorax, a striking look against the greens and browns of a pond edge. Females and immatures are brown and tan, which is why the pink reads as a male's signal.
It is a hardy, adaptable insect, at home on ponds, roadside ditches, retention basins, and other still or slow water, and it has spread comfortably through the warm parts of the country.

As a predator it follows the dragonfly playbook: adults hunt small flying insects on the wing, gathering prey in a basket made of their bristly legs, while the aquatic young hunt small creatures (including mosquito larvae) underwater before climbing out to transform.

quick_hits: A tiny dragonfly with glowing amber-orange wings hovering low over the pond — one of the smallest dragonflies in North America.
At about an inch long it can pass for a wasp, and it reinforces the impression by bobbing its abdomen while perched.
Males have entirely amber wings; females show patchy brown-and-clear wings instead.
The aquatic young eat mosquito larvae, so the species works on biting insects at both stages of its life.
species.range_and_origin: Native and widespread across the eastern and central United States. In Florida it is common near still and slow waters through the warm months.
more_information: The eastern amberwing is a study in small-package boldness. Males have wings washed a warm amber-orange, unusual among local dragonflies, and a body not much over an inch long.

That small size and orange-banded look pay off as mimicry. Perched amberwings bob the abdomen and flick the wings in a way that resembles a wasp tidying itself, and the resemblance is thought to make birds and other predators think twice — a harmless dragonfly borrowing a wasp's reputation.

For all the bluff, it earns its keep as a predator. Adults hawk tiny flying insects over the water, and the aquatic young (naiads) hunt mosquito larvae and other small prey beneath the surface, making amberwings quiet allies against biting insects.

quick_hits: A Black Witch can span five to seven inches across the wings. By day it often rests flat in a dark sheltered place; in flight at dusk, its size can make it look briefly batlike.

The Black Witch carries very different traditions across its range. Some Mexican and Central American folklore associates it with death, while traditions elsewhere associate the same moth with money or good fortune.
Despite its size, the adult cannot sting and poses no danger to people. It feeds on juices from ripe or fermenting fruit and tree sap.
Black Witches are strong long-distance wanderers. Individuals regularly move north from tropical breeding areas and have been recorded far beyond the species' usual range.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the American tropics, from South America up through Mexico, and a regular warm-season wanderer into Florida and across the southern United States.
more_information: The black witch is a moth built on a grand scale, with a wingspan that can top seven inches — broad, dark, and scalloped, with a small comma-and-number-eight marking on each forewing. Seen flapping at dusk, it is easy to mistake for a bat.

Few insects carry as much folklore. Across its range it has gathered names and beliefs that pull in opposite directions: in much of Mexico and Central America it is the butterfly of death, an ill omen if it enters a home where someone is sick; in parts of the Caribbean and South Texas, by contrast, one landing over your doorway is said to bring money or luck. The same big dark moth, read as a curse in one place and a blessing in another.

Behind the stories is a gentle, mobile insect. Adults feed on rotting fruit and sap, not blood or nectar exclusively, and they have no interest in people. Each year individuals drift far north of the tropics, which is how a tropical giant ends up resting under a Florida eave or bridge.

quick_hits: The Green Anole is Florida's only native anole. It can change from bright green to brown, and adult males display a pink throat fan called a dewlap.
Color change is influenced by temperature, light and the lizard's physiological state. It is not the rapid background-matching trick associated with chameleons.
Where introduced Brown Anoles become abundant, Green Anoles often shift toward higher perches in shrubs and trees, reducing overlap between the two species.
Its expanded toe pads are covered with microscopic structures that help it cling to leaves, stems and smooth surfaces while climbing.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States and the only anole native to Florida.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Bright green to brown, sometimes changing between the two. It is the only anole at Palma Sola that turns true green.

blocks.label: Throat fan
blocks.text: Adult males have a pink to reddish dewlap that they extend during displays.

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Slender, with a pointed snout and long tail. Brown Anoles are usually stockier and more heavily patterned.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look on shrubs, vines and tree trunks for a slender lizard that may be bright green or brown. Adult males sometimes perform head bobs and push-ups while extending a pink dewlap.

species.diet: Mostly insects, spiders and other small invertebrates caught among leaves, branches and trunks.
species.behavior: Active by day. Green Anoles climb through vegetation hunting small prey, bask in exposed spots and retreat into cover when threatened. Males communicate with head bobs, push-up displays and extensions of the dewlap.
species.ecological_role: A small predator of insects and spiders in shrubs and trees, and prey for birds, snakes and larger animals.
species.plant_connections: Plants are the Green Anole's hunting ground, basking platform and shelter. Broad leaves, vines, shrubs and tree branches provide surfaces for climbing and places to ambush insects. Dense, vertically layered vegetation also gives the lizard more choices of perch height and escape cover.

size.length: Usually about five to eight inches from snout to tail tip.

species.habitat: Shrubs, vines, trees, and garden plantings with sun and cover, from woodland edges to landscaped beds.
species.where_to_look: Look on shrubs, vines, tree trunks and leafy garden plantings, especially where vegetation provides both sunny perches and dense cover. Where Brown Anoles are abundant, Green Anoles often use higher vegetation.
species.when_to_see: Present in Florida year-round and most active during warm weather. Palma Sola currently has too few records to say how regularly it is seen here.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to people. Avoid handling; a frightened anole may bite in self-defense.
danger.pets: No meaningful danger to pets. Cats and dogs may chase them.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling or feeding. Dense shrubs, vines and tree cover provide useful habitat for native anoles.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida — the state's only native anole. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern overall. In parts of Florida, introduced Brown Anoles have changed how Green Anoles use habitat, often shifting them toward higher perches.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Brown Anoles remain brown, tan or gray and are usually stockier and more heavily patterned. Green Anoles can turn bright green and are more slender. Where both occur, Green Anoles also tend to use higher vegetation.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day, climbing through vegetation to hunt small prey, basking in exposed spots and retreating into cover when threatened.
Males communicate with head bobs, push-up displays and extensions of the pink dewlap.

at_a_glance.text: The Green Anole is Florida's only native anole. It can change from bright green to brown, and adult males display a pink throat fan called a dewlap.
Color change is influenced by temperature, light and the lizard's physiological state. It is not the rapid background-matching trick associated with chameleons.
Where introduced Brown Anoles become abundant, Green Anoles often shift toward higher perches in shrubs and trees, reducing overlap between the two species.
Its expanded toe pads are covered with microscopic structures that help it cling to leaves, stems and smooth surfaces while climbing.

species.teaser: A Green Anole can change from bright green to brown, but it is not trying to match whatever it is sitting on.

quick_hits: A Mourning Dove is a slim gray-brown dove with black wing spots, a small head and a long pointed tail edged with white.
Its low coo is often mistaken for an owl. The mournful quality of that call gave the bird its English name.
The sharp whistle heard when a Mourning Dove takes off comes from the wings, not the voice.
Both parents feed newly hatched young with crop milk, a fat- and protein-rich secretion produced in the crop.
species.range_and_origin: Native and abundant across North America. In Florida it is a common year-round resident of open country, farmland, suburbs, and parks.
more_information: Few birds are as widespread or as numerous as the mourning dove; it is found coast to coast and is among the most plentiful birds on the continent. Much of that success comes from a simple diet of seeds and a long breeding season that lets pairs raise several broods a year.
The call does most of the work of naming it. The slow, drawn-out "coo-OO-oo-oo-oo" carries a melancholy tone that people regularly mistake for an owl, especially at dawn and dusk.

The whistling wings are a separate trick. The narrow outer wing feathers vibrate in flight, producing a sharp twitter on takeoff and landing that may also serve as an alarm, alerting the flock when one bird flushes in a hurry.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Soft gray-brown, with a few black spots on the wings and a pinkish wash on the breast.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: Slim and streamlined, with a small head and a long, pointed tail edged in white.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Fast and direct, wings whistling on takeoff.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Often seen feeding on the ground or perched on wires.

identification.what_to_look_for: A trim, plain dove with a long pointed tail, either walking and pecking on open ground or perched quietly. The mournful coo and the whistling wing-twitter on takeoff confirm it.

species.diet: Almost entirely seeds — grasses, weeds, and grains — gathered from the ground and stored in the crop to digest later.
species.behavior: Active by day, feeding on the ground and resting on wires, branches, and rooftops. Often in pairs or loose flocks. Flushes fast with whistling wings when startled, then settles nearby.
species.sounds: The signature low, mournful "coo-OO-oo-oo-oo," most often heard at dawn and dusk, plus the whistling twitter of the wings in flight.
species.ecological_role: An abundant seed-eater that helps move and process plant seeds, and a key prey species for hawks, falcons, and other predators.
species.plant_connections: Feeds on the seeds of many grasses and weedy plants, gleaned from open and disturbed ground.

size.length: 9 to 13 inches
size.lifespan: commonly a few years, occasionally much longer.

species.habitat: Open and semi-open places — fields, roadsides, lawns, gardens, and parks — with bare ground for feeding and scattered perches.
species.where_to_look: On open lawns and paths, on wires and bare branches, and around any seeding plants. Listen for the mournful coo to locate one.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, present and calling in every season.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Watch and enjoy, and please do not feed park wildlife. Doves find plenty of seed on their own.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Extremely abundant and widespread.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident; formal Palma Sola records are sparse.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Larger and paler, with a squared tail and a narrow black collar on the back of the neck. Mourning Doves have a long pointed tail and black spots on the wings.
Larger and heavier-bodied, with a bold white wing patch visible even when perched. Mourning Doves are slimmer and lack the broad white wing stripe.

how_it_lives.text: Seeds make up nearly the entire diet. A feeding bird swallows them whole and stores them temporarily in its crop, then can leave the exposed feeding area and digest the meal from a safer perch.
Birds often occur in pairs or loose groups and fly away rapidly when startled.

how_it_lives.label: A very simple nest
how_it_lives.text: Mourning Doves build very simple nests from twigs, pine needles and grass stems, usually on a branch or other supported surface. Both parents care for the young.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Gray-brown to buff, with black spots on the wings and a pale peach wash on the breast.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: Small head, plump body and long pointed tail with white outer tips.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Fast and direct, often with a sharp wing whistle at takeoff.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A low, drawn-out series of coos. The sharp whistling sound heard during takeoff and landing is made by the wings rather than the voice.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About a foot long, with a wingspan around a foot and a half.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look on lawns, paths and other open ground for a slim brown dove picking up seeds. On a perch, the small head and long pointed tail are distinctive.

how_to_know_it.label: Wing whistle
how_to_know_it.text: The whistling comes from the wings rather than the voice. Narrow outer flight feathers vibrate on takeoff and landing, and the sharp twitter may double as an alarm when one bird flushes in a hurry.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look on lawns, paths and other open ground with scattered trees or shrubs nearby. Mourning Doves also perch conspicuously on bare branches, wires and other exposed sites.
A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola's formal observation record is currently too small to measure how regularly it is seen in the park.

what_it_does_here.text: A major consumer of grass and weed seeds and an important prey species for hawks, falcons and other predators.

what_it_does_here.label: Seeds and nest material
what_it_does_here.text: Plants supply both food and nest material. Mourning Doves gather seeds from grasses, weeds and other low plants on open ground, then place simple nests in trees, shrubs or vines, building the platform from twigs, pine needles and grass stems.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people.
Watch without feeding. Give ground-feeding birds room to move away naturally rather than flushing them repeatedly.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern.

Its low coo is often mistaken for an owl. The mournful quality of that call gave the bird its English name.
The sharp whistle heard when a Mourning Dove takes off comes from the wings, not the voice.
Both parents feed newly hatched young with crop milk, a fat- and protein-rich secretion produced in the crop.

species.teaser: Mourning Doves feed newly hatched chicks a nutrient-rich substance called crop milk, produced by both parents.

quick_hits: A Blue Jay is a large crested songbird patterned blue, white and black, often detected first by its loud calls.
The blue color comes from microscopic feather structure rather than blue pigment. When light passes through the feather instead of reflecting from it, the blue disappears and the feather looks brown.
Blue Jays cache thousands of acorns in autumn. Many are recovered later, but unretrieved acorns can germinate, making jays important long-distance dispersers of oaks.
Blue Jays frequently imitate Red-shouldered and Red-tailed Hawk calls. Why they do it is not completely clear; the calls may warn other jays or sometimes deceive other birds.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern and central North America. In Florida it is a common year-round resident of woodlands, parks, and leafy neighborhoods, especially where oaks grow.
more_information: Blue jays are members of the crow family, and it shows in their intelligence. They are curious, social, and quick to learn, with a wide vocabulary of calls and a knack for problem-solving.

They are also unsung foresters. In autumn a jay gathers acorns and other nuts and buries them across its territory for winter — far more than it can ever eat. The forgotten caches sprout, and over centuries jays have helped oaks spread across the continent, a quiet partnership written into whole forests.

That famous blue is structural, not pigmented. Microscopic structures in the feathers scatter light so we see blue, which is why a backlit or crushed feather loses the color entirely. Jays round out their reputation with mimicry, especially convincing imitations of hawk calls that can clear rivals away from food.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Blue above, white to pale gray below, with a black necklace across the chest.

blocks.label: Wings and tail
blocks.text: Barred with black and white and tipped with white.

blocks.label: Crest
blocks.text: A pointed blue crest that rises and lowers with the bird's mood.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Loud, bold, and often in small noisy groups.

identification.what_to_look_for: A crested blue-and-white bird, larger than a cardinal, calling loudly from the trees or visiting feeders. The black necklace and white-tipped wings and tail confirm it.

species.diet: Mainly acorns, nuts, and seeds, plus insects, fruits, and the occasional egg or nestling. Caches large numbers of acorns for winter.
species.behavior: Active by day, social, and noisy, often moving in family groups. Bold at feeders and quick to mob hawks, owls, and cats as a group. Raises and lowers its crest to signal alarm or excitement.
species.sounds: Loud and varied: a ringing "jay-jay" scream, a musical "queedle" like a squeaky gate, and dead-on imitations of hawk calls.
species.ecological_role: A key seed disperser, especially of oaks, and a sharp-eyed alarm system whose calls alert other animals to predators.
species.plant_connections: Closely tied to oaks and other nut trees — it eats their acorns and, by burying and forgetting them, plants the next generation of trees.

size.length: 9 to 12 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 7 years or more in the wild.

species.habitat: Forests, woodland edges, and well-treed parks and neighborhoods, especially where oaks and other nut trees grow.
species.where_to_look: Around the park's oaks and larger trees, often announcing itself with loud calls before you spot the flash of blue.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, conspicuous in every season and especially busy caching acorns in fall.

danger.people: Harmless to people, though a bold jay near a nest may scold loudly. It poses no real threat.

interaction.guidance: Watch and enjoy, and please do not feed park wildlife. Jays are confident enough to approach on their own — no encouragement needed.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common, adaptable, and widespread.

seasonality.note: Year-round resident in Florida. Current Palma Sola records come from a single observation event, so local frequency is not established.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Lacks a crest and black necklace and lives in specialized scrub habitat. Blue Jays are crested, strongly patterned black-and-white, and common in wooded parks and neighborhoods.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day and often social. Blue Jays forage in trees and on the ground, cache nuts and seeds for later use, and may join other birds in mobbing hawks or owls.
Acorns, other nuts, seeds, fruit and insects make up most of the diet. Eggs or nestlings are occasionally taken but are a minor food source.
They are crow family, and it shows — curious, social, quick to learn, and good enough at imitating a hawk's call to clear rivals off a food source.
The blue is not a pigment. Structure in the feathers scatters light, which is why a crushed or backlit jay feather loses the colour completely.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Blue above, white to pale gray below, with a black necklace across the chest.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings and tail
how_to_know_it.text: Blue, black and white, with conspicuous white tips and corners.

how_to_know_it.label: Crest
how_to_know_it.text: A pointed blue crest that can be raised or flattened during social interactions.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A wide variety of calls, including the loud jeer most people associate with the species. Blue Jays also imitate hawks, especially Red-shouldered Hawks.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a large crested blue-and-white bird with a black necklace and white-tipped wings and tail. Loud jeer calls often reveal it before the bird comes into view.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look around oaks and other large trees, especially along woodland edges. Listen for the loud calls and watch for birds carrying acorns or other food between trees.
A year-round Florida resident. Blue Jays are common in well-treed landscapes regionally, but Palma Sola's current formal observation record is too small to describe local reliability.

what_it_does_here.text: An important disperser of acorns and other large seeds. By carrying nuts away from the parent tree and caching them in the ground, Blue Jays can establish new oak seedlings.

what_it_does_here.label: Planting oaks by accident
what_it_does_here.text: Oaks are one of the Blue Jay's strongest plant relationships. Jays carry and bury acorns for later use, often moving them well away from the parent tree; unrecovered caches can become new oaks. Trees also provide nesting sites, and Blue Jay nests are built mainly from twigs and lined with grasses and rootlets.

Blue Jays plant oaks. Through autumn a jay gathers acorns and buries them one at a time across its territory, far more than it can ever eat, and the caches it forgets sprout. Over centuries that habit helped oaks spread across the continent.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people.
Watch without feeding. Natural foods such as acorns, seeds, fruit and insects already support Blue Jays in the park.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern.

The blue color comes from microscopic feather structure rather than blue pigment. When light passes through the feather instead of reflecting from it, the blue disappears and the feather looks brown.
Blue Jays cache thousands of acorns in autumn. Many are recovered later, but unretrieved acorns can germinate, making jays important long-distance dispersers of oaks.
Blue Jays frequently imitate Red-shouldered and Red-tailed Hawk calls. Why they do it is not completely clear; the calls may warn other jays or sometimes deceive other birds.

species.teaser: A Blue Jay feather is not actually filled with blue pigment. Its microscopic structure scatters light so that the feather appears blue.

quick_hits: A small, plump brown waterbird that dives and vanishes the moment you notice it.
It can sink rather than dive, compressing its feathers to lose buoyancy and slip under with barely a ripple.
The short, thick bill is unlike a duck's — in the breeding season it carries a black band that gives the bird its name.
It is rarely seen flying or on land. Almost everything it does happens on or under the water.
species.range_and_origin: Native across the Americas. In Florida it is a common winter visitor and a year-round breeder on ponds, lakes, and marshes with plenty of vegetation.
more_information: The pied-billed grebe is a diver first and a flier last. Rather than burst into the air like a duck, it usually escapes trouble by submerging — and it can control how it sinks, trapping or releasing air in its plumage to ride high or settle low in the water, sometimes leaving only its head showing like a tiny periscope.

Those diving skills come from a body that is all wrong for land. Its lobed toes and far-back legs make it a powerful underwater swimmer but an awkward walker, so it spends nearly all its time on the water.

Grebe chicks are striped like little humbugs and often ride on a parent's back, even diving along while hitching a ride. Adults also do something odd and useful: they eat their own feathers, which seems to help protect the stomach and form pellets they later cough up.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: Small and stocky, with a short neck and almost no visible tail.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Plain brown overall, paler on the throat.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Short, thick, and pale, with a black vertical ring in breeding season.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Dives constantly and sits low in the water.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small brown waterbird riding low on a pond, repeatedly diving and popping back up somewhere unexpected. The stubby, ringed bill separates it from ducks and other divers.

species.diet: Mostly crayfish, small fish, aquatic insects, and other small water creatures, caught on underwater dives.
species.behavior: Active by day on open and weedy water, diving frequently to feed or to escape. Rarely seen flying or on land. Often solitary or in small numbers, slipping into cover when disturbed.
species.sounds: Surprisingly loud for its size in the breeding season: a far-carrying series of hollow "kuk-kuk-kuk-cow-cow-cow" calls from marshy cover.
species.ecological_role: A small diving predator that helps keep crayfish, insect, and small-fish numbers in check on quiet, vegetated waters.
species.plant_connections: Lives among emergent and floating marsh plants, which give it cover, nesting material, and the still water it prefers.

size.length: 12 to 15 inches
size.lifespan: commonly several years.

species.habitat: Ponds, lakes, and marshes with open water and plenty of submerged and emergent vegetation for cover and nesting.
species.where_to_look: On the open water of the ponds, often near the weedy edges. Watch for a small brown bird that keeps diving and reappearing — and be patient, because it spends a lot of time underwater.
species.when_to_see: Most numerous in fall and winter, with some present year-round. Active throughout the day on the ponds.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Watch and enjoy, and please do not feed park wildlife. Grebes are shy — if one keeps diving away, you are simply a bit too close.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and the Americas. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Widespread and common on suitable waters.
