how_it_lives.text: Dives frequently to feed or to escape, taking crayfish, small fish, aquatic insects and other small water creatures.

how_it_lives.label: Sinking without a splash
how_it_lives.text: A Pied-billed Grebe can compress its plumage and reduce its buoyancy, settling quietly lower in the water instead of making a conspicuous dive. At times almost the whole body disappears while the head stays above the surface.

The legs sit far back on the body and the toes carry broad lobes that push against the water. That makes the grebe a strong underwater swimmer and an awkward walker, so it spends very little time on land.
how_it_lives.label: Built for water

how_to_know_it.label: Size and shape
how_to_know_it.text: Small and stocky, with a short neck and almost no visible tail. About a foot long.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Plain brown overall, paler on the throat.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Short and thick rather than flat like a duck's, with a black band across it in the breeding season.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Surprisingly loud for its size in the breeding season — a far-carrying series of hollow kuk-kuk-kuk-cow-cow-cow calls from marshy cover.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Watch for a small brown bird that keeps diving and reappearing somewhere else. Be patient; it spends a lot of time underwater.

where_to_find_it_here.text: On the open water of the ponds, often near the weedy edges where it can slip into cover.
Most numerous in autumn and winter, with some present year-round.

what_it_does_here.label: Cover, nest and calm water
what_it_does_here.text: Emergent and floating marsh plants do three jobs at once for a grebe: they screen it from view, they supply the material for its floating nest, and they keep the water still enough for a bird that hunts by sight below the surface.

what_it_does_here.label: Chicks ride aboard
what_it_does_here.text: Newly hatched chicks often climb onto a parent's back and ride tucked among the feathers. A parent may dive with them still aboard.

what_it_does_here.label: Why eat feathers?
what_it_does_here.text: Grebes deliberately swallow their own feathers and feed feathers to their chicks. The feathers collect in the stomach along with hard, indigestible material and are eventually brought back up as pellets. They may help protect the gut from sharp fish bones and other remains.

at_a_glance.text: A small, plump brown waterbird that dives and vanishes the moment you notice it.
It can sink rather than dive, compressing its feathers to lose buoyancy and slip under with barely a ripple.
The short, thick bill is unlike a duck's — in the breeding season it carries a black band that gives the bird its name.
Chicks ride on a parent's back, and adults swallow their own feathers — two of the odder habits on the pond.

species.teaser: It would rather sink than fly. By squeezing air out of its feathers it can settle below the surface without a splash, leaving only the head showing.

quick_hits: A stocky, hunch-shouldered heron with a black cap and back, pale gray wings and red eyes is a Black-crowned Night Heron.
It feeds mostly from late afternoon through the night, when most other herons have stopped.
It hunts by ambush, standing motionless at the water's edge and waiting rather than walking prey down.
Young birds are brown and heavily spotted, and are difficult to separate from young Yellow-crowned Night Herons.
species.range_and_origin: Native and among the most widespread herons in the world. In Florida it is a fairly common year-round resident of marshes, pond edges and wooded swamps.

blocks.label: Adult
blocks.text: Black crown and back over pale gray wings, white underparts, red eyes and short yellow legs.

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Stocky and short-necked, with a hunched look that is obvious even at a distance.

blocks.label: Juvenile
blocks.text: Brown, heavily streaked and spotted with white, with orange-yellow eyes.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look low and still rather than out in the open. A compact hunched heron tucked against waterside shrubs near dawn or dusk is usually this bird.

species.diet: Fish, frogs, crayfish and aquatic insects, with eggs and nestlings taken occasionally.
species.behavior: Most active from late afternoon through the night, roosting quietly in trees and shrubs by day. Hunts by standing still and ambushing prey rather than stalking. Often nests in colonies with other wading birds.
species.sounds: A harsh barking quok, usually given in flight and often heard at dusk as birds leave the roost to feed. It is frequently the first sign the bird is there at all.
species.ecological_role: A nocturnal predator of fish, amphibians and crustaceans in shallow water.
species.plant_connections: Waterside trees and shrubs are what make the night shift possible. The heron spends the day roosting in dense cover close to the water it will hunt after dark, and nests colonially in the same kind of vegetation. A pond with bare banks offers it nowhere to wait out the daylight.

size.length: About two feet tall, with a wingspan around three and a half feet.

species.habitat: Almost any wetland with cover — marshes, pond and lake edges, wooded swamps, and mangroves — with trees or shrubs nearby for daytime roosting.
species.where_to_look: Check pond margins and the shrubs overhanging them, especially in the low light of early morning and evening. By day the bird is usually roosting quietly in cover.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident, most likely to be seen in low light at either end of the day. Palma Sola has only a single record, so it is an occasional visitor here.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle an injured or trapped heron; the pointed bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. A roosting bird disturbed during the day loses the rest it needs before a night of hunting.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-18 from iNaturalist gap analysis (June 2026 batch). Anchor obs #182494203 (pammy63); Unique ID written to iNat. Content drafted and ready; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local pattern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Adults are straightforward: Black-crowned has a black back over pale gray wings, while Yellow-crowned is gray-bodied with a strongly patterned black-and-white face. Juveniles of the two are much harder to separate and may need a close view.
Green Herons are much smaller with a chestnut neck and dark cap, and they crouch far lower over the water.

how_it_lives.text: It works the shift the other herons do not. Through the day it sits still in a tree or a shrub, easy to walk straight past; from late afternoon into the night it hunts.

And it hunts by ambush rather than stalking — standing motionless at the water's edge and waiting, rather than walking prey down. Fish, frogs, crayfish, aquatic insects, and the occasional egg or nestling.

how_to_know_it.label: Adult
how_to_know_it.text: Black crown and back over pale gray wings, white underparts, red eyes and short yellow legs.

how_to_know_it.label: Build
how_to_know_it.text: Stocky and short-necked, with a hunched look that is obvious even at a distance.

how_to_know_it.label: Juvenile
how_to_know_it.text: Brown, heavily streaked and spotted with white, with orange-yellow eyes. Separating young Black-crowned and Yellow-crowned Night Herons can be genuinely difficult; build, bill shape and head pattern become more useful with a good view.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A harsh barking quok, usually given in flight and often heard at dusk as birds leave the roost to feed. It is frequently the first sign the bird is there at all.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About two feet tall, with a wingspan around three and a half feet.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look low and still rather than out in the open. A compact hunched heron tucked against waterside shrubs near dawn or dusk is usually this bird.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Check pond margins and the shrubs overhanging them, especially in the low light of early morning and evening. By day the bird is usually roosting quietly in cover.
A year-round Florida resident, most likely to be seen in low light at either end of the day. Palma Sola has only a single record, so it is an occasional visitor here.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local pattern.

what_it_does_here.text: Waterside trees and shrubs are what make the night shift possible. The heron spends the day roosting in dense cover close to the water it will hunt after dark, and nests colonially in the same kind of vegetation. A pond with bare banks offers it nowhere to wait out the daylight.

at_a_glance.text: A stocky, hunch-shouldered heron with a black cap and back, pale gray wings and red eyes is a Black-crowned Night Heron.
It feeds mostly from late afternoon through the night, when most other herons have stopped.
It hunts by ambush, standing motionless at the water's edge and waiting rather than walking prey down.
Young birds are brown and heavily spotted, and are difficult to separate from young Yellow-crowned Night Herons.

species.teaser: It works the shift the other herons do not. Most feeding happens from dusk into the night, when the shallows are largely empty.

quick_hits: A slim gray bird singing a long series of changing phrases from an exposed perch is likely a Northern Mockingbird, Florida's state bird.
A male may learn around 200 song types over its lifetime, incorporating imitations of other birds and frogs into its own long performances.
Unpaired males may sing well into the night during the breeding season, sometimes from brightly lit perches.
Mockingbirds defend nests and feeding territories aggressively, sometimes swooping at cats, hawks or people that approach too closely.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America and resident across the southern and eastern United States. In Florida it is an abundant year-round resident of yards, parks, roadsides, and open areas with scattered shrubs — and the official state bird.
more_information: The mockingbird is a born mimic. It builds its song from snatches of whatever it hears, repeating each borrowed phrase several times before moving to the next, and it keeps adding new material throughout its life. Males with the largest repertoires tend to win the best territories and mates, so there is real payoff in being a good copycat.

That drive to sing can run around the clock. Unpaired males in spring will sing on into the night, often from a high, lit perch — beautiful or maddening depending on how close it is to your bedroom window.

Mockingbirds are also famously bold. They defend nests and feeding territories with relentless dive-bombing runs at anything they see as a threat, and they have a long memory for individual people who have come too close before.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Plain gray above, paler below, with two thin white wing bars.

blocks.label: Wing flash
blocks.text: Large white patches burst into view when it flies or flicks its wings open.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Long, with white outer feathers.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Sings from high, open perches and runs in short bursts across lawns.

identification.what_to_look_for: A slender gray bird with a long tail singing from a fence, wire, or treetop, flashing white wing patches when it flies. If it is reeling off many different songs in a row, that is the giveaway.

species.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates in the warm months, shifting to fruits and berries in fall and winter. Often forages on open lawns.
species.behavior: Active by day and conspicuous. Sings from exposed perches, runs and hops across short grass, and aggressively defends its territory and nest year-round. Frequently flashes its white wing patches while foraging, which may help startle insects.
species.sounds: The reason for the name — long, varied songs of repeated, imitated phrases, delivered by day and sometimes at night. Also a harsh "chack" scold note.
species.ecological_role: A widespread songbird that helps control insects and, by eating fruits, spreads the seeds of many shrubs and small trees through its droppings.
species.plant_connections: Eats the berries and fruits of many native shrubs and trees and nests in dense shrubbery — so fruiting plants and thick cover both draw it in.

size.length: 8 to 10 inches
size.lifespan: commonly up to 8 years in the wild.

species.habitat: Open and semi-open country with scattered shrubs and trees — yards, parks, hedgerows, roadsides, and woodland edges.
species.where_to_look: Almost anywhere in the open parts of the park — singing from treetops and fence lines, or running across the lawns. Listen for a long, ever-changing song.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident and one of the park's most reliable singers, vocal in every season and sometimes after dark in spring.

danger.people: Harmless to people, though a parent defending a nest may swoop close to warn you off. It cannot hurt you.
danger.pets: No real danger to pets, but a nesting mockingbird may dive at a cat or dog that wanders too close.

interaction.guidance: Watch and enjoy, and please do not feed park wildlife. If one is dive-bombing, you are simply near its nest — step away and it will settle.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common, adaptable, and comfortable around people.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-18 from iNaturalist gap analysis (June 2026 batch). Anchor obs #328061189 (jerseymeg); Unique ID written to iNat. Content drafted and ready; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident. Current Palma Sola wildlife records are too limited to measure local reliability.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The loggerhead shrike wears a black bandit mask and has a hooked bill; the mockingbird has a plain face, a slim straight bill, and bold white wing flashes in flight.

how_it_lives.text: Mockingbirds spend much of their time in open and semi-open habitat, singing from exposed perches and dropping to lawns or low vegetation to forage. They defend nesting and feeding territories aggressively.

how_it_lives.label: The wing flash
how_it_lives.text: While foraging on the ground, a mockingbird often opens its wings in quick flashes that expose the large white patches. One hypothesis is that the movement startles insects, but researchers do not yet know the display's exact function.
Insects and other small invertebrates dominate during warmer months; fruit and berries become more important at other times of year.
Unpaired males in spring will sing straight through the night, usually from a high, lit perch.
They defend a nest or a feeding patch with relentless dive-bombing runs, and they remember individual people who have come too close before.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Plain gray above and pale below, with narrow white wing bars.

how_to_know_it.label: Wing flash
how_to_know_it.text: Large white wing patches show dramatically in flight and during wing-flashing displays on the ground.

how_to_know_it.label: Tail
how_to_know_it.text: Long, with white outer feathers.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A long series of varied phrases, usually repeating each phrase several times before switching to another. Mockingbirds imitate many other birds and frogs and continue adding sounds throughout life.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a slim gray bird with a long tail, conspicuous white wing patches and a habit of singing from exposed perches. A long song made of short phrases repeated several times before changing is characteristic.

how_to_know_it.label: Behavior cue
how_to_know_it.text: Often sings from exposed treetops, poles, fences or wires and forages on short grass.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in open areas with scattered shrubs and trees. Mockingbirds often sing from the highest exposed perch available, then drop to lawns and other short vegetation to forage.
A year-round Florida resident. Mockingbirds are common in parks and neighborhoods regionally, but Palma Sola currently has only one formal wildlife record.

what_it_does_here.text: An insect predator and fruit-eater. Seeds from some fruits pass through the bird and can be dispersed away from the parent plant.

what_it_does_here.label: Berries and open ground
what_it_does_here.text: Mockingbirds depend on both open ground and dense vegetation. Fruiting shrubs and small trees provide food, while thick shrubs and low trees provide nest sites and defensive cover. Plantings that combine berry-producing plants with open lawn or ground layer suit the species particularly well.

A mockingbird builds its song out of whatever it hears, repeating each borrowed phrase several times before moving on, and it keeps adding new material all its life. Males with the largest repertoires tend to hold the best territories, so there is a real payoff in copying well.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger. A nesting bird may swoop close if you approach its nest, and may scold or swoop at a pet nearby.
If a mockingbird repeatedly swoops or scolds you, move farther away; a nest or fledgling may be nearby. Do not feed or approach the nest.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern.

at_a_glance.text: A slim gray bird singing a long series of changing phrases from an exposed perch is likely a Northern Mockingbird, Florida's state bird.
A male may learn around 200 song types over its lifetime, incorporating imitations of other birds and frogs into its own long performances.
Unpaired males may sing well into the night during the breeding season, sometimes from brightly lit perches.
Mockingbirds defend nests and feeding territories aggressively, sometimes swooping at cats, hawks or people that approach too closely.

species.teaser: A Northern Mockingbird keeps adding sounds to its repertoire throughout its life, mixing imitations into songs that can continue for minutes.

quick_hits: A Pileated Woodpecker is nearly crow-sized, mostly black, with a tall red crest and bold white stripes on the face and neck.
Its loud laughing calls, heavy chopping and deep drumming often carry through the trees before the bird comes into view.
Pileated Woodpeckers make distinctive rectangular excavations in dead and decaying wood while following carpenter-ant tunnels.
Large cavities excavated by Pileated Woodpeckers can later provide roosting or nesting space for animals that cannot carve such holes themselves.
species.range_and_origin: Native to forests across much of the eastern United States and Canada, west into the Pacific Northwest. In Florida it is an uncommon but year-round resident of mature woods, wooded suburbs, and parks with large trees.
more_information: The pileated is the heavyweight of North American woodpeckers — about the size of a crow, with a wingspan close to two and a half feet. For a long time the only larger woodpecker on the continent was the ivory-billed, now almost certainly extinct, which leaves the pileated at the top of the list.

Its signature is the rectangular excavation. Working with a chisel-tipped bill and a long, barbed, sticky tongue, it digs deep squared-off holes into rotting wood to pull out carpenter ants and beetle larvae. A single foraging tree can end up looking as if someone went at it with a hand axe.

Those abandoned cavities matter to the whole forest. Wood ducks, screech-owls, flying squirrels, and many other animals nest in old woodpecker holes they could never excavate themselves, which makes the pileated a kind of habitat engineer for everything around it. (And yes — its flopping crest and laughing call helped inspire Woody Woodpecker.)

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: Crow-sized, with a long neck and a pointed red crest.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Mostly black with bold white stripes on the face and neck; white shows under the wings in flight.

blocks.label: Male vs. female
blocks.text: Males have a red "mustache" stripe; females show black there.

blocks.label: Sign left behind
blocks.text: Large rectangular holes chiseled into tree trunks.

identification.what_to_look_for: A big black-and-white woodpecker with a tall red crest, working a tree trunk or flying with deep, slow wingbeats that flash white underwing patches. If you find fresh rectangular holes in a dead trunk, a pileated is likely nearby.

species.diet: Mostly carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae dug out of dead and dying wood, rounded out with other insects, wild fruits, and nuts.
species.behavior: Active by day, usually alone or in pairs, working steadily up and around tree trunks and fallen logs. Pairs hold a large territory year-round. The flight is strong and slightly undulating, and the bird often calls in flight.
species.sounds: Loud and far-carrying: a ringing, laughing "kuk-kuk-kuk-kuk" that rises and falls, plus deep, resonant drumming on hollow wood used to claim territory.
species.ecological_role: A keystone forager. By chiseling into dead wood it controls carpenter-ant and beetle populations, and the cavities it leaves behind become nest and shelter sites for a long list of other animals.
species.plant_connections: Depends on mature trees and standing dead wood (snags) for both food and nest cavities — so leaving old and dying trees standing directly supports it.

size.length: 16 to 19 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 9 to 12 years.

species.habitat: Mature forests and well-treed parks and neighborhoods with plenty of large, old, and dead trees for feeding and nesting.
species.where_to_look: Among the park's larger trees and any standing dead trunks. Listen for the loud laughing call and slow drumming, and scan big trunks for a crow-sized bird with a red crest.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Often heard before it is seen; most active foraging in the morning.

danger.people: Harmless to people. It keeps to the trees and has no interest in visitors.

interaction.guidance: Watch and enjoy from a distance, and please do not feed park wildlife. Give a foraging bird room and it will carry on working.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Populations are stable and have slowly expanded as forests have regrown.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-18 from iNaturalist gap analysis (June 2026 batch). Anchor obs #362821784 (randall_carter); Unique ID written to iNat. Content drafted and ready; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident, but the park currently has only one documented observation.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much smaller and lacks the Pileated's long pointed crest and large white wing patches. Pileated Woodpeckers are nearly crow-sized and leave much larger rectangular excavations.
Tiny by comparison — sparrow-sized rather than crow-sized.

how_it_lives.text: Forages on standing and fallen wood, chiseling deeply into decaying areas for carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae. Other insects, fruit and nuts are also eaten.
Usually encountered alone or in pairs.

The excavations are rectangular, and nothing else here makes them. Working with a chisel-tipped bill and a long barbed tongue, it digs deep squared-off holes into rotting wood after carpenter ants and beetle larvae. A tree it has worked over can look as though someone took a hand axe to it.

how_to_know_it.label: Size and shape
how_to_know_it.text: Nearly crow-sized, with a long neck and tall red crest.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Mostly black with bold white stripes on the face and neck; large white patches show in the wings during flight.

how_to_know_it.label: Male and female
how_to_know_it.text: Males have a red cheek or 'mustache' stripe; females have black there.

how_to_know_it.label: Sign left behind
how_to_know_it.text: Large rectangular or oblong excavations in dead or decaying wood.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A loud, laughing series of calls plus deep, rolling drumming. Even the chopping sounds of feeding can carry through the woods.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a crow-sized black woodpecker with a red crest on large trunks, snags or fallen logs. Rectangular excavations are strong evidence that a Pileated Woodpecker has been feeding there.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Check the park's largest trees, standing dead trunks, stumps and fallen logs. Look for rectangular feeding holes and listen for the loud call or deep drumming.

where_to_find_it_here.caption: Down at the back of our park — the southern end — a Pileated working a big pine. The rectangular holes it leaves behind are usually easier to find than the bird itself.

where_to_find_it_here.text: A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola currently has only one documented observation, so sightings here should be considered occasional.

what_it_does_here.text: Its excavations change the physical structure of dead wood. Feeding holes expose insect-rich wood, while larger abandoned cavities can later be used by other birds and mammals.

what_it_does_here.label: Dead wood is habitat
what_it_does_here.text: Large trees and dead wood are central to the Pileated Woodpecker's life. It digs for ants and beetle larvae in decaying trunks, snags, stumps and fallen logs, and excavates nesting cavities in large trees — often dead ones. Retaining safe standing snags and fallen wood therefore preserves habitat that living ornamental trees alone do not provide.

The holes outlast the bird. Wood Ducks, screech-owls, flying squirrels and a long list of others nest in abandoned pileated cavities they could never cut for themselves, which makes this one woodpecker a housing supply for much of the forest around it.

take_care.text: Watch from a distance and leave feeding trees, cavities and dead wood undisturbed.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern. Large trees, snags and downed wood remain important habitat.

at_a_glance.text: A Pileated Woodpecker is nearly crow-sized, mostly black, with a tall red crest and bold white stripes on the face and neck.
Its loud laughing calls, heavy chopping and deep drumming often carry through the trees before the bird comes into view.
Pileated Woodpeckers make distinctive rectangular excavations in dead and decaying wood while following carpenter-ant tunnels.
Large cavities excavated by Pileated Woodpeckers can later provide roosting or nesting space for animals that cannot carve such holes themselves.

species.teaser: A large rectangular hole in a dead tree may be easier to find than the bird that made it. Pileated Woodpeckers excavate deeply into decaying wood for carpenter ants.

quick_hits: A bright orange butterfly with black markings above and an underside scattered with elongated, mirror-like silver spots.
Its caterpillars eat only passionflower vines — the same host the Zebra Longwing depends on, so one native passionvine supports both butterflies.
The caterpillar is bright orange with rows of black branching spines. The spines look alarming but do not sting.
Despite the name it belongs to the longwing group rather than the true fritillaries.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southern United States and the Americas. In Florida it is a common, year-round resident, with numbers rising in fall as butterflies move south down the peninsula.
more_information: The gulf fritillary is one of the most familiar orange butterflies in Florida gardens, and despite the name it belongs to the longwing group rather than the true fritillaries.

Its caterpillars feed only on passionflower vines — the very same Passiflora the zebra longwing uses — so a single planting of native passionvine can support both of Florida's beloved longwings at once. The caterpillars take in the vine's compounds, which makes them and the adults unpalatable to many predators.
The undersides of its wings are the real surprise: long, gleaming silver-white spots that flash like little mirrors when the butterfly basks or nectars with its wings closed.

blocks.label: Upper side
blocks.text: Bright orange with black spots and markings.

blocks.label: Underside
blocks.text: Brown with elongated, iridescent silver-white spots.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: Somewhat long-winged, like its longwing relatives.

identification.what_to_look_for: A bright orange butterfly nectaring in the open; when it closes its wings, look for the unmistakable rows of shiny silver spots underneath. The caterpillar is orange with branching black spines, found on passionflower vines.

species.diet: Caterpillars feed only on passionflower (Passiflora) vines. Adults nectar at many flowers, including lantana, Spanish needles, and other open blooms.
species.behavior: Active by day in sunny, open areas. Breeds through several generations a year and joins a southward movement into the Florida peninsula in fall. Often nectars with wings held closed, flashing its silver underside.
species.ecological_role: A common garden pollinator and, with the zebra longwing, a passionflower specialist — together they make native passionvine a high-value plant for supporting butterflies.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillars feed only on passionflower vines (Passiflora spp.) — the same host as the zebra longwing — so one native passionvine planting supports both butterflies.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks; several generations are produced each year.

species.habitat: Open, sunny places — gardens, fields, roadsides, edges, and parks — wherever passionflower vines and nectar flowers grow.
species.where_to_look: In sunny, flowery spots, nectaring with wings closed to show the silver underside. Check passionflower vines for the spiny orange caterpillars. Most numerous in late summer and fall.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, most numerous during the fall southward movement into Florida.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people. The caterpillar's spines look intimidating but do not sting.

interaction.guidance: Just watch and enjoy. Native passionflower vine supports both the gulf fritillary and the zebra longwing, making it a standout butterfly plant.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread, and a frequent visitor to butterfly gardens.

species.internal_notes: Promoted into Top 30. Ties to passionvine plant pages (host plant). Recent genus from Agraulis.

seasonality.note: Present year-round in Florida, with numbers rising in autumn.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The monarch is broader-winged with heavy black veins and no silver; the gulf fritillary is narrower with bright silver spots on the underside.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day in sunny, open areas, often nectaring with the wings held closed so the silver underside shows.
Several generations are produced each year, and adults join a southward movement into the Florida peninsula in autumn.

how_it_lives.label: The caterpillar
how_it_lives.text: Bright orange with rows of black branching spines. The spines look formidable but do not sting. It feeds on passionflower leaves.

how_to_know_it.label: Upperside
how_to_know_it.text: Bright orange with black spots and markings.

how_to_know_it.label: Underside
how_to_know_it.text: Large, elongated silver-white spots cover the brown underside and can flash almost metallic when they catch the light.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: Somewhat long-winged, like its longwing relatives.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan around three inches.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: A bright orange butterfly in a sunny, flowery spot. If it settles with wings closed, look for the silver flecks underneath.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in sunny, flowery spots, and check any passionflower vine for the spiny orange caterpillars.
A year-round Florida resident. More are on the wing in autumn, when butterflies move south down the peninsula.

what_it_does_here.label: One vine, two butterflies
what_it_does_here.text: The caterpillars eat nothing but passionflower vines. The Zebra Longwing uses the same host, so a single native passionvine planting supports both species — one of the highest-value butterfly plants a Florida garden can grow.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Native passionflower vine is the surest way to keep this butterfly around, and the Zebra Longwing with it.

at_a_glance.text: A bright orange butterfly with black markings above and an underside scattered with elongated, mirror-like silver spots.
Its caterpillars eat only passionflower vines — the same host the Zebra Longwing depends on, so one native passionvine supports both butterflies.
The caterpillar is bright orange with rows of black branching spines. The spines look alarming but do not sting.
Despite the name it belongs to the longwing group rather than the true fritillaries.

species.teaser: Closed wings show the trick: the underside is scattered with elongated silver spots that catch the light like tiny mirrors.

quick_hits: Florida's state butterfly is easy to recognize: long, narrow black wings crossed by pale yellow stripes.
Zebra Longwings feed on pollen as well as nectar, an unusual ability among butterflies. Nutrients from the pollen help adults live for several months rather than only a few weeks.

The caterpillars feed on passionflower vines and acquire chemical defenses associated with those plants. Both caterpillars and adults are distasteful to many predators, and the bold wing pattern serves as a warning.
At dusk, Zebra Longwings gather at communal roosts and may return to the same sheltered spot night after night.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas, reaching north into Florida and southern Texas. It is common throughout peninsular Florida, favoring shaded hammocks, woodland edges, and gardens — and it has been the state butterfly since 1996.
more_information: The zebra longwing is unusual on several counts. Most butterflies live only two to four weeks, but the zebra longwing can live several months. The secret is its diet: along with nectar, it gathers and digests pollen, a rare ability among butterflies that supplies extra protein and greatly extends its life.

Its whole life cycle runs through passionflower vines. The caterpillars eat only Passiflora, and in doing so absorb compounds that make the adult butterfly distasteful, even toxic, to predators — which is what the bold black-and-yellow stripes advertise.

It is also social in a way few butterflies are. At dusk, zebra longwings return to shared roosting spots, clustering together overnight for safety, sometimes in groups of dozens, then dispersing again to feed by day with their slow, drifting flight.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Long and narrow, black with pale-yellow stripes.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Slow, graceful, and floating, usually in shade.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Medium-large, with that distinctive elongated wing shape.

identification.what_to_look_for: A black butterfly with thin yellow stripes drifting slowly through a shady garden or wood edge. The long, narrow wings and unhurried, floating flight are unmistakable. At dusk, look for several roosting together.

species.diet: Caterpillars eat only passionflower (Passiflora) leaves. Adults take both nectar and pollen — the pollen-feeding is what gives them their unusually long lives.
species.behavior: Active by day with a slow, graceful flight, favoring shade. Gathers in communal night roosts. Females lay eggs on passionflower vines. Produces several generations a year.
species.ecological_role: A pollinator with a twist — by feeding on pollen it moves it efficiently between flowers — and a passionflower specialist whose presence reflects the health of native vine habitat.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillars feed only on passionflower vines (Passiflora spp.) such as corkystem and purple passionflower — the same vines that support the gulf fritillary. Adults also gather pollen from many flowers.

size.lifespan: up to roughly six months — far longer than most butterflies — thanks to its pollen diet.

species.habitat: Shaded hammocks, woodland edges, thickets, and gardens, especially where passionflower vines grow in dappled light.
species.where_to_look: Drifting slowly through shaded plantings and wood edges, especially near passionflower vines. At dusk, check sheltered spots for small groups roosting together.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident through much of central and southern Florida, active in every month in warm areas.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.
danger.pets: Not a concern; a pet that ate one might find it bitter, but it poses no real danger.

interaction.guidance: Just watch and enjoy, and avoid handling the delicate wings. Planting native passionflower vine is the single best way to support them.

conservation.status: Least Concern, and a point of state pride as Florida's official butterfly.

species.internal_notes: FLORIDA STATE BUTTERFLY — include regardless of count. Re-keyed 2026-06-19 from subspecies H. c. tuckeri (taxon 49765) to species Heliconius charithonia (taxon 49766); Florida race kept in also_known_as and noted in text. obs_stats still reflect the old subspecies key — recompute at species taxon on next pipeline run (likely undercount).

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Bright orange above with large silver-white spots underneath. Zebra Longwings are black with narrow pale-yellow stripes and much longer, narrower wings.

how_it_lives.label: Eating pollen
how_it_lives.text: At flowers, a Zebra Longwing gathers both nectar and pollen. It collects pollen on the proboscis and extracts nutrients from it, giving the adult access to protein and other nutrients that most butterflies do not obtain this way.
Females lay eggs on passionflower vines. The caterpillars feed on the new growth, linking the butterfly's entire reproductive cycle to Passiflora.
Toward evening, individuals gather at sheltered communal roosts.
At dusk they return to shared roosts and cluster together overnight, sometimes dozens at a time, then scatter again to feed by day.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings
how_to_know_it.text: Long and narrow, black with pale yellow stripes.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Slow and floating compared with many other butterflies, often through shaded vegetation.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan about three to four inches.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a black butterfly with narrow pale-yellow stripes and unusually long wings, often moving slowly through shaded gardens and woodland edges. Several may gather at a sheltered roost near dusk.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in shaded gardens, woodland edges and hammock-like plantings, especially around passionflower vines and flowering plants. Near dusk, check sheltered vegetation for communal roosts.
A year-round resident through much of central and southern Florida.

what_it_does_here.label: Passionflower is the whole cycle
what_it_does_here.text: Passionflower vines are essential host plants. Zebra Longwings lay their eggs on Passiflora, and the caterpillars eat the leaves and young growth. Adults are much less specialized and visit many flowers for nectar and pollen. A planting that combines passionflower with a succession of nectar- and pollen-producing blooms supports both stages of the butterfly's life.

Most butterflies live two to four weeks. A Zebra Longwing can live several months, and the difference is pollen: it gathers and digests pollen as well as nectar, which is rare among butterflies, and the extra protein buys it the longer life.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Native passionflower vines are what keep this butterfly here. The caterpillars feed on little else.

at_a_glance.text: Florida's state butterfly is easy to recognize: long, narrow black wings crossed by pale yellow stripes.
Zebra Longwings feed on pollen as well as nectar, an unusual ability among butterflies. Nutrients from the pollen help adults live for several months rather than only a few weeks.

The caterpillars feed on passionflower vines and acquire chemical defenses associated with those plants. Both caterpillars and adults are distasteful to many predators, and the bold wing pattern serves as a warning.
At dusk, Zebra Longwings gather at communal roosts and may return to the same sheltered spot night after night.

species.teaser: Most butterflies live on sugar-rich nectar as adults. Zebra Longwings also collect and digest pollen, gaining nutrients that help them live for several months.

quick_hits: The Green Heron is a small, stocky heron with a dark green-gray back, chestnut neck and dark cap.
It sometimes uses bait, dropping insects, feathers or other small objects onto the water to bring fish within striking range.
It often hunts from a bank or low branch, crouched almost horizontally over the water and partly hidden by vegetation.
At rest the neck looks very short. During a strike it extends suddenly, revealing how much neck was folded into that compact body.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North and Central America. In Florida it occurs year-round around small ponds, marshes, mangroves and other wetlands with dense waterside vegetation.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Small and stocky, only about a foot and a half tall.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Dark green-gray back, chestnut neck and breast, dark cap and yellowish legs.

blocks.label: Posture
blocks.text: Often crouched low and horizontal at the water's edge. The neck is usually drawn in, making the bird look almost neckless until it strikes.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look at shaded, vegetated pond edges for a small dark heron crouched low on a bank or branch. The chestnut neck, dark cap and compact shape separate it from the taller wading birds.

species.diet: Mostly small fish, with insects, crustaceans, frogs and other small animals also taken.
species.behavior: Usually hunts alone from the water's edge, standing or crouching on a bank, root, branch or shallow perch. It waits for prey to approach, then lunges with the bill.
species.sounds: A sharp, explosive skeow is often given as the bird flushes from cover.
species.ecological_role: A predator of small fish and other aquatic animals along vegetated pond and wetland edges.
species.plant_connections: Green Herons use plants as hunting cover as well as nesting structure. Low branches and dense shrubs let them wait directly above the water while remaining concealed, and pairs build stick nests in trees or shrubs near wetlands.

size.length: About a foot and a half tall, with a wingspan a little over two feet.

species.habitat: Small freshwater wetlands, pond and stream edges, marshes, and mangroves with dense vegetation and overhanging branches for cover.
species.where_to_look: Search quiet, vegetated pond margins rather than open water. Green Herons often perch on low branches, roots or banks partly hidden by foliage while watching the water below.
species.when_to_see: Green Herons occur in Florida year-round. Palma Sola has only a few older records, so the park does not yet have enough observations to define local frequency or a seasonal peak.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle an injured or trapped heron; the pointed bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch quietly from a distance and do not feed it. If a bird leaves its perch as you approach, give it more space.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

species.internal_notes: One of the few birds documented to use tools (drops bait to catch fish) — strong 'wow that's good to know' fact for research.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola records are too limited to establish local seasonality.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Larger, gray overall and much heavier-billed, with a bold black-and-white face. Green Herons are smaller, chestnut-necked and usually crouch much lower.
Larger and longer-legged, with a uniform slate-blue adult body. Green Herons are stockier with a chestnut neck.

how_it_lives.text: It usually hunts alone from a bank, root or low branch at the water's edge, waiting for small fish, insects, frogs and other prey to move within reach.

how_it_lives.label: Fishing with bait
how_it_lives.text: Green Herons sometimes place an insect, feather or other small object on the water. A fish approaching the object may move within striking range.
Pairs build stick nests in trees or shrubs near water, usually as isolated pairs or small groups rather than in the large mixed colonies many other herons favor.

how_to_know_it.text: Small and stocky, only about a foot and a half tall, with a wingspan a little over two feet.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Dark green-gray back, chestnut neck and breast, dark cap and yellowish legs.

how_to_know_it.text: A sharp, explosive skeow is often given as the bird flushes from cover — frequently the first sign it was there at all.
