how_to_know_it.text: Look at shaded, vegetated pond edges for a small dark heron crouched low on a bank or branch. The chestnut neck, dark cap and compact shape separate it from the taller wading birds.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Search quiet, vegetated pond margins rather than open water. Green Herons often perch on low branches, roots or banks partly hidden by foliage while watching the water below.
Occurs in Florida year-round, but Palma Sola has only a few older records, so local frequency is not established.

what_it_does_here.label: Cover is the hunting perch
what_it_does_here.text: Green Herons use plants as hunting cover as well as nesting structure. Low branches and dense shrubs let them wait directly above the water while remaining concealed, and pairs build stick nests in trees or shrubs near wetlands.

at_a_glance.text: The Green Heron is a small, stocky heron with a dark green-gray back, chestnut neck and dark cap.
It sometimes uses bait, dropping insects, feathers or other small objects onto the water to bring fish within striking range.
It often hunts from a bank or low branch, crouched almost horizontally over the water and partly hidden by vegetation.
At rest the neck looks very short. During a strike it extends suddenly, revealing how much neck was folded into that compact body.

species.teaser: Green Herons sometimes place an insect, feather or other small object on the water and wait for a fish to approach it.

quick_hits: A large, clear lemon-yellow butterfly crossing gardens and open spaces with a quick, restless flight.
The species name sennae comes from Senna, the group of pea-family plants its caterpillars eat.
Its long tongue reaches into deep tubular flowers that many other insects cannot use — red blooms especially.
Numbers rise noticeably in autumn as butterflies move south down the peninsula.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas and common across the southern United States, ranging north in summer. In Florida it is a year-round resident and breeder, with numbers swelling in fall as northern butterflies move south.
more_information: The cloudless sulphur is one of Florida's most familiar butterflies — those flickering patches of pure yellow crossing a lawn or garden are usually this species.

Its life is tied to plants in the genus Senna (and the closely related Cassia), members of the pea family. The caterpillars feed on their leaves and flowers, and a caterpillar munching yellow blossoms often turns yellow itself, blending neatly into its meal. The butterfly's scientific name, Phoebis sennae, even records the connection.

In autumn, cloudless sulphurs join a broad southward movement of butterflies down the peninsula. With an extra-long proboscis, the adults can drink from long, tubular flowers — they are especially fond of red ones — that shorter-tongued butterflies cannot use.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Large and lemon-yellow; males clear yellow, females yellow to whitish with a dark wing border and a small dark spot.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Among the larger common yellow butterflies.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Fast and somewhat erratic.

identification.what_to_look_for: A big, bright yellow butterfly moving quickly across open ground or nectaring at tubular flowers. The clear, unmarked yellow of the male is the easiest clue; females are paler with darker edges.

species.diet: Caterpillars feed on Senna and Cassia plants. Adults nectar at many flowers, favoring long, tubular blooms — especially red ones — that suit their long tongue.
species.behavior: Active by day with a fast, restless flight. Breeds through several generations a year and joins a southward migration in fall. Males often gather at damp ground to 'puddle,' sipping water and minerals.
species.ecological_role: A wide-ranging pollinator that reaches deep flowers other insects cannot, and a specialist on Senna plants that ties it to the pea family.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillar host plants are Senna and Cassia (pea family) — including native privet senna (Senna ligustrina) and partridge pea — the very plants the butterfly is named for.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks; several generations are produced each year.

species.habitat: Open, sunny places — gardens, fields, roadsides, edges, and parks — wherever Senna host plants and nectar flowers grow.
species.where_to_look: Flitting across open, sunny areas and visiting nectar flowers, especially anywhere Senna or Cassia plants are growing. Most numerous in late summer and fall.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, with a noticeable increase during the fall southward migration.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Just watch and enjoy. Planting native Senna (such as privet senna or partridge pea) gives the caterpillars a home.

conservation.status: Least Concern. One of Florida's most common and widespread butterflies.

seasonality.note: Present year-round in Florida, with numbers rising in autumn.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day with a fast, restless flight, breeding through several generations a year.

how_it_lives.label: Puddling
how_it_lives.text: Males often gather on damp ground, sipping water and dissolved minerals — a source of salts they cannot get from nectar.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Large and lemon-yellow. Males clear yellow; females yellow to whitish with a dark wing border and a small dark spot.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Among the larger common yellow butterflies, with a wingspan up to about three inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Fast and restless, rarely settling for long.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: A flickering patch of pure yellow crossing a lawn or bed. Most of the yellow butterflies moving quickly across open ground here are this one.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Watch open, sunny areas and nectar flowers, especially anywhere Senna or Cassia is growing.
Present year-round in Florida, with more on the wing during the autumn movement south.

what_it_does_here.label: Named for its host plant
what_it_does_here.text: The caterpillars eat Senna and Cassia — pea-family plants including native privet senna and partridge pea. The butterfly is literally named after them, and without those plants in the landscape it cannot complete its life cycle here.
A caterpillar feeding on yellow Senna blossoms often turns yellow itself and vanishes into its meal.

In autumn they join a broad southward movement of butterflies down the peninsula. An extra-long proboscis lets the adults drink from long tubular flowers, including many red and orange ones, that shorter-tongued butterflies cannot reach.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Native Senna — privet senna or partridge pea — gives the caterpillars a home.

at_a_glance.text: A large, clear lemon-yellow butterfly crossing gardens and open spaces with a quick, restless flight.
The species name sennae comes from Senna, the group of pea-family plants its caterpillars eat.
Its long tongue reaches into deep tubular flowers that many other insects cannot use, including many red and orange blooms.
In autumn they join a broad southward movement of butterflies down the Florida peninsula.

species.teaser: Its scientific name gives away its host plant: sennae, for the Senna it cannot breed without.

quick_hits: A pale, chalky-white butterfly with faint tan markings, dark eyespots and scalloped, orange-edged wings.
It stays low, flying just above the ground in damp, open places like pond edges, ditches and wet fields.
Its caterpillars feed on low native groundcovers — frogfruit and water hyssop — the same plants that carpet moist pond margins.
Males defend small territories around the host plants, patrolling a patch of damp ground.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, the Caribbean, Mexico, and South America. In Florida it is a common, year-round resident of low, moist, open habitats, especially in the central and southern parts of the state.
more_information: The white peacock is a butterfly of wet, open ground. You will rarely see it high in the air; instead it flutters low over damp fields, ditches, and pond margins, close to the small plants its caterpillars depend on.

Those host plants — frogfruit and water hyssop especially — are humble, low-growing natives that thrive at the water's edge, exactly the kind of groundcover a pond-side planting provides. Where they grow, white peacocks tend to follow.

Male white peacocks are notably territorial for a butterfly, staking out a small area around the host plants and actively driving off rival males and other insects that intrude — a lot of bustle from such a delicate-looking creature.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Chalky white with faint light-brown markings.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Scalloped edges trimmed in orange, with small dark eyespots.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Low and close to the ground.

identification.what_to_look_for: A pale, whitish butterfly flying low over damp, open ground near water, showing orange-trimmed, scalloped wings and small dark spots. Its habit of staying near the ground around pond edges is a good clue.

species.diet: Caterpillars feed on low native plants, chiefly frogfruit and water hyssop. Adults sip nectar from low-growing flowers such as Spanish needles and frogfruit.
species.behavior: Active by day, flying low to the ground. Males defend small territories around host plants. Breeds through multiple generations across the warm months.
species.ecological_role: A pollinator of low, moist-ground flowers and a specialist on creeping native groundcovers — a small but telling member of the pond-edge community.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillar host plants are low native groundcovers — frogfruit (Phyla nodiflora) and water hyssop (Bacopa monnieri) — the same plants that carpet moist pond edges.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks; several generations are produced each year.

species.habitat: Low, damp, open places — pond and marsh edges, ditches, wet fields, and parks — wherever its low-growing host plants occur.
species.where_to_look: Flying low around the moist edges of the ponds and in damp open ground, especially near frogfruit and other low groundcovers.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, most numerous in the warm months. Look low to the ground near water.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Just watch and enjoy. Low plantings of native frogfruit and water hyssop near water are the best way to invite them in.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and secure in Florida, though always tied to the moist, low habitats it needs.

seasonality.note: Present year-round in Florida, most numerous in the warm months.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day, flying low to the ground. Males defend small territories around host plants, and several generations follow one another through the warm months.
Adults sip nectar from low-growing flowers such as Spanish needles and frogfruit.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Chalky white with faint light-brown markings.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings
how_to_know_it.text: Scalloped edges trimmed in orange, with small dark eyespots.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Low and close to the ground, rarely rising far above the vegetation.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan around two to two and a half inches.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: A pale, whitish butterfly working low over damp open ground near water. Look down rather than up.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Flying low around the moist edges of the ponds and in damp open ground, especially near frogfruit and other low groundcovers.
Present year-round in Florida and most numerous in the warm months.

what_it_does_here.label: Groundcover is the habitat
what_it_does_here.text: The caterpillars eat frogfruit and water hyssop — creeping native plants easy to mistake for weeds. Where those groundcovers are left to spread along a damp margin, this butterfly follows; where the same ground is mown short or cleared, it does not.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Low plantings of native frogfruit and water hyssop near water are the best way to invite them in.

at_a_glance.text: A pale, chalky-white butterfly with faint tan markings, dark eyespots and scalloped, orange-edged wings.
It stays low, flying just above the ground in damp, open places like pond edges, ditches and wet fields.
Its caterpillars feed on low native groundcovers — frogfruit and water hyssop — the same plants that carpet moist pond margins.
Males defend small territories around the host plants, patrolling a patch of damp ground.

species.teaser: It flies only a foot or so above the ground, tied to the low creeping plants that carpet damp pond edges.

quick_hits: The Florida red-bellied cooter is a large, dark basking turtle named for the reddish wash on its underside and shell.
It is a Florida native, at home in the state's ponds, lakes, and slow rivers.
Adults are mostly vegetarian, grazing on underwater plants — turtles that essentially tend the pond's vegetable garden.
It has an unusual nesting trick: females sometimes lay their eggs right in the warm nest mounds of alligators, where the guarding gator unintentionally protects them.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Florida and a bit of southern Georgia. It is one of the common large freshwater turtles across the Florida peninsula.
more_information: The red-bellied cooter is one of the big, dark turtles hauled out to bask alongside sliders and other cooters on sunny days, told apart by the reddish tones on its shell and the red wash on its underside (the plastron).
Like its cousin the peninsular cooter, the adult is largely a plant-eater, grazing submerged vegetation — a useful role in keeping pond plant growth in balance.

Its most surprising habit is where it nests. Females will sometimes dig their nests directly into the mounded nests of American alligators. The female gator, fiercely guarding her own eggs, ends up shielding the turtle eggs too — an accidental partnership that gives the cooter's eggs protection they would not have on an open bank.

blocks.label: Shell
blocks.text: High-domed and dark, with reddish vertical bars on the side scutes.

blocks.label: Underside (plastron)
blocks.text: Washed with orange to reddish color.

blocks.label: Head
blocks.text: Dark with yellow stripes, including an arrow-shaped stripe between the eyes.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Large, with females bigger than males.

identification.what_to_look_for: A big, dark, high-domed turtle basking at the pond, showing reddish bars on the shell. The red-tinted underside and the arrow-shaped head stripe help separate it from the similar sliders and peninsular cooter.

species.diet: Adults are mostly herbivorous, grazing on submerged aquatic plants and algae; young turtles also take some insects and other small animals.
species.behavior: Active by day. Alternates basking on logs and banks with feeding dives. Wary, sliding into the water when approached. Nests on land, sometimes within alligator nest mounds.
species.ecological_role: A plant-grazing turtle that helps shape underwater vegetation, with eggs and young that feed many predators — and an unusual nesting link to alligators.
species.plant_connections: Adults graze largely on submerged aquatic plants and algae, making this cooter one of the pond's natural plant-grazers.

size.shell_length: 8 to 13 inches, with large females reaching about 15 inches
size.lifespan: long-lived, often 20 to 30 years or more.

species.habitat: Freshwater ponds, lakes, marshes, springs, and slow rivers with abundant aquatic plants and good basking spots.
species.where_to_look: Basking on logs and banks at the ponds on sunny days, often among sliders and peninsular cooters. Look for the reddish tones on the shell.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Most visible basking on warm, sunny days.

danger.people: Harmless if left alone; may nip if handled, so it is best not to pick one up.
danger.pets: No real danger to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not handle or feed it. Let basking turtles keep their sunning spots.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common in suitable Florida fresh water.

seasonality.note: Most visible basking on warm, sunny days.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The peninsular cooter has yellow hairpin-loop stripes on the head; the red-bellied cooter has a reddish belly and a red arrow mark between the eyes.
Sliders are smaller with a colored ear patch behind the eye; the red-bellied cooter is larger and lacks it.

how_it_lives.text: Day after day it alternates basking on a log or bank with diving to feed, and it is wary — approach and it is gone into the water.
Adults graze on submerged plants and algae; young turtles take some insects and small animals as well.

how_to_know_it.label: Shell
how_to_know_it.text: High-domed and dark, with reddish vertical bars on the side plates.

how_to_know_it.label: Underside
how_to_know_it.text: Washed with orange to red.

how_to_know_it.label: Head
how_to_know_it.text: Dark with yellow stripes, including an arrow-shaped mark between the eyes.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Large, with females bigger than males.
From above, look for the reddish bars on the shell and the arrow-shaped mark on the head. The reddish underside is useful when you can see it, but a basking turtle often will not show it.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Basking on logs and banks at the ponds on sunny days, usually among sliders and peninsular cooters. Look for the reddish tones in the shell.
A year-round resident, most visible when the sun is out.

what_it_does_here.text: Adults graze underwater plants and algae, which is unusual for a pond turtle and makes this one of the pond's plant-grazers. Young turtles take insects and other small animals before shifting over to a plant diet.

Females sometimes dig their nests straight into the mounds built by American Alligators. The mound is warm, and a female alligator guarding her own eggs may incidentally discourage predators that would otherwise dig up the turtle eggs alongside them.
what_it_does_here.label: Alligator nest mounds

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Watch from a distance and do not handle or feed them. A basking turtle driven off its log has lost the sun time it came for, and like any turtle it may nip if picked up.

at_a_glance.text: A large, dark basking turtle named for the reddish wash on its shell and underside.
Females sometimes lay their eggs inside an alligator's nest mound, where the guarding gator shelters them without meaning to.
Adults are almost entirely vegetarian, grazing on underwater plants.
Told from the park's other big turtles by the red arrow between the eyes and the reddish bars along the shell.

quick_hits: Pond Sliders are medium-sized freshwater turtles that often bask on logs and banks, dropping quickly into the water when disturbed.

Two forms occur in Florida. Yellow-bellied Sliders, with a large yellow cheek patch, are native only to northern Florida. Red-eared Sliders, with a red stripe behind the eye, are introduced in Florida and widespread through the peninsula.
Red-eared Sliders spread largely through released pets. In Florida they compete with native turtles for food and basking sites and can hybridize with native Yellow-bellied Sliders.
Young sliders eat more animal prey; vegetation becomes increasingly important as they mature.
species.range_and_origin: The native yellow-bellied slider (Trachemys scripta scripta) belongs to the southeastern U.S., including north Florida. The red-eared slider (Trachemys scripta elegans) is native to the Mississippi Valley, not Florida — but released pets have spread it across much of the peninsula and beyond.
more_information: 'Pond slider' covers two subspecies that look similar but tell very different stories in Florida. The yellow-bellied slider is a true native. The red-eared slider — the little green turtle once sold by the millions in pet stores — comes from farther west and does not naturally belong here.

The trouble starts when people release pet turtles they can no longer keep. Red-eared sliders are hardy and adaptable, and in the wild they compete with native turtles for basking sites and food, and can interbreed with the native yellow-bellied slider, blurring its genetic line. Globally, the red-eared slider is listed among the world's worst invasive species, largely because of the pet trade.

The takeaway for visitors is simple: enjoy the turtles basking on the park's logs, but never release a pet turtle into a pond. What looks like a kindness can quietly harm the native wildlife already living there.

blocks.label: Shell
blocks.text: Smooth, oval, olive-green to brown with yellow markings, darkening with age.

blocks.label: Head stripe
blocks.text: A yellow patch behind the eye (yellow-bellied) or a red stripe behind the eye (red-eared) — the key to telling the two apart.

blocks.label: Skin
blocks.text: Dark with yellow stripes.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Females larger than males.

identification.what_to_look_for: A medium turtle basking on a log, with yellow stripes on the head and neck. Check just behind the eye: a yellow blotch points to the native yellow-bellied slider; a red stripe points to the introduced red-eared slider.

species.diet: Omnivorous. Young sliders eat mostly insects, tadpoles, snails, and small fish; adults shift toward aquatic plants and algae.
species.behavior: Active by day. Spends long stretches basking on logs and banks to warm up, sliding quickly into the water when disturbed, and forages in between.
species.ecological_role: A basking pond turtle that grazes vegetation and scavenges. The native yellow-bellied slider is part of Florida's natural pond life, while released red-eared sliders can crowd out native turtles.
species.plant_connections: Adults graze on submerged aquatic plants and algae (younger turtles eat more animal prey) and bask among pond-edge vegetation.

size.shell_length: up to roughly 12 inches; females larger than males
size.lifespan: commonly 20 to 30 years, longer in captivity.

species.habitat: Almost any quiet fresh water — ponds, lakes, marshes, canals, and slow rivers — with basking logs and soft, vegetated bottoms.
species.where_to_look: Basking on logs, banks, and debris at the ponds on sunny days, often several together. Look behind the eye to tell native from introduced.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Most visible basking on warm, sunny days.

danger.people: Harmless if left alone; like any turtle it may nip if handled, so it is best not to pick one up.
danger.pets: No real danger to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance, and never release a pet turtle into the park or any wild pond — released red-eared sliders harm native turtles. Do not handle or feed them.

invasive.notes: Mixed at the species level. Yellow-bellied Sliders are native to northern Florida but not naturally to the Bradenton area. Red-eared Sliders are introduced and invasive in Florida, spread largely through the pet trade. They compete with native turtles and can hybridize with native Yellow-bellied Sliders.

conservation.status: The species overall is Least Concern and abundant. The concern is local and genetic: released red-eared sliders pressuring native yellow-bellied sliders and red-bellied turtles.

species.internal_notes: Species-level entry spanning two subspecies: native yellow-bellied slider and introduced red-eared slider (released pets). Invasive flag = Yellow to reflect the red-eared subspecies; Conservation = Green because the species overall is abundant. Strong responsible-pet-ownership teaching animal. native:false is intentional and reflects the introduced red-eared subspecies that dominates released-pet populations here; the native yellow-bellied subspecies is acknowledged in the species text. Do not 'correct' native to true.

seasonality.note: Present year-round in Florida. Most visible while basking in warm, sunny weather; Palma Sola currently has too few records to estimate local frequency.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Larger and lacks the prominent red or yellow patch behind the eye. Peninsular Cooters instead show fine yellow striping on the head.
Usually larger, without an ear patch, and often shows reddish color on the underside of the shell.

how_it_lives.text: Basking lets a slider raise its body temperature before returning to the water to feed. An approached turtle usually drops quickly from its perch into the pond.
Young sliders eat insects and other small aquatic animals more heavily. As they mature, aquatic vegetation makes up a larger part of the diet.

how_to_know_it.label: Shape
how_to_know_it.text: A medium-sized, fairly rounded pond turtle with yellow stripes on the head, neck and legs. The shell reaches about a foot long, and females grow larger than males.

how_to_know_it.label: Red-eared form
how_to_know_it.text: A broad red stripe behind the eye. The shell is usually olive to dark brown with yellow patterning.

how_to_know_it.label: Yellow-bellied form
how_to_know_it.text: A large yellow patch behind the eye rather than a red stripe.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look behind the eye. A red stripe identifies a Red-eared Slider, an introduced form in Florida. A large yellow cheek patch indicates a Yellow-bellied Slider, whose natural Florida range is farther north.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look for sliders basking on logs, banks or floating debris around the ponds on warm sunny days. Check the colored patch behind the eye before deciding which form you are seeing.
Present year-round in Florida and easiest to notice while basking in warm, sunny weather. Palma Sola currently has too few records to estimate local frequency.

what_it_does_here.label: Two forms, two geographies
what_it_does_here.text: The Yellow-bellied Slider is native to the southeastern United States and reaches only northern Florida naturally. The Red-eared Slider is native farther west in the Mississippi drainage but has been introduced widely through the pet trade and now occurs throughout much of Florida. A slider basking here is unlikely to be a naturally occurring animal either way.

what_it_does_here.label: Plants in the pond
what_it_does_here.text: Aquatic plants become increasingly important food as sliders mature. Dense submerged and shoreline vegetation also provides cover for young turtles and the small aquatic animals they eat.

take_care.text: Do not handle. A frightened turtle may bite in self-defense. Keep dogs from approaching or chasing turtles on land.

Watch without handling or feeding. Never release a pet turtle into a park pond or other natural waterway. Florida's Exotic Pet Amnesty Program provides an alternative for owners who can no longer keep nonnative pets.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: The species as a whole is widespread. In Florida, the conservation issue is not scarcity of sliders but the effect of introduced Red-eared Sliders on native freshwater turtles and on the genetic integrity of native Yellow-bellied Slider populations.

at_a_glance.text: Pond Sliders are medium-sized freshwater turtles that often bask on logs and banks, dropping quickly into the water when disturbed.

Two forms occur in Florida. Yellow-bellied Sliders, with a large yellow cheek patch, are native only to northern Florida. Red-eared Sliders, with a red stripe behind the eye, are introduced in Florida and widespread through the peninsula.
Red-eared Sliders spread largely through released pets. In Florida they compete with native turtles for food and basking sites and can hybridize with native Yellow-bellied Sliders.
Young sliders eat more animal prey; vegetation becomes increasingly important as they mature.

species.teaser: The red patch behind many Florida pond turtles tells a human story: Red-eared Sliders were spread far beyond their native range through the pet trade.

quick_hits: Adults are gray with a black head, broad white cheek patch and pale yellow crown.
Crabs and crayfish dominate the diet, which helps explain the species' unusually stout, heavy bill.
Despite the name, Yellow-crowned Night Herons feed in daylight as well as after dark. In coastal habitats, feeding activity may follow the tides more closely than the clock.
Young birds are brown and spotted and can look surprisingly similar to young Black-crowned Night Herons.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. In Florida it occurs year-round in coastal wetlands, mangroves, swamps and inland areas where crabs or crayfish are abundant.

blocks.label: Adults
blocks.text: Gray body, black head, broad white cheek patch and pale yellow crown. Breeding birds grow long pale head plumes.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Thick, heavy and black.

blocks.label: Young
blocks.text: Brown with pale spots and streaks. Young birds lack the adult's bold face pattern and are much harder to separate from young Black-crowned Night Herons.

identification.what_to_look_for: Adults are compact gray herons with a bold black-and-white face and thick black bill. They often walk slowly with the body angled forward while searching shallow water, mud or wet ground for crustaceans.

species.diet: Mostly crabs and crayfish, with fish, insects and other small aquatic animals also taken.
species.behavior: Forages alone much of the time, walking slowly and leaning forward as it searches shallow water and wet ground. Feeding can occur by day or at night.
species.ecological_role: A predator specialized heavily on crabs and crayfish in coastal and inland wetlands.
species.plant_connections: Yellow-crowned Night Herons roost and nest in trees and shrubs near water. Documented nest sites include oaks, pines, mangroves, myrtles and other woody plants. The stick platform may be lined with leaves, vines or Spanish moss.

size.length: About two feet tall, with a wingspan around three and a half feet.

species.habitat: Coastal marshes, mangroves, estuaries, and tidal flats, plus inland swamps, wooded wetlands, and pond edges with crabs or crayfish.
species.where_to_look: Look along pond margins, wet ground and other shallow areas where crayfish or crabs are available. During rest periods, check waterside trees and shrubs.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola has only a few records, so local frequency and peak timing are not yet established.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle an injured or trapped heron; the pointed bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Give feeding and roosting birds enough room to remain in place.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently state-listed in Florida or considered globally threatened.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local seasonal pattern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Adults are straightforward: Black-crowned has a black back over pale gray wings, while Yellow-crowned is gray-bodied with a strongly patterned black-and-white face. Juveniles of the two species are much harder to separate and may require a close view of bill shape, leg proportions and spotting.

how_it_lives.text: It walks slowly through shallow water and wet ground, searching mainly for crabs and crayfish. Feeding may occur in daylight or after dark.
It roosts and nests in trees and shrubs, either alone or in colonies. Some nesting sites are reused for many years.

how_to_know_it.label: Adults
how_to_know_it.text: Gray body, black head, broad white cheek patch and pale yellow crown. Breeding birds grow long pale plumes off the back of the head.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Thick, heavy and black.

how_to_know_it.label: Young birds
how_to_know_it.text: Brown with pale spots and streaks, without the adult's bold face pattern.
A feeding bird walks slowly with its body tilted forward, watching shallow water and wet ground ahead of it.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Pond margins and wet ground where crayfish are available. When the bird is resting rather than feeding, check the waterside trees and shrubs instead.
In Florida year-round. The park has only a few records — too few to say anything useful about the time of year.

what_it_does_here.text: The heavy bill explains the diet. This is a crab and crayfish specialist, and the bill is built to crack them rather than to spear fish.
The name is only half right. They feed in daylight as readily as after dark, and on the coast the timing follows the tide more closely than the clock.
They roost and nest in waterside trees and shrubs — oaks, pines, mangroves and myrtles have all been used — building a stick platform lined with leaves, vines or Spanish moss.

at_a_glance.text: Adults are gray with a black head, a broad white cheek patch and a pale yellow crown.
Crabs and crayfish dominate the diet, which is why the bill is so unusually heavy.
Young birds are brown and spotted, and can be very hard to tell from young Black-crowned Night Herons.

species.teaser: The heavy bill tells you what it eats: Yellow-crowned Night Herons specialize on crabs and crayfish.

quick_hits: Males are bright red with a pointed crest, a black face mask and a stout orange-red bill.
Females are warm buff-brown with red tinges on the crest, wings and tail, and the same heavy orange bill.
Both sexes sing. In many North American songbirds only the male does.
Cardinals hold the same territory all year rather than migrating, so a pair may be the same birds you saw last season.
species.range_and_origin: Native and widespread across the eastern and central United States; a common, year-round resident throughout Florida. It does not migrate, holding the same territory all year.
more_information: The cardinal is a year-round neighbor rather than a seasonal visitor — pairs often hold the same territory through every season, which is part of why they feel so familiar.

They are unusual among songbirds in that the female sings as readily as the male, and the two will trade phrases back and forth. During courtship you may also catch a tender behavior called mate-feeding, where the male passes a seed to the female beak-to-beak.
Everything about that heavy, conical bill is built for seeds: it lets the cardinal crack tough seed coats many birds cannot, so it thrives wherever seed-bearing plants and feeders are found.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Bright red overall, with a pointed crest, black face mask, and stout orange-red bill.

blocks.label: Female
blocks.text: Warm buff-brown with reddish tinges on the crest, wings, and tail, and the same orange bill.

blocks.label: Both
blocks.text: A tall crest and a short, thick, cone-shaped bill.

identification.what_to_look_for: A crested songbird with a heavy orange bill — vivid red if a male, soft brown with red accents if a female. Listen for clear, whistled 'cheer-cheer-cheer' and 'birdy-birdy-birdy' phrases from both sexes.

species.diet: Mainly seeds and grains, plus fruits, berries, and insects — especially in summer, when insects feed the growing young.
species.behavior: Active by day, year-round, usually in pairs or small family groups. Forages on or near the ground and in shrubs, and comes readily to feeders. Males may even attack their own reflection in a window during breeding season, mistaking it for a rival.
species.sounds: Clear, whistled songs — phrases like 'cheer-cheer-cheer' and 'birdy-birdy-birdy' — sung by both sexes, plus a sharp metallic 'chip' note.
species.ecological_role: A seed- and fruit-eater that helps disperse the seeds of native plants, and an insect-eater that helps keep bug numbers down while raising young.
species.plant_connections: Eats the seeds, fruits, and berries of many native shrubs and trees and nests in dense shrubbery — so seed- and berry-bearing native plantings draw cardinals in.

size.length: 8 to 9 inches
size.lifespan: commonly up to roughly 3 years, sometimes much longer.

species.habitat: Woodland edges, thickets, shrubby gardens, and backyards with dense cover for nesting and seed-bearing plants for food.
species.where_to_look: In shrubs, hedges, and woodland edges, often near the ground. The male's red is easy to spot; listen for the loud, clear whistles of both sexes.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, active by day in every season.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Simply enjoy them. A feeder with seeds is the easiest way to welcome cardinals, but they do just fine on natural food in the park.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Abundant and even expanding its range, and one of the most familiar birds in the region.

how_it_lives.text: Usually in pairs or small family groups, foraging on or near the ground and in shrubs. Cardinals do not migrate and defend the same territory through the year.
Mostly seeds and grain, with fruit, berries and insects added — insects especially while raising young.
The female sings as readily as the male, which is unusual among songbirds, and a pair will trade phrases back and forth. In courtship the male passes her a seed beak-to-beak.
The heavy conical bill does the work of a nutcracker, splitting seed coats too tough for most birds its size.

how_to_know_it.label: Male
how_to_know_it.text: Bright red overall, with a pointed crest, black face mask and stout orange-red bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Female
how_to_know_it.text: Warm buff-brown with reddish tinges on the crest, wings and tail, and the same heavy orange bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About eight or nine inches long, with a wingspan around a foot.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Clear whistled phrases — cheer-cheer-cheer, birdy-birdy-birdy — sung by both sexes, plus a sharp metallic chip note.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look low in shrubs and along woodland edges rather than high in the canopy. The whistles carry further than the bird is visible.

where_to_find_it_here.text: In shrubs, hedges and woodland edges, often near the ground. Listen for the loud clear whistles of either sex.
A year-round resident, active by day in every season.

what_it_does_here.label: Seeds and thickets
what_it_does_here.text: Cardinals need two things from plants at once: seed- and berry-bearing shrubs and trees for food, and dense shrubbery to nest in. A planting that supplies both — fruiting natives with thick cover beneath — is what keeps a pair resident rather than passing through.

at_a_glance.text: Males are bright red with a pointed crest and black face mask; females are warm buff-brown with red tinges. Both carry the same stout orange-red bill.
Both sexes sing. In many North American songbirds only the male does.
That heavy conical bill is a seed-cracker, opening tough seeds many birds cannot manage.
Cardinals hold the same territory all year rather than migrating, so a pair may be the same birds you saw last season.

species.teaser: Both sexes sing, which is unusual among North American songbirds — and a female often sings from the nest.

quick_hits: Eastern Screech-Owls have been found roosting in Palma Sola's fruit trees, sitting motionless against bark where their patterned feathers make them easy to overlook.
Despite the name, its familiar songs are not screeches. Listen for a descending whinny or a steady, even trill after dark.
It is only about eight or nine inches tall — roughly the height of a soda can — with feather tufts on the head that look like ears but are not.
Eastern Screech-Owls occur in gray and reddish-brown forms. Both are patterned with streaks and bars that blend closely with tree bark.
species.range_and_origin: The Eastern Screech-Owl ranges across the eastern United States; the form here is the Florida subspecies. It is a common, year-round resident of woodlands, suburbs, and parks anywhere there are trees with cavities for nesting.
more_information: The screech-owl is a master of staying hidden. By day it tucks into a tree cavity or sits tight against a trunk, where its bark-patterned feathers make it nearly invisible. Many people live alongside screech-owls for years without ever noticing one.
It comes in two color morphs, a gray form and a reddish form, and both can turn up in the same area, even within the same family.

Though it is a capable predator of insects, small mammals, birds, and reptiles, its voice is anything but fearsome. The usual calls are a soft, horse-like whinny that falls in pitch and a steady trilling purr — far gentler than the word 'screech' suggests. Like many owls, it nests in tree cavities and will readily take to a nest box.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Small — roughly eight to nine inches tall, about the size of a soda can.

blocks.label: Ear tufts
blocks.text: Two feather tufts that can be raised or flattened (not actually ears).

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Either gray or reddish-brown, both heavily patterned to mimic bark.

blocks.label: Eyes
blocks.text: Yellow.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small, stocky owl with ear tufts, roosting quietly in a tree cavity or against a trunk by day. It is far more often heard than seen — listen at dusk for a soft, descending whinny or a steady trill.

species.diet: A varied hunter — large insects, spiders, earthworms, small rodents, lizards, frogs, and small birds, caught mostly at night.
species.behavior: Active at night, roosting by day in cavities or tucked against bark. Hunts from a perch, dropping onto prey below. Nests in tree cavities and nest boxes. Generally solitary or in pairs.
species.sounds: Two main calls, neither a true screech: a soft, descending whinny like a small horse, and an even, trilling purr on one pitch. Most often heard at dusk and after dark.
species.ecological_role: A nighttime predator that helps keep insect and rodent numbers in check, and a cavity-dependent species — a good reason hollow and dead trees have real value in a healthy woodland.
species.plant_connections: Depends on trees with natural cavities — often old oaks and other hardwoods — for roosting and nesting, and readily uses nest boxes where old trees are scarce.

size.length: about 8.5 inches
size.lifespan: commonly up to roughly 8 to 10 years in the wild.

species.habitat: Woodlands, forest edges, swamps, suburbs, and parks with mature trees and natural cavities for roosting and nesting.
species.where_to_look: Among mature trees — scan cavities and quiet, shaded trunks by day, and listen for soft whinnies and trills at dusk. Far more often heard than seen.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Active at night; daytime sightings usually mean a roosting bird tucked into a cavity or against bark.

danger.people: Harmless to visitors. Screech-owls are small, secretive, and pose no threat to people.
danger.pets: No danger to pets under normal circumstances.

interaction.guidance: If you find a roosting owl, enjoy it quietly from a distance and move on — daytime disturbance robs it of rest. Never disturb a nest cavity.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and adaptable, though it depends on trees with natural cavities and benefits from nest boxes where old trees are scarce.

species.internal_notes: Owl = high visitor appeal. Re-keyed 2026-06-19 from subspecies M. a. floridanus (taxon 725930) to species Megascops asio (taxon 19765); Florida race kept in also_known_as and noted in text. obs_stats updated from project view (2 obs / 2 observers: robcarr52 species-level + brice_c subspecies-level — the latter was all the old subspecies key was catching).

seasonality.note: Year-round resident in Florida. Palma Sola has only a few documented records, so local frequency is not yet well established.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much larger, with a wingspan measured in feet rather than inches. Both have ear tufts and yellow eyes, but an Eastern Screech-Owl is only about soda-can height.

how_it_lives.text: Hunts mainly at night from low or middle-height perches, dropping or flying out after prey. Large insects, spiders, earthworms, small rodents, lizards, frogs and small birds are all taken.
By day it roosts in tree cavities or against bark. Pairs nest in natural cavities and readily use nest boxes.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Small — about eight to nine inches tall.

how_to_know_it.label: Ear tufts
how_to_know_it.text: Two feather tufts can be raised or flattened. They are not the owl's ears.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Either gray or reddish-brown, with heavy streaking and barring that breaks up the bird's outline against bark. The eyes are yellow.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The two familiar songs are a descending whinny and an even-pitched trill. Eastern Screech-Owls also give other calls, including alarm barks and occasional screeches.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: By day, look closely at tree cavities and shaded trunks for a small, stocky owl with ear tufts. At night, the descending whinny or steady trill is usually the easier way to find one.

how_to_know_it.label: Two colours
how_to_know_it.text: It comes in a gray form and a reddish form, and both can turn up in the same area — sometimes in the same family.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Nothing about the voice matches the name. The usual calls are a soft, horse-like whinny that falls away in pitch, and a steady trilling purr.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in mature trees, especially around natural cavities and shaded trunks. At dusk and after dark, listen in wooded parts of the park for whinnies and trills.

A year-round Florida resident, active mainly at night. A daytime sighting usually involves a bird resting in or near a tree cavity. Palma Sola has only a few documented records, so local frequency is not yet well established.

what_it_does_here.text: Everything depends on holes in trees. The owl cannot cut its own, so it roosts and nests in cavities made by woodpeckers or opened by decay, which makes standing dead wood the limit on whether a screech-owl can live somewhere at all.

what_it_does_here.label: Why old trees matter
what_it_does_here.text: Trees are essential habitat. Eastern Screech-Owls roost and nest in natural cavities, often in mature hardwoods, and use the surrounding branches as hunting perches. Old trees, snags and trees with cavities therefore provide habitat that younger, uniformly pruned plantings cannot replace.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle or approach a nesting or injured owl.
If you find a roosting owl, watch quietly from a distance and let it rest. Never approach a nest cavity or repeatedly draw other visitors to a roosting bird.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern. The species depends on natural cavities and can benefit where mature cavity-bearing trees are retained.

at_a_glance.text: Eastern Screech-Owls have been found roosting in Palma Sola's fruit trees, sitting motionless against bark where their patterned feathers make them easy to overlook.
Despite the name, its familiar songs are not screeches. Listen for a descending whinny or a steady, even trill after dark.
It is only about eight or nine inches tall — roughly the height of a soda can — with feather tufts on the head that look like ears but are not.
Eastern Screech-Owls occur in gray and reddish-brown forms. Both are patterned with streaks and bars that blend closely with tree bark.

species.teaser: An Eastern Screech-Owl can spend the entire day pressed against bark or sitting at a tree-cavity entrance while people walk past without noticing it.

quick_hits: A large, dark skipper marked with bright blue or blue-purple streaks across the wings.
Its caterpillars feed on red mangrove, tying the butterfly closely to warm coastal mangrove habitat.
The adult is a powerful flier, but the caterpillar's world is one mangrove leaf: it folds the leaf with silk and feeds from inside the shelter.
Red mangrove provides both larval food and shelter; adult skippers leave the mangroves to visit nearby flowers for nectar.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Florida, the Caribbean, and nearby regions. The Florida form (subspecies okeechobee) is found along both coasts of the southern two-thirds of the peninsula, roughly as far north as Pinellas County on the Gulf and Volusia on the Atlantic — placing our area near the northern edge of its range.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Large for a skipper, dull blackish-brown, with bold electric-blue streaks.

blocks.label: Head and body
blocks.text: Dark with a white face and blue markings.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Fast and powerful; often perches under leaves.

identification.what_to_look_for: A big, dark, fast butterfly near mangroves or flowers, flashing surprising streaks of bright blue. Those neon-blue marks on an otherwise dark butterfly are the giveaway — no other Florida skipper looks like it.

species.diet: Caterpillars eat only red mangrove leaves. Adults sip nectar from a range of flowers, including mangrove blossoms, Spanish needles, citrus, and bougainvillea.
species.behavior: Active by day, especially in warm sun. A fast, strong flier that stays close to its mangrove host and nearby nectar flowers. The caterpillar builds a folded-leaf shelter on red mangrove and feeds from within it.
species.ecological_role: A pollinator of coastal flowers and a specialist tied to red mangrove — a living link in the mangrove ecosystem and a small indicator of healthy coastal habitat.
species.plant_connections: Red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) is the only larval host plant — the butterfly lives only where it grows. Adults nectar at mangrove blossoms, Spanish needles, and other flowers.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks; active in Florida much of the year.

species.habitat: Coastal mangrove forests and edges, especially where red mangrove grows, plus nearby flowers for nectar. Restricted to warm, frost-free shorelines.
species.where_to_look: Near any mangrove or coastal plantings and at nectar-rich flowers on warm days. A localized find, since the butterfly stays close to its mangrove host.
species.when_to_see: Present in southern Florida year-round; here, near its northern Gulf limit, it is a more localized and seasonal find tied to warm weather and mangroves.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people.

interaction.guidance: Just watch and enjoy. Avoid handling butterflies, whose wings are delicate, and remember that mangroves themselves are legally protected in Florida.

conservation.status: Not formally listed, but localized and entirely dependent on red mangrove. Its future is tied to the protection of mangrove habitat, which is safeguarded under Florida law.

Prose was updated 09-08 and deliberately avoids asserting either name.

seasonality.note: Closely tied to coastal mangrove habitat. Palma Sola records are currently too limited to define local seasonality.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The long-tailed skipper is smaller with two long tails on the hindwings; the mangrove skipper is larger, tail-less, with bolder neon-blue streaks.

how_it_lives.text: Red mangrove is the larval host. A caterpillar folds part of a leaf into a silk-bound shelter and feeds on the surrounding leaf tissue.
Adults are less specialized, leaving the host plant to take nectar from flowers near the mangrove edge.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings
how_to_know_it.text: Large for a skipper, dark brown to blackish with bright blue or blue-purple streaks.

how_to_know_it.label: Head and body
how_to_know_it.text: Dark-bodied with pale markings on the face and blue markings on the body.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan about two to three inches.

how_to_know_it.label: Flight
how_to_know_it.text: Fast and strong, often settling beneath leaves.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look near mangroves and nearby flowers for a large, fast dark skipper flashing bright blue streaks across the wings.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look around red mangroves and nearby flowering plants. Adults may leave the mangrove foliage to nectar, but eggs and caterpillars should be searched for on red mangrove leaves.
Southern Florida supports adults through much of the year. Palma Sola currently has too few records to define a reliable local season.

what_it_does_here.label: One butterfly, one mangrove
what_it_does_here.text: Red mangrove is the larval host plant. Females lay eggs on the foliage, and the caterpillar eats the leaves while using them to build a silk-bound shelter. Adults feed at flowers nearby. The butterfly's distribution in Florida is therefore closely tied to mangrove habitat.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Leave folded or silk-bound mangrove leaves intact. One may hold a caterpillar.

at_a_glance.text: A large, dark skipper marked with bright blue or blue-purple streaks across the wings.
Its caterpillars feed on red mangrove, tying the butterfly closely to warm coastal mangrove habitat.
The adult is a powerful flier, but the caterpillar's world is one mangrove leaf: it folds the leaf with silk and feeds from inside the shelter.
Red mangrove provides both larval food and shelter; adult skippers leave the mangroves to visit nearby flowers for nectar.

species.teaser: The Mangrove Skipper's caterpillar eats red mangrove and folds a mangrove leaf into the shelter where it lives.

quick_hits: One of the largest birds in North America, with a wingspan approaching nine feet.
Unlike the Brown Pelican it never plunge-dives. It feeds from the surface, often in coordinated groups that drive fish together.
It is a winter visitor here. Birds breed on inland lakes far to the north and west, then come south for the cool months.
In flight the black flight feathers show against a white body, and flocks soar in long lines and V formations.
species.range_and_origin: Breeds on inland lakes of western Canada and the northwestern United States, and winters along the Gulf Coast, including Florida, and other warm regions. In Florida it is a non-breeding winter visitor.
more_information: Despite sharing a name with the familiar brown pelican, the white pelican lives very differently. It is far larger, mostly white, and tends to favor inland lakes and shallow coastal waters, often soaring in high, wheeling flocks.

Its feeding is a group effort. Rather than diving, white pelicans swim together and herd fish into shallow water, then dip their great bills in unison to scoop them up — a coordinated technique that makes them effective without ever leaving the surface.

Because Florida is a wintering ground rather than a breeding home, white pelicans appear mainly in the cooler months and then head north to nest. They are mostly silent here, drifting in serene formations on the water and in the sky.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Bright white overall, with black flight feathers that show mainly in flight.

blocks.label: Bill and pouch
blocks.text: Long and yellow-orange.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Enormous — among the largest birds on the continent.

blocks.label: Feeding
blocks.text: Floats and scoops; does not dive.

identification.what_to_look_for: A huge white bird with black wingtips, floating in groups on open water or soaring high in slow circles. If a pelican is plunge-diving at the coast, that is the smaller, darker brown pelican; the white pelican scoops from the surface, usually inland.

species.diet: Mainly fish, scooped from the water at the surface, often while fishing cooperatively in groups.
species.behavior: Active by day and highly social. Fishes in coordinated groups on the water and soars in high flocks, often in V-formation. Spends the Florida season feeding and resting before migrating north to breed.
species.ecological_role: A large surface-feeding fish predator that, as a seasonal visitor, links Florida's waters to the interior North American lakes where it breeds.

size.length: 50 to 65 inches
size.lifespan: commonly 12 to 16 years, sometimes longer.

species.habitat: Shallow inland lakes, reservoirs, estuaries, and calm coastal waters. In winter it favors large, quiet bodies of water with abundant fish.
species.where_to_look: On open pond water in the cooler months, usually in a group. A seasonal treat rather than a bird you will see in summer.
species.when_to_see: Winter visitor, typically present from late fall into early spring, then gone north to breed. Sightings are occasional and seasonal.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. White pelicans are shy and easily flushed, and discarded fishing line is a serious hazard to them — pack it out.

invasive.notes: Native to North America and a natural winter visitor to Florida. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Populations are generally stable, though the species can be sensitive to disturbance at its northern breeding colonies and to fishing-line entanglement.

species.internal_notes: Winter visitor — single sighting Dec 2025. Confirm seasonality; do not imply year-round.

seasonality.note: Breeds far to the north and west; gone for the summer.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: In flight both are white with black wing edges, but the white pelican has a huge orange bill and pouch and short legs; the wood stork has long trailing legs, a bare dark head, and a down-curved bill.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day and highly social. It fishes from the surface rather than from the air, and groups will sometimes work together, driving fish into shallower water where they are easier to take.
Between feeding bouts it rests on open water or sandbars, and flocks soar high on rising warm air, often in V formation.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Bright white overall. The black flight feathers show strongly on spread wings and all but disappear on a bird sitting on the water.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Long and yellow-orange, with the pouch beneath it.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Enormous — a wingspan of up to about nine feet.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a group rather than a single bird, either resting on open water or soaring high in a line. The size alone settles it.
Brown Pelicans are gray-brown and plunge-dive from the air. American White Pelicans are much larger, mostly white, and usually feed while swimming.

where_to_find_it_here.text: On open pond water in the cooler months, usually in a group rather than alone.
A winter visitor, typically present from late autumn into early spring and then gone north to breed. Sightings here are occasional and seasonal.

what_it_does_here.label: Open water, not vegetation
what_it_does_here.text: This is one of the few birds here whose habitat is defined by the absence of plants. It needs large, quiet, open water to fish cooperatively, and undisturbed sandbars or shorelines to rest on — dense marsh vegetation is of no use to it.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people.
Watch from a distance and do not feed it. White Pelicans are easily flushed, and discarded fishing line is a serious hazard — pack it out.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Not currently threatened, though the species is sensitive to disturbance at its northern breeding colonies and to fishing-line entanglement.

at_a_glance.text: One of the largest birds in North America — almost entirely white, with a wingspan approaching nine feet.
It never plunge-dives the way a Brown Pelican does. It feeds from the surface while swimming.
Groups will sometimes work together, driving fish into shallower water where they are easier to scoop up.
Florida is wintering territory. Birds breed on inland lakes far to the north and west, then come south for the cool months.

species.teaser: It does not dive. White Pelicans fish in coordinated groups, herding fish into the shallows and scooping them from the surface together.

quick_hits: An Osprey is a large fish-eating raptor with a white underside, white head and bold dark stripe through the eye.
It hunts live fish by diving feet-first into the water, sometimes disappearing completely below the surface.
A reversible outer toe and rough pads on the soles help the feet hold slippery fish.
Osprey populations fell sharply during the DDT era and rebounded strongly after the pesticide was banned in 1972.
species.range_and_origin: Found near fish-bearing water on every continent except Antarctica. Florida supports year-round residents as well as seasonal migrants.

blocks.label: Underside
blocks.text: Mostly white, with a white head crossed by a bold dark eye stripe.

blocks.label: Upperparts
blocks.text: Dark brown.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Long, narrow wings bend sharply at the wrists, creating a shallow M shape.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large brown-and-white raptor flying over water on long, kinked wings or hovering briefly before a feet-first dive. The bold dark eye stripe is visible when perched.

species.diet: Almost entirely live fish.
species.behavior: Hunts over open water, sometimes hovering briefly before plunging feet-first after fish. Ospreys build large stick nests on exposed supports and frequently reuse the same nest site.
species.sounds: A series of high, sharp whistles, especially around a nest.
species.ecological_role: A highly specialized predator of live fish.
species.plant_connections: Ospreys need an open, elevated nest support near fish-bearing water. Natural sites include tall trees and dead snags, but the birds also readily use poles, channel markers and purpose-built platforms. Large branches and sticks form the bulky nest, which may be reused and enlarged over many years.

size.length: Wingspan around five to six feet.

species.habitat: Near almost any fish-bearing water — lakes, rivers, reservoirs, estuaries, and coasts — with tall, open structures or trees for nesting.
species.where_to_look: Look overhead near ponds and surrounding waterways, and check tall open trees, snags, poles and platforms for perched birds or large stick nests.
species.when_to_see: Ospreys occur in Florida year-round, with additional migrants present during part of the year. Palma Sola currently has only a few records, so local sightings should be considered occasional.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to visitors when observed normally.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not approach an active nest. If adults become agitated or leave the nest because of your presence, move farther away.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and found nearly worldwide. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and currently of low conservation concern. Osprey populations declined sharply during the DDT era, then rebounded after the U.S. ban in 1972. Artificial nest platforms and other open structures have also provided important nesting sites in developed landscapes.

species.internal_notes: Osprey sits in its own family (Pandionidae), not with the other hawks/eagles — nice 'good to know' angle.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident with additional migrants. Palma Sola currently has too few observations to define local abundance or a seasonal peak.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Bald Eagles are bulkier, with broader wings and a much heavier body. Adult eagles have a white head and tail but a dark underside; Ospreys are white below with a dark eye stripe and hold their wings with a pronounced kink.

how_it_lives.text: An Osprey patrols over water and may hover briefly before dropping toward a fish with its feet extended. It can strike the surface hard enough to become completely submerged.

how_it_lives.label: Feet built for fish
how_it_lives.text: The outer toe can rotate backward, allowing a two-forward, two-back grip. Rough pads beneath the toes help hold slippery prey, and a caught fish is usually turned head-first for flight.

how_to_know_it.label: Plumage
how_to_know_it.text: White below and on the head, crossed by a bold dark stripe through the eye. Dark brown above.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Long narrow wings kinked sharply at the wrist, held in a shallow M.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: A series of high, sharp whistles, most often around a nest.
Look for a big brown-and-white raptor working over water, or hovering a moment before it drops.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look up over the ponds and the waterways around the park, then check tall open trees, snags, poles and platforms for a perched bird or a bulky stick nest.

One bird made a habit of the Kapok tree by the Cypress pond. It would rest there between trips, carry tilapia over from the Big Pond, and drop the bones onto the mulch below — often enough that on a morning walk underneath, you could have one land near you.

where_to_find_it_here.caption: Look up. The Kapok tree by the Cypress pond — a perch this Osprey came back to again and again.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Ospreys are in Florida year-round, with additional migrants passing through. The park has only a few formal records, so most visits will not turn one up.

what_it_does_here.text: An Osprey hunts live fish and almost nothing else. It dives feet-first, and the feet are built for the job: the outer toe reverses so the bird can hold a fish with two toes forward and two back, and the soles are covered in rough spines that bite into a slippery body.

Nesting comes down to a single requirement — an open support high above fish-bearing water. Tall trees and dead snags are the natural version, but the birds take just as readily to poles, channel markers and purpose-built platforms. A nest gets reused and added to over many years until it becomes a substantial pile of sticks.

what_it_does_here.caption: Not a fish — a branch. This one is hauling nest material over our ponds, carried in the same talons built to grip a slippery catch.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Keep well back from an active nest. If the adults start calling or leave the nest because you are there, you are too close — move away.

at_a_glance.text: A large fish-eating raptor, white below with a white head and a bold dark stripe through the eye.
It hunts by diving feet-first, sometimes disappearing completely under the surface.
Osprey numbers fell sharply during the DDT years and climbed back after the pesticide was banned in 1972.

species.teaser: An Osprey can reverse one outer toe and grip a fish with two toes facing forward and two backward.

quick_hits: Bald Eagles nearly disappeared from much of the lower 48 during the twentieth century. After DDT was banned and legal protections increased, the population recovered enough for the species to leave the federal endangered-species list in 2007.
Florida has the densest Bald Eagle population of any state except Alaska. Nearly 1,500 nests were recorded in 55 Florida counties during the 2023–24 breeding season.
A Bald Eagle nest near St. Petersburg holds the record for the largest bird nest measured: about nine and a half feet wide, twenty feet deep and estimated at more than two tons.
The name 'Bald Eagle' refers to the adult's white head, not a lack of feathers. Young birds remain mostly brown and mottled for several years before developing the familiar white head and tail.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America and found across much of the continent, especially near large bodies of water. Florida supports one of the continent's densest Bald Eagle populations outside Alaska.

blocks.label: Adults
blocks.text: Adults have a dark brown body, white head and tail, heavy yellow hooked bill and yellow feet.

blocks.label: Young birds
blocks.text: Young Bald Eagles lack the white head and tail. They are mostly dark brown with varying amounts of white mottling and gradually acquire adult plumage over several years.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Very large, with broad wings usually held flat while soaring and a large head projecting well ahead of the wings. Turkey Vultures hold their wings in a shallow V and often rock from side to side.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look high in large trees near water or scan the sky for a very large raptor with broad, flat wings. Adults show the familiar white head and tail; immature birds are mostly brown and mottled. Turkey Vultures soar with their wings held in a shallow V.

species.diet: Fish are important food, but Bald Eagles also take birds and mammals and readily scavenge carrion.
species.behavior: Fish are an important food, but Bald Eagles are opportunistic and also take birds and mammals and readily eat carrion. They sometimes chase Ospreys until the smaller bird drops its catch.
species.sounds: The Bald Eagle's real call is a surprisingly high series of chirps and whistles. The powerful 'eagle scream' used in movies is often the call of a Red-tailed Hawk.
species.ecological_role: Bald Eagles are both predators and scavengers in aquatic and coastal food webs, taking live prey and feeding readily on carrion.
species.plant_connections: Large trees are essential nesting and perching structures. In Florida, most Bald Eagle nests are built in living native pines, although cypress, oaks and mangroves are also used. A nest may be reused and enlarged for years, so the tree must support an enormous load while giving the birds open access to nearby water.

size.length: Wingspan about six to seven feet. Females are larger than males.

species.habitat: Lakes, rivers, reservoirs, and coastlines with tall trees for nesting and perching and plenty of fish and waterbirds.
species.where_to_look: Look overhead or high in large trees near ponds, bays and other open water. At Palma Sola this is an occasional sighting, not a bird visitors should expect on every visit.
species.when_to_see: Bald Eagles occur in Florida year-round, but numbers and movements change with the breeding cycle. Florida's nesting activity is concentrated from fall through spring. Palma Sola has only a single recorded sighting, so the park does not yet have enough observations to define a local peak.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to visitors when observed from a distance. Do not approach or disturb an eagle or nest.
danger.pets: Bald Eagles generally avoid people and domestic animals. Keep pets under normal control around wildlife.

interaction.guidance: Never approach or disturb an active nest. Watch from a distance with binoculars or a long lens and leave if the birds change their behavior in response to you. Bald Eagles and their nests remain protected by federal law even though the species is no longer listed as endangered.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: The Bald Eagle is one of the best-known U.S. wildlife recoveries. By the early 1960s only a few hundred breeding pairs remained in the lower 48 states. After DDT was banned and legal protections increased, populations recovered dramatically, and the species was removed from the federal endangered-species list in 2007. Bald Eagles remain federally protected.

species.internal_notes: Single sighting (Mar 2026). Verify it's a recurring visitor before promising it on signage.

seasonality.note: Bald Eagles occur in Florida year-round and nest primarily from fall through spring. Palma Sola currently has only one documented sighting, so no local seasonal peak can be established.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Ospreys are smaller and slimmer, white below with a dark eye-stripe, and hold their wings with a distinct kink at the wrist. A Bald Eagle is bulkier, dark-bodied, and holds its broad wings flat.
Turkey Vultures have much smaller heads, longer narrower wings held in a shallow V, and often rock while soaring. Bald Eagles look heavier and usually hold their broad wings flatter.

how_it_lives.text: Fish are an important food, but Bald Eagles are opportunistic. They also take birds and mammals and readily eat carrion.

how_it_lives.label: Taking a fish from an Osprey
how_it_lives.text: Bald Eagles sometimes chase Ospreys carrying fish until the Osprey drops its catch, then take the falling fish. This kind of food theft is called kleptoparasitism.

how_it_lives.label: Nesting on a Florida calendar
how_it_lives.text: Florida eagles begin nesting activities in fall, and young are raised through winter and spring. This early schedule takes advantage of Florida's mild winter.

how_to_know_it.text: Adults have a dark brown body, white head and tail, heavy yellow hooked bill and yellow feet.

how_to_know_it.label: Young birds

In Florida, most Bald Eagle nests are built in living native pines, although cypress, oaks and mangroves are also used. A nest may be reused and enlarged for years, so the tree must support an enormous load while giving the birds open access to nearby water.
Florida holds one of the densest Bald Eagle populations anywhere outside Alaska. The park has only a single record, but the birds are genuinely around.

take_care.text: Never approach or disturb an active nest. Watch from a distance with binoculars or a long lens and leave if the birds change their behavior in response to you. Bald Eagles and their nests remain protected by federal law even though the species is no longer listed as endangered.

Florida has the densest Bald Eagle population of any state except Alaska. Nearly 1,500 nests were recorded in 55 Florida counties during the 2023–24 breeding season.
A Bald Eagle nest near St. Petersburg holds the record for the largest bird nest measured: about nine and a half feet wide, twenty feet deep and estimated at more than two tons.
