species.teaser: The largest bird nest on record was built by Bald Eagles near St. Petersburg: about nine and a half feet wide, twenty feet deep and estimated to weigh more than two tons.

quick_hits: Most waterfowl nest on the ground. Wood Ducks nest high inside tree cavities, often old woodpecker holes.
They have strong claws and perch readily in trees, which almost no other duck here does.
The male is one of the most strongly patterned ducks in North America; the female is gray-brown with a white teardrop around the eye.
Acorns are a favourite food in autumn and winter, which ties this duck to oaks as much as to water.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America, common across the eastern United States and the Pacific Northwest. In Florida it is a year-round resident, and winter brings additional birds from the north.
more_information: The wood duck is a bird of wooded swamps and shaded water, and its whole life is tied to trees. It nests in natural cavities, often old woodpecker holes, which sets it apart from the ground-nesting ducks of open marshes.

That cavity-nesting habit leads to a remarkable sight. A day or so after hatching, the tiny ducklings climb to the cavity entrance and jump, tumbling to the ground or water below and bouncing unharmed thanks to their light, downy bodies, then trailing their mother off to feed.

By the early 1900s, unregulated hunting and the clearing of bottomland forests had pushed wood ducks to the brink. Hunting limits under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, habitat protection, and a huge volunteer nest-box effort turned the species around — one of conservation's quieter success stories.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Boldly patterned — a glossy green and chestnut head with white stripes, a swept-back crest, and red eyes.

blocks.label: Female
blocks.text: Soft gray-brown with a distinctive white teardrop around the eye.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: A slim duck with a boxy, crested head, often holding the head low.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a slim, boxy-headed duck moving through deeply shaded, wooded water rather than out in the open. Wood ducks favor tucked-away spots near overhanging branches — and if approached too closely, they'll flush fast with a loud, rising squeal.

species.diet: Seeds, acorns, fruits, and aquatic plants, along with insects and other small invertebrates. Acorns are a favorite in fall and winter.
species.behavior: Active by day, usually in pairs or small groups, often staying near cover at the edge of shaded water. Perches readily in trees — unusual for a duck — and nests in tree cavities or nest boxes.
species.sounds: The female gives a loud, rising 'oo-eek' squeal when flushed; the male a softer, thin whistle.
species.ecological_role: Spreads the seeds of wetland and bottomland plants and is part of the food web as both forager and prey. Its reliance on tree cavities makes it a flagship for protecting wooded wetlands.
species.plant_connections: Eats acorns, seeds, fruits, and aquatic plants, and nests in tree cavities (often old woodpecker holes) in wooded wetlands.

size.length: 19 to 21 inches
size.lifespan: usually 3 to 4 years, occasionally much longer.

species.habitat: Wooded swamps, shaded ponds, slow wooded streams, and marshes with nearby trees for nesting. Favors quiet water with overhanging cover.
species.where_to_look: On quieter, shadier stretches of the ponds and wooded edges, often in pairs near overhanging cover rather than out in open water.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, with more birds present in winter. Most likely along sheltered, wooded water.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Wood ducks are shy and stick to cover; bread and snacks harm waterfowl health.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern today, and a notable comeback from near-collapse in the early 1900s thanks to hunting limits, habitat protection, and nest-box programs.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day, usually in pairs or small groups and often close to cover at the edge of shaded water.

how_it_lives.label: Nesting off the ground
how_it_lives.text: It nests in tree cavities, frequently old woodpecker holes, and will readily use a nest box. Ducklings leave by jumping down within a day of hatching, before they can fly.
Seeds, acorns, fruits and aquatic plants make up most of the diet, with insects and other small invertebrates added.

how_to_know_it.label: Male
how_to_know_it.text: Boldly patterned — a glossy green and chestnut head with white stripes, a swept-back crest and red eyes.

how_to_know_it.label: Female
how_to_know_it.text: Soft gray-brown with a distinctive white teardrop around the eye.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About twenty inches long, with a wingspan around two and a half feet.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: The female gives a loud rising oo-eek squeal when flushed; the male a softer, thin whistle.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Check shaded, sheltered water rather than open ponds, and look up — a duck perched on a branch is almost certainly this one.

where_to_find_it_here.text: On quieter, shadier stretches of the ponds and wooded edges, often in pairs near overhanging cover rather than out in open water.
A year-round resident, with more birds present in winter.

what_it_does_here.label: It needs trees as much as water
what_it_does_here.text: Acorns are a major autumn and winter food, and the nest is a cavity in a living or dead tree beside the water. A pond with no trees around it supports no Wood Ducks, however good the water is — which is why nest boxes worked so well where the old trees had gone.
A day or so after hatching, the ducklings climb to the cavity entrance and jump. They are light and downy enough to bounce, and they follow their mother off to water from wherever they land.

By the early 1900s, unregulated hunting and the clearing of bottomland forest had taken Wood Ducks to the brink. Hunting limits, habitat protection and an enormous volunteer nest-box effort brought them back.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people.
Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Wood Ducks are shy and stick to cover, and bread harms waterfowl.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Not currently threatened, and a notable recovery from near-collapse in the early 1900s through hunting limits, habitat protection and nest-box programs.

They have strong claws and perch readily in trees, which almost no other duck here does.
The male is one of the most strongly patterned ducks in North America; the female is gray-brown with a white teardrop around the eye.
Acorns are a favourite food in autumn and winter, which ties this duck to oaks as much as to water.

species.teaser: A duck that nests in a tree. Ducklings leave the cavity by jumping — sometimes from well above the ground — within a day of hatching.

quick_hits: A Tricolored Heron is blue-gray and purple above but bright white below. It is the only dark Florida heron with a clean white belly.
It often hunts actively, running, lunging and turning sharply through shallow water after small fish.
Small fish dominate the diet, and the bird sometimes crouches so low before striking that its belly nearly touches the water.
Tricolored Herons are State-designated Threatened in Florida, although the species remains globally classified as Least Concern.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. In Florida it is a year-round resident of coastal and freshwater wetlands.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Blue-gray upperparts with purple tones, contrasted with a bright white belly.

blocks.label: Neck
blocks.text: Long and slender, with a white stripe down the front in adults. Juveniles are much rustier on the neck and upperparts.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Long, narrow and pointed.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Often feeds with quick runs, turns and lunges rather than remaining still for long periods.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a slim, medium-sized heron that is dark blue-gray above and unmistakably white below. Feeding birds often move quickly through shallow water, chasing small fish.

species.diet: Mostly small fish, with aquatic insects, crustaceans and amphibians also taken.
species.behavior: Tricolored Herons hunt small fish in shallow water by stalking, running and making quick turns and lunges. Their feeding style is generally more active than that of Little Blue Herons.
species.ecological_role: A predator specialized largely on small fish in shallow wetlands.
species.plant_connections: Tricolored Herons nest in dense shrubs and small trees, often on islands or over standing water. Males gather sticks, and females arrange them into a platform; some nests are lined with finer twigs or cordgrass. Wetland vegetation also provides cover for the small fish the birds hunt.

size.length: Roughly two feet tall, with a wingspan around three feet.

species.habitat: Fresh and saltwater marshes, estuaries, mangrove swamps, lagoons, and pond edges with shallow water for hunting.
species.where_to_look: Look in shallow pond edges and other open wetlands. Tricolored Herons usually hunt small fish in shallow or semi-open water, often with much more movement than Little Blue or Great Blue Herons.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident and an occasional visitor at Palma Sola.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle an injured or trapped heron; the pointed bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Give feeding birds enough room to continue hunting without moving away.

conservation.status: State-designated Threatened in Florida and globally classified as Least Concern. FWC identifies wetland development, altered hydrology, reduced prey, contaminants and disturbance among threats.

seasonality.note: Occurs year-round in Florida. Palma Sola records are too limited to define a local seasonal pattern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Adult Little Blue Herons are dark underneath as well as above and move more deliberately. Tricolored Herons have a bright white belly and often feed more actively.
Much larger and heavier, with a pale head and thick yellowish bill. Tricolored Herons are slimmer and less than half the bulk.

how_it_lives.text: Tricolored Herons hunt small fish in shallow water by stalking, running and making quick turns and lunges. Their feeding style is generally more active than that of Little Blue Herons.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Blue-gray upperparts with purple tones, against a bright white belly.

how_to_know_it.label: Neck
how_to_know_it.text: Long and slender, with a white stripe down the front in adults. Young birds are much rustier on the neck and upperparts.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Long, narrow and pointed.
The white belly is the whole identification. No other dark heron here is clean white underneath.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Shallow pond edges and open wetland. This is the dark heron that keeps moving — quick runs, sharp turns and lunges, where a Little Blue Heron would be picking its way slowly.
A year-round Florida resident and an occasional visitor here.

what_it_does_here.text: Small fish are the target, and the hunting is built around chasing rather than waiting. A bird will sometimes crouch so low before striking that its belly nearly touches the water.

They nest in dense shrubs and small trees, usually on islands or standing over water. The male gathers sticks and the female builds, and some nests are lined with finer twigs or cordgrass. That same wetland vegetation is what gives the small fish their cover.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Tricolored Herons are listed as Threatened in Florida, though the species is not considered at risk globally. The state points to wetland development, altered water flow, reduced prey and disturbance at nesting colonies as the pressures behind the listing.

at_a_glance.text: Blue-gray and purple above but bright white below — the only dark Florida heron with a clean white belly.
It hunts on the move, running, turning and lunging through shallow water after small fish.
Listed as Threatened in Florida, though the species is not considered at risk globally.

species.teaser: Most dark herons are dark underneath too. The Tricolored Heron's bright white belly is the field mark that separates it.

quick_hits: A Florida Softshell has a broad, flattened body, a leathery shell and a long tubular snout.
The flat shell and strongly webbed feet make it a fast swimmer, very different from the heavy, domed shape of many familiar pond turtles.
The long nose lets the turtle breathe at the surface while most of its body remains underwater.
Females grow much larger than males, and a large softshell has a long neck and powerful jaws. Never try to pick one up.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Florida and neighboring parts of the Southeast. It is widespread in Florida's freshwater ponds, lakes, marshes and slow-moving waterways.

blocks.label: Shell
blocks.text: Broad, flat and leathery, without the hard scutes that form the shell plates of most turtles.

blocks.label: Snout
blocks.text: Long and narrow, ending in a small pair of nostrils.

blocks.label: Feet
blocks.text: Large and strongly webbed.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Females can become very large; males remain much smaller.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a broad, flat turtle with a long pointed nose. In the water you may see only the head or nose at the surface. On land, the leathery flattened shell makes it easy to separate from the park's hard-shelled cooters and sliders.

species.diet: Mostly animal prey, including snails, crayfish, aquatic insects, fish and other small animals; carrion may also be eaten.
species.behavior: Most of its life is spent in water. The flattened body and webbed feet make it a strong swimmer, and it can bury itself in soft bottom sediment while waiting for prey or hiding.
species.ecological_role: A predator and scavenger in freshwater food webs, feeding on aquatic invertebrates, fish and other small animals. Eggs and young turtles in turn become food for many predators.
species.plant_connections: Aquatic vegetation helps shape the habitat around a softshell even though the turtle is mainly carnivorous. Plant beds and shoreline vegetation provide cover for fish, crayfish and other prey, while muddy or sandy openings along the bank give females places to leave the water and nest.

size.length: Large females can have shells more than a foot and a half long; males are much smaller.

species.habitat: Ponds, lakes, canals, marshes, and slow rivers with soft, sandy or muddy bottoms it can burrow into.
species.where_to_look: Look in freshwater ponds and along muddy or sandy shorelines. Softshells spend most of their time in the water and may bury themselves in soft bottom sediment with only the head exposed.
species.when_to_see: Present in Florida year-round. Most likely to be noticed when a turtle surfaces to breathe, basks near the water or comes onto land.

danger.people: Do not handle a Florida Softshell. It has powerful jaws and a long, flexible neck that can reach surprisingly far around the sides of the shell. A defensive bite can cause a serious wound.
danger.pets: Keep dogs from approaching or cornering a softshell on land. A frightened turtle may defend itself by biting.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and never pick one up. If a softshell is crossing a path or moving on land, give it room to continue in the direction it is already traveling.

conservation.status: Common and widespread in Florida and not currently considered a species of conservation concern.

species.internal_notes: Distinctive pancake-flat turtle — easy pond spotting.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Has a hard, domed shell with yellow markings and a conventionally shaped turtle head. The Florida Softshell is much flatter, with a leathery shell and long tubular nose.
Also a large pond turtle, but has a hard shell and a striped head. The softshell's flat leathery shell and long nose separate it at close range.
Smaller and hard-shelled, usually with a colored patch behind the eye. Softshells lack the hard shell plates and have a much longer snout.

how_it_lives.text: Most of its life is spent in water. The flattened body and webbed feet make it a strong swimmer, and it can bury itself in soft bottom sediment while waiting for prey or hiding.

how_it_lives.label: Coming ashore
how_it_lives.text: Females leave the water to lay eggs on land, so a softshell seen crossing open ground may be moving between water and a nesting site.

how_to_know_it.label: Shell
how_to_know_it.text: Broad, flat and leathery, without the hard plates that form most turtles' shells.

how_to_know_it.label: Snout
how_to_know_it.text: Long and narrow, ending in a small pair of nostrils.

how_to_know_it.label: Feet
how_to_know_it.text: Large and strongly webbed.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Large females can have shells more than a foot and a half long. Males stay much smaller.
In the water you may see nothing but the nose. On land the flat leathery shell separates it instantly from the park's cooters and sliders.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Freshwater ponds and muddy or sandy shorelines. Softshells spend most of their time in the water and often bury themselves in soft bottom sediment with only the head showing, so the usual sighting is a nose at the surface rather than a turtle up on a log.
Present year-round. Most often noticed when one surfaces to breathe or comes out onto land.

what_it_does_here.text: Unlike the cooters it shares the pond with, this one is a hunter — snails, crayfish, aquatic insects, fish, and whatever carrion turns up. The flat body and webbed feet make it fast enough to run prey down, and it can also lie buried in the bottom and wait.

Plants matter to it at one remove. Beds of aquatic vegetation and shoreline cover hold the fish and crayfish it hunts, while bare muddy or sandy openings along the bank give females somewhere to leave the water and nest.

take_care.label: The risk
take_care.text: Do not handle a Florida Softshell. It has powerful jaws and a long, flexible neck that can reach surprisingly far around the sides of the shell, and a defensive bite can cause a serious wound.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Watch from a distance and never pick one up. If one is crossing a path, give it room to keep going the way it was already heading, and keep dogs from cornering it.

at_a_glance.text: A broad, flattened turtle with a leathery shell and a long tubular snout.
The flat shell and heavily webbed feet make it a fast swimmer — nothing like the domed pond turtles.
The long nose lets it breathe at the surface with the rest of the body still underwater.
Females grow much larger than males, and a big one has a long neck and powerful jaws.

species.teaser: A Florida Softshell can stay almost completely submerged and reach the surface with only the tip of its long nose.

quick_hits: Roseate Spoonbills occur around Tampa Bay as well as farther south in Florida. The region supports important breeding colonies of these large pink wading birds.
The pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the spoonbill's diet. Young birds are much paler and develop stronger pink coloration as they mature.
The flattened bill works partly by touch. The bird sweeps it through shallow water and snaps it shut when sensitive tissue inside contacts prey.

By the 1930s, plume hunting had reduced Florida's population to roughly 30 to 40 breeding pairs in Florida Bay. The species recovered after legal protection, but it remains State-designated Threatened in Florida.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas, from the southern United States through the Caribbean and Central and South America. In Florida, important populations occur in Florida Bay and around Tampa Bay.
more_information: The spoonbill belongs to the ibis family, and the resemblance shows once you look past the pink and the bill: long legs, a long neck carried straight out in flight, and the same steady flap-and-glide as a White Ibis.

Nesting is a communal business. Spoonbills build bulky stick nests in trees and shrubs standing over or beside water, usually alongside herons, egrets and ibises rather than in colonies of their own. Sites on islands or above open water are harder for raccoons and other climbing predators to reach, which is part of why the surrounding trees matter as much as the shallow water does.

blocks.label: Overall
blocks.text: A large pink wading bird with a white neck, bare pale head and a long bill that widens into a flat spoon shape at the tip.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Adults are pink with deeper rose-red on parts of the wings. Young birds are much paler.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Flies with the neck stretched straight out, unlike herons that pull the neck back.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large pink wading bird sweeping a flattened bill from side to side through shallow water. Adults have a bare pale head and white neck. In flight, the neck remains extended.

species.diet: Small fish, shrimp, crayfish, crabs and aquatic insects caught in shallow water.
species.behavior: A spoonbill wades through shallow water with its bill partly open, sweeping its head from side to side. Contact with a fish, shrimp or other small animal triggers the bill to close. Spoonbills feed and roost socially and nest in colonies with other wading birds.
species.ecological_role: Spoonbill feeding and nesting success depend strongly on water depth and the concentration of small aquatic prey. For that reason, biologists use breeding performance in places such as Florida Bay to track how wetland hydrology is functioning.
species.plant_connections: Mangroves and other waterside trees and shrubs provide nesting structure, often on islands or over water where colonies gain some protection from land predators. The plants around a wetland therefore matter even though the spoonbill's food comes from the water.

size.length: Roughly two and a half feet tall, with a wingspan a little over four feet.

species.habitat: Shallow fresh and brackish water — mangrove edges, estuaries, coastal lagoons, marshes, and mudflats — with the small aquatic prey it sweeps up.
species.where_to_look: Look in shallow water along pond margins and other open wetland edges. Spoonbills move frequently as water depth and prey availability change, so a park sighting is an occasional event rather than something to expect every visit.
species.when_to_see: Present in Florida year-round, but it wanders widely in search of feeding areas, so park sightings are more occasional than for the resident herons.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed or approach a spoonbill. Never approach a nesting colony; repeated disturbance can cause adults to leave eggs or young exposed. Roseate Spoonbills are State-designated Threatened in Florida.

conservation.status: State-designated Threatened in Florida and globally classified as Least Concern. Florida spoonbills recovered dramatically after plume hunting ended, but wetland alteration, nesting disturbance and changing water conditions remain concerns.

species.internal_notes: High visitor 'wow' factor. Recent genus from Ajaia — current name used.

seasonality.note: Wanders widely in search of feeding areas, so sightings are sporadic.

how_it_lives.text: A spoonbill wades through shallow water with its bill partly open, sweeping its head from side to side. Contact with a fish, shrimp or other small animal triggers the bill to close.
Spoonbills feed and roost in company, usually alongside other wading birds rather than alone.

how_to_know_it.text: A large pink wading bird with a white neck, bare pale head and a long bill that widens into a flat spoon shape at the tip.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Adults are pink with deeper rose-red on parts of the wings. Young birds are much paler.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Flies with the neck stretched straight out, unlike herons that pull the neck back.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Roughly two and a half feet tall, with a wingspan a little over four feet.

how_to_know_it.text: Look for a large pink wading bird sweeping a flattened bill from side to side through shallow water. Adults have a bare pale head and white neck. In flight, the neck remains extended.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in shallow water along pond margins and other open wetland edges. Spoonbills move frequently as water depth and prey availability change, so a park sighting is an occasional event rather than something to expect every visit.
Present in Florida year-round, but the birds wander widely in search of feeding areas.

what_it_does_here.text: Everything turns on water depth. A spoonbill needs prey concentrated into shrinking shallow pools to feed successfully, which ties its breeding directly to how water moves through the system. That is why biologists track spoonbill nesting as a measure of whether Everglades restoration is working.

what_it_does_here.label: Mangroves hold the colony
what_it_does_here.text: Mangroves and other waterside trees and shrubs provide nesting structure, often on islands or over water where colonies gain some protection from land predators. The plants around a wetland therefore matter even though the spoonbill's food comes from the water.

what_it_does_here.text: The spoonbill belongs to the ibis family, and the resemblance shows once you look past the pink and the bill: long legs, a long neck carried straight out in flight, and the same steady flap-and-glide as a White Ibis.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people.
Watch from a distance and do not feed or approach a spoonbill. Never approach a nesting colony; repeated disturbance can cause adults to leave eggs or young exposed.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: State-designated Threatened in Florida and globally classified as Least Concern. Florida spoonbills recovered dramatically after plume hunting ended, but wetland alteration, nesting disturbance and changing water conditions remain concerns.

at_a_glance.text: Roseate Spoonbills occur around Tampa Bay as well as farther south in Florida. The region supports important breeding colonies of these large pink wading birds.
The pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the spoonbill's diet. Young birds are much paler and develop stronger pink coloration as they mature.
The flattened bill works partly by touch. The bird sweeps it through shallow water and snaps it shut when sensitive tissue inside contacts prey.

By the 1930s, plume hunting had reduced Florida's population to roughly 30 to 40 breeding pairs in Florida Bay. The species recovered after legal protection, but it remains State-designated Threatened in Florida.

species.teaser: A Roseate Spoonbill can feed in water too cloudy to see through. Sensitive tissue inside the bill detects prey by touch as the bird sweeps it from side to side.

quick_hits: The peninsular cooter is a large, dark freshwater turtle you will most often spot basking on a log or bank, soaking up the sun — often several piled together.
Look for the bright yellow pinstripes running along its dark neck and shell; they are the easiest way to recognize it.
Adults are almost entirely vegetarian, grazing on underwater plants, which is unusual among Florida's pond turtles.

All that basking has a purpose: warming in the sun helps the cold-blooded turtle digest its fibrous, plant-based meals. Approach too quickly and you will hear a series of quiet plops as the whole row slips back into the water.
species.range_and_origin: Native to peninsular Florida and found almost exclusively here. A close relative of other cooters and sliders found across the southeastern United States.
more_information: The peninsular cooter is one of the big, dark turtles you will see hauled out and basking on logs, banks, and floating debris on sunny days. Basking is not just for show — it helps the turtle warm up, dry off, and fight skin parasites and algae.

While young cooters eat some insects and other small animals, adults shift to a largely plant-based diet, grazing on submerged aquatic vegetation. That makes them important grazers in the pond ecosystem.
Cooters are long-lived and slow to mature, so the adults basking at the park's ponds may well be older than many of the visitors watching them.

blocks.label: Shell
blocks.text: Domed and dark olive to brown, often with faint yellowish markings, growing dull and worn with age.

blocks.label: Skin
blocks.text: Dark with thin yellow stripes on the head, neck, and legs.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Large — clearly bigger than a slider when full grown; females larger than males.

identification.what_to_look_for: A big, dark turtle basking on a log or bank, or just its head poking above the water as it swims. The combination of large size, domed dark shell, and yellow head stripes points to a cooter rather than the smaller, more boldly marked pond slider.

species.diet: Adults are mostly herbivorous, grazing on submerged aquatic plants and algae. Young turtles also eat insects, snails, and other small aquatic animals.
species.behavior: Active by day. Spends much of its time basking to regulate temperature, alternating with feeding dives. Wary of people and quick to drop into the water when approached.
species.ecological_role: As a plant-grazing turtle, the cooter helps shape underwater vegetation, and its eggs and young feed a range of predators. A healthy basking population is a good sign of a healthy pond.
species.plant_connections: Adults graze on submerged native vegetation such as eelgrass (tapegrass) and pondweeds, along with algae — making the cooter one of the pond's natural plant-grazers.

size.shell_length: 9 to 13 inches, with large females reaching about 15 inches
size.lifespan: long-lived, often 30 years or more.

species.habitat: Freshwater ponds, lakes, slow rivers, springs, and canals with plenty of aquatic plants and good basking spots like logs and banks.
species.where_to_look: Basking on logs, banks, and debris at the ponds on sunny days, or as a dark head moving across the water's surface.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Most visible while basking on warm, sunny days.

danger.people: Harmless if left alone. Like any turtle it may nip if picked up, so it is best not to handle it.
danger.pets: No real danger to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not handle or feed it. Basking turtles need their sun time; approaching just sends them diving off their logs.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common in suitable Florida freshwater habitat.

species.internal_notes: Count includes 1 genus-level 'Cooters' observation folded in.

seasonality.note: Most visible basking on warm, sunny days.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The red-bellied cooter shows a reddish wash below and a red arrow-shaped mark on the head; the peninsular cooter has yellow hairpin-loop stripes and no red.
Sliders are smaller and wear a colored patch just behind the eye; the peninsular cooter is larger with no ear patch.

how_it_lives.text: Much of the day is spent basking — a cooter uses the sun to run its body temperature — alternating with dives to feed. Wary of people, and quick to drop off a log at any movement.
Adults graze on submerged aquatic plants and algae. Young turtles also take insects, snails and other small animals.

how_to_know_it.label: Shell
how_to_know_it.text: Domed and dark olive to brown, often with faint yellowish markings, growing dull and worn with age.

how_to_know_it.label: Head
how_to_know_it.text: Fine yellow stripes run across the dark head and neck, forming looping or hairpin-shaped marks behind the eyes.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Large — clearly bigger than a slider when full grown, and females larger than males.
Size, the dark domed shell and the yellow head stripes point to a cooter rather than the smaller, more boldly marked pond slider.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Basking on logs, banks and floating debris at the ponds on sunny days, or as a dark head crossing the open water.
A year-round resident, most visible when it is warm and bright.

what_it_does_here.text: Basking raises the turtle's body temperature, which supports digestion and other body functions. Drying in the sun can also help reduce algae and some external parasites on the shell and skin.
Adults graze submerged native vegetation such as eelgrass and pondweeds, along with algae, which makes them one of the pond's grazers. Young turtles eat insects and snails before shifting over.
Cooters are long-lived and slow to mature. A large adult may have been using the same pond for decades.

take_care.label: What to do
take_care.text: Watch from a distance and do not handle or feed them. If basking turtles begin dropping into the water as you approach, give them more room.

at_a_glance.text: A large, dark freshwater turtle, most often seen basking on a log or bank — frequently several piled together.
Look closely at the head. Yellow stripes form looping, hairpin-like marks behind the eyes — no red ear patch, and no red arrow between the eyes.
Adults are almost entirely vegetarian, which is unusual among Florida's pond turtles.
Approach too quickly and you get a row of quiet plops as the whole line slides back into the water.

quick_hits: A Double-crested Cormorant is a dark, heavy-bodied waterbird that dives completely underwater after fish.
It chases fish underwater using its large webbed feet for propulsion, rather than spearing prey from ambush like an Anhinga.
After diving, cormorants often perch with their wings spread. Their feathers become waterlogged more readily than those of most waterbirds, which can aid underwater diving.
Cormorants have a hooked bill and shorter tail; Anhingas have a straight daggerlike bill and long fan-shaped tail.
species.range_and_origin: Native and widespread across North America. In Florida it occurs on ponds, lakes, rivers, estuaries and coastal waters throughout the year.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Dark brown to blackish, with orange-yellow bare skin around the base of the bill.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Long and narrow with a noticeable hook at the tip.

blocks.label: In the water
blocks.text: Swims low and repeatedly disappears underwater during feeding dives.

blocks.label: Breeding crest
blocks.text: Adults briefly grow two small tufts on the head during breeding season; they are absent or difficult to see most of the year.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a dark waterbird repeatedly diving in open water or perched with its wings spread. The hook-tipped bill, orange facial skin and relatively short tail separate it from an Anhinga.

species.diet: Mostly fish, with occasional crayfish, amphibians and other aquatic prey.
species.behavior: Dives repeatedly in pursuit of fish, propelling itself underwater with its webbed feet. Between feeding bouts it rests on exposed perches and may hold its wings open to dry.
species.ecological_role: A pursuit predator of fish in both freshwater and coastal habitats.
species.plant_connections: Cormorants nest colonially in trees, shrubs, on the ground or on human structures. In large tree colonies, accumulated droppings can damage or eventually kill nesting trees, changing the vegetation beneath and around the colony. At Palma Sola the species is an occasional visitor rather than a known nesting colony.

size.length: Wingspan about four feet.

species.habitat: Fresh and salt water of almost any kind — ponds, lakes, rivers, reservoirs, and coastlines — with fish to catch and perches for drying.
species.where_to_look: Scan open pond water for diving birds, then check snags, banks and other exposed perches for cormorants resting or drying their wings.
species.when_to_see: Double-crested Cormorants occur in Florida year-round. Palma Sola has only a few records, so sightings here should be considered occasional.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Give perched birds enough room to rest and dry their feathers without being forced back into the water.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

species.internal_notes: Recent genus change from Phalacrocorax — current name reflected here.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident. Palma Sola currently has too few records to define a local seasonal pattern.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Anhingas are slimmer, with longer fan-shaped tails and straight daggerlike bills. Double-crested Cormorants are heavier-bodied, with shorter tails and bills that hook at the tip.

how_it_lives.text: Cormorants pursue fish underwater rather than waiting for them. Their large webbed feet provide most of the propulsion, and the hooked bill grips the catch.
Because the plumage becomes waterlogged, a bird often rests afterward on an exposed perch with its wings spread while the feathers dry.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Dark brown to blackish, with orange-yellow bare skin around the base of the bill.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Long and narrow with a distinct hook at the tip.

how_to_know_it.label: In the water
how_to_know_it.text: Swims low, and disappears under again and again while feeding.
The bird it gets confused with is the Anhinga. The hooked bill and the short tail settle it.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Scan the open pond water for a dark bird that keeps vanishing, then check snags, banks and other exposed perches where one may be resting with its wings held open.
In Florida year-round, but with only a few park records — an occasional visitor here.

what_it_does_here.text: A cormorant catches fish by running them down underwater, driving itself with big webbed feet rather than ambushing from above.

The spread-wing pose afterward is the cost of that. Cormorant feathers wet through more readily than most waterbirds', which cuts buoyancy and helps underwater, but leaves the bird needing to dry out before it flies well.

Where they nest in numbers, cormorants reshape the trees they use: droppings build up under a colony heavily enough to damage and eventually kill them, changing what grows underneath. At Palma Sola they are visitors, not a colony.

at_a_glance.text: A dark, heavy-bodied waterbird that dives completely underwater after fish.
It chases fish down with its webbed feet rather than spearing them from ambush like an Anhinga.
Adults grow the two small head tufts of the name only briefly in breeding season. Most of the year there is no crest to see.

species.teaser: The 'double crest' is easy to miss. Adults grow two small head tufts only during the breeding season.

quick_hits: Eastern Gray Squirrels spend much of the day moving between the ground and tree canopy, feeding heavily on acorns, nuts, seeds, buds and fruit.
Instead of storing all its food in one place, a Gray Squirrel buries nuts separately across its home range — a strategy called scatter-hoarding.
Some buried acorns are never recovered. Those that survive can germinate, making squirrels important dispersers of oak seeds.
Its hind feet can rotate far enough backward to grip bark while the squirrel climbs down a trunk headfirst.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the eastern United States, including all of Florida. It is a familiar year-round resident of forests, parks, and neighborhoods anywhere there are trees, especially oaks.
more_information: The gray squirrel's whole lifestyle revolves around food storage. In fall it gathers acorns and other nuts and buries them one by one across its territory — a strategy called scatter-hoarding — then recovers them through winter using a sharp memory and an even sharper sense of smell.

It is far from perfect at the recovery part, and that is good news for the forest. The acorns a squirrel forgets are effectively planted, buried at just the right depth to sprout. In a very real sense, some of the oaks shading this park owe their start to generations of forgetful squirrels.

They are also built for life in the trees. A gray squirrel can rotate its hind feet nearly 180 degrees, letting it grip the bark and head down a trunk face-first, and its long tail serves as a counterbalance, a rudder in mid-leap, a sunshade, and a blanket.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Usually gray above with a paler, whitish belly; some individuals are unusually dark or reddish-brown.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Long, broad, and very bushy, often held in a curve over the back.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Clearly larger than a chipmunk, smaller than a cat.

identification.what_to_look_for: A gray, bushy-tailed rodent bounding across the ground or spiraling up an oak. The big, flicking tail and the habit of freezing, then dashing, are dead giveaways.

species.diet: Mostly acorns, nuts, and seeds, plus buds, flowers, fungi, berries, and the occasional insect or egg. Quick to take advantage of bird feeders and picnic leftovers.
species.behavior: Active by day, year-round (it does not hibernate). Spends its time foraging, caching food, and chasing other squirrels through the trees. Builds leafy nests called dreys high in the branches, and stays constantly alert for hawks, owls, and other predators.
species.sounds: Surprisingly vocal — sharp kuk-kuk barks and chatters, plus a buzzy alarm call given with flicks of the tail to warn others of danger.
species.ecological_role: A keystone tree-planter: by burying and forgetting nuts, gray squirrels help oaks and other trees regenerate. They are also important prey for hawks, owls, and snakes, linking the treetops to the rest of the food web.
species.plant_connections: Oaks and other nut trees — the squirrel eats their acorns and nuts and, by burying and forgetting them, helps plant new trees.

size.length: 17 to 20 inches, including the tail
size.lifespan: often only a few years in the wild, but can exceed 10 years.

species.habitat: Forests and woodlands with nut-bearing trees, especially oaks, plus parks, campuses, and leafy neighborhoods. Needs trees for nesting and escape.
species.where_to_look: In and under the oaks and other large trees — on the ground foraging, racing up trunks, or leaping between branches. Active throughout the day.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, active in every season and through most of the daylight hours.

danger.people: Harmless if left alone. Like any wild animal, a squirrel can bite if cornered or hand-fed, so it is best not to try to touch or feed them.
danger.pets: No real danger to pets, though dogs love to give chase. The squirrel is far quicker and usually well out of reach.

interaction.guidance: Enjoy them, but do not hand-feed. Fed squirrels lose their wariness, can become nippy, and a human diet is not good for them.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Abundant and adaptable, and one of the most commonly seen mammals in the state.

species.internal_notes: The land-mammal crowd-pleaser, especially for kids.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident. The park's formal observation record is sparse and probably underrepresents this familiar species.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much larger and heavier-bodied, with a longer tail and highly variable coloration. Eastern Gray Squirrels are smaller and usually gray with a pale underside.

how_it_lives.text: Much of the year revolves around stored food. A squirrel carries individual nuts away from the parent tree and buries them in separate caches, returning later to recover many of them.
Its feet are adapted for climbing in either direction on vertical bark, and the long tail helps with balance while running and leaping through branches.
Active by day throughout the year. Gray Squirrels build leafy nests high in branches and also use tree cavities for shelter.
It can rotate its hind feet nearly 180 degrees to grip the bark and come down a trunk head-first. The tail does the rest of the work — counterbalance, rudder in mid-leap, sunshade and blanket.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Usually gray above and whitish below. Some individuals can be darker or show reddish tones.

how_to_know_it.label: Tail
how_to_know_it.text: Long and very bushy, often held curved over the back when the animal pauses.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Much larger than a chipmunk and smaller than a house cat.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Sharp barks, chatters and buzzy alarm calls, often accompanied by rapid tail flicking.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a gray, bushy-tailed squirrel feeding beneath trees, running along branches or spiraling around a trunk. Gray Squirrels can descend a trunk headfirst, a useful clue when you see one moving vertically.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look in and beneath large trees, especially oaks. Squirrels forage on the ground for fallen nuts, run along trunks and branches, and build leafy nests high in the canopy.
A year-round Florida resident active during daylight. The park's formal observation record is sparse and probably underrepresents this familiar species.

what_it_does_here.text: Squirrels plant trees by forgetting. They bury acorns and other large seeds one at a time and fail to recover a good many of them, leaving those seeds exactly where a seedling needs to be — underground, and well away from the parent tree.

what_it_does_here.label: The oak and the squirrel
what_it_does_here.text: Trees provide nearly everything the Gray Squirrel needs. Oaks and other nut-bearing trees supply much of its food; branches provide travel routes and support leafy nests; cavities offer shelter. By carrying and burying acorns away from the parent tree, squirrels also influence where new oaks become established.

take_care.text: Do not handle or hand-feed squirrels. A wild squirrel can bite or scratch if cornered or accustomed to taking food from people. Keep dogs from chasing wildlife.
Watch without hand-feeding. Feeding encourages squirrels to approach people and to seek food from them persistently.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

at_a_glance.text: Eastern Gray Squirrels spend much of the day moving between the ground and tree canopy, feeding heavily on acorns, nuts, seeds, buds and fruit.
Instead of storing all its food in one place, a Gray Squirrel buries nuts separately across its home range — a strategy called scatter-hoarding.
Some buried acorns are never recovered. Those that survive can germinate, making squirrels important dispersers of oak seeds.
Its hind feet can rotate far enough backward to grip bark while the squirrel climbs down a trunk headfirst.

species.teaser: A Gray Squirrel burying an acorn may be determining where the next oak grows.

quick_hits: Florida's Mottled Duck is a nonmigratory subspecies found only in peninsular Florida.
Males and females are both mottled brown. Males have olive-green to yellow bills; females have orange-brown bills marked with dark spots.
A female Mallard can look similar, but Mottled Ducks have a paler, plainer head and usually lack the broad white borders around the blue wing patch.
Released domestic Mallards breed with Florida Mottled Ducks, producing fertile hybrids. FWC considers this genetic mixing the biggest immediate threat to the Florida population.
species.range_and_origin: The Florida Mottled Duck is a nonmigratory subspecies found only in peninsular Florida. A separate Mottled Duck population occurs along the western Gulf Coast.

blocks.label: Plumage
blocks.text: Warm mottled brown overall, with a noticeably paler, plainer head and neck.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Male: olive-green to yellow. Female: orange-brown with dark spots or blotches.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: The blue-purple wing patch usually lacks the broad white border above that is typical of a female Mallard.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a warm brown duck with a paler, plainer head. Bill color separates adult males and females. Birds showing Mallard-like traits — stronger white wing markings, green on the head or domestic-looking plumage — may be hybrids, but some birds cannot be identified confidently in the field.

species.diet: Marsh-plant seeds, stems and roots, plus insects, snails, crayfish, mollusks and small fish.
species.behavior: Usually seen in pairs or small groups, feeding by dabbling and tipping forward in shallow water. Females nest on the ground in dense vegetation near water.
species.ecological_role: An omnivorous marsh duck that feeds on both wetland plants and small aquatic animals.
species.plant_connections: Wetland plants provide both food and nesting cover. Mottled Ducks eat seeds, stems and roots of marsh plants, and females hide ground nests in dense grasses, rushes or palmetto near water.

size.length: About the size of a Mallard, with a wingspan around two and a half feet.

species.habitat: Florida's fresh and brackish marshes, ponds, lakes, canals, ditches, and stormwater impoundments — wherever there is shallow water and marsh vegetation.
species.where_to_look: Look on shallow ponds and along marshy edges, often for pairs or small groups. Mottled Ducks use fresh and brackish wetlands with abundant shoreline and marsh vegetation.
species.when_to_see: Florida Mottled Ducks are nonmigratory and occur in the state year-round. Palma Sola has several Mottled Duck and hybrid records, but the local dataset is too small to estimate how consistently pure Mottled Ducks are present.

interaction.guidance: Do not feed or release domestic ducks. Released Mallards that remain in Florida can breed with native Mottled Ducks and produce fertile hybrids. Florida regulates possession and prohibits unauthorized release of Mallards.

invasive.notes: Mottled Ducks are native. Wild migratory Mallards occur naturally in Florida during winter, but released domestic Mallards that remain year-round are non-native and can hybridize with Mottled Ducks.

conservation.status: Not federally listed, but a major Florida conservation concern. FWC identifies hybridization with released domestic Mallards as the biggest immediate threat to the Florida Mottled Duck. Wetland loss and alteration are additional concerns.

species.internal_notes: Count includes 3 Mallard × Mottled Duck hybrid obs + 1 genus-level Anas. Hybridization is a real FL conservation story worth telling.

seasonality.note: Nonmigratory Florida resident. Some Palma Sola records involve Mallard × Mottled Duck hybrids, so the current dataset does not establish reliable local frequency for pure Mottled Ducks.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Female Mallards are similarly brown but usually have less contrast between the head and body and show stronger white borders around the blue wing patch. Wild male Mallards have the familiar green head. Hybrids can combine traits of both species.

how_it_lives.text: Mottled Ducks feed in shallow water by dabbling and tipping forward. They usually occur in pairs or small groups rather than the large winter flocks formed by many migratory ducks.
Their diet includes marsh-plant seeds, stems and roots along with insects, snails, crayfish, mollusks and small fish.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look on shallow ponds and along marshy edges, often for pairs or small groups. Mottled Ducks use fresh and brackish wetlands with abundant shoreline and marsh vegetation.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Palma Sola's wildlife records include birds identified as Mallard × Mottled Duck hybrids. That makes the statewide hybridization problem visible here at the park.

species.teaser: Some of the brown ducks at Palma Sola carry visible signs of a statewide conservation problem: interbreeding between native Mottled Ducks and released Mallards.

quick_hits: The Wood Stork is the only stork that breeds in the United States. Adults are large white birds with black flight feathers, a bare dark head and a heavy downcurved bill.
It feeds mainly by touch, sweeping an open bill through shallow water and snapping it shut when prey makes contact.
Wood Storks feed most efficiently where falling water levels concentrate fish in shallow pools. Their breeding success therefore depends heavily on the timing of wet and dry conditions.
The U.S. breeding population was listed as endangered in 1984, improved enough to be downlisted to threatened in 2014, and was removed from the federal endangered-species list in March 2026.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. In the United States it breeds mainly in the Southeast, especially Florida, Georgia and South Carolina, with the breeding range expanding northward during its recovery.
more_information: Wood Storks often travel between wetlands by soaring on rising warm air, sometimes circling high overhead with other large birds.

blocks.label: Body
blocks.text: Large and white, with black flight feathers that become especially obvious when the wings are spread.

blocks.label: Head
blocks.text: Adults have a bare, dark gray, scaly-looking head and neck.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Long, thick and curved downward.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Black trailing edges contrast strongly with the white wings, and the long legs extend behind the tail.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large white wading bird with a bare dark head and heavy downcurved bill. In flight, broad black areas show along the wings and the long legs trail behind.

species.diet: Mostly small fish, plus other aquatic animals such as crayfish, frogs and large insects.
species.behavior: The bird walks slowly through shallow water with its bill partly open. Instead of aiming visually at individual fish, it waits for prey to touch the bill and then closes it.
species.ecological_role: A shallow-water predator whose feeding success depends on fish being concentrated by changing water levels. Because nesting and feeding respond strongly to wetland hydrology, Wood Storks have also been used to evaluate wetland restoration.
species.plant_connections: Trees and wetlands have to work together for a Wood Stork colony. The birds build large stick nests in trees or shrubs over water or on wetland islands, while nearby shallow wetlands provide the concentrated fish needed to feed adults and young. Protecting a colony therefore means protecting both the nesting trees and the surrounding feeding wetlands.

size.length: About three feet tall, with a wingspan around five feet.

species.habitat: Fresh and brackish wetlands — marshes, swamps, flooded fields, and pond edges — especially those that dry down seasonally to concentrate fish. Nests in trees, including cypress and mangroves.
species.where_to_look: Look in shallow pond margins, marshy edges and other places where fish become concentrated in receding water. Wood Storks often feed with other wading birds.
species.when_to_see: Wood Storks occur in Florida year-round. Their movements follow changing water conditions, so they may appear where shallow water has concentrated fish. At Palma Sola they are an occasional visitor rather than a bird to expect on any given day.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched from a distance. Do not approach or handle an injured Wood Stork; its large bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed or approach the bird. Never enter or closely approach a nesting colony; repeated disturbance can cause adults to leave nests.

conservation.status: Removed from the federal endangered-species list in March 2026 after decades of recovery. The U.S. breeding population had been listed as endangered in 1984 and threatened since 2014. Federal biologists will continue monitoring the population for ten years after delisting.

species.internal_notes: Federally listed history. Status verified 2026-06-19: ESA-delisted (Southeast U.S. DPS), effective March 2026, with a 10-year post-delisting monitoring plan; content reflects this.

seasonality.note: Present in Florida year-round, but local numbers shift with water levels. Recorded at Palma Sola only a handful of times.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Also white with black in the wings, but has an enormous orange bill and short legs that do not trail far behind the tail.
Entirely white in flight, with a yellow bill, feathered head and black legs. The Wood Stork has black flight feathers and a bare dark head.

how_it_lives.label: Travelling by thermal
how_it_lives.text: Wood Storks often move between wetlands by soaring on rising warm air, sometimes circling high overhead with other large birds.

Feeling for prey by touch only pays where the water has drawn down enough to crowd the fish together, so nesting success reads directly off wetland hydrology — and biologists use it to judge how restoration is going.

species.teaser: A Wood Stork hunts without needing to see its prey. It walks through shallow water with the bill open and snaps it shut when a fish touches it.

also_known_as: Great White Heron (white form, south Florida)
quick_hits: Great Blue Herons stand close to four feet tall and can span more than six feet from wingtip to wingtip, making them the largest herons in North America.
A hunting bird may stand motionless for minutes before driving its head and neck forward in a sudden strike.
Fish dominate the diet, but Great Blue Herons also hunt frogs, snakes, insects, turtles and small mammals, including prey caught on lawns and open ground.
In extreme southern Florida, Great Blue Herons also occur in an all-white form known as the Great White Heron.
species.range_and_origin: Native across much of North and Central America. In Florida it occurs year-round around fresh, brackish and coastal water and also feeds in nearby fields and lawns.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Very large, standing around four feet tall with long legs and a heavy bill.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Blue-gray body, pale head and neck, and a broad black stripe extending behind the eye.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Flies with the neck folded back and the long legs trailing behind.

blocks.label: White morph
blocks.text: The Great White Heron of southern Florida is entirely white but retains the Great Blue's massive size, heavy bill and pale legs.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a very large blue-gray heron standing or walking slowly along the water's edge. In flight, the folded neck separates a heron from Wood Storks and cranes, which fly with their necks extended.

species.diet: Mostly fish, plus amphibians, reptiles, large insects and small mammals.
species.behavior: Usually solitary while feeding. Great Blue Herons alternate between standing still and walking slowly as they hunt. They may feed by day or after dark and gather in colonies to nest.
species.ecological_role: A large predator of fish and other wetland animals that also carries its hunting onto dry ground for reptiles and small mammals.
species.plant_connections: Great Blue Herons nest colonially, usually high in trees but sometimes in mangroves, shrubs or other structures. Their large stick nests may be reused and enlarged. The nest cup can be lined with pine needles, reeds, grass, moss, mangrove leaves or smaller twigs.

size.length: About four feet tall, with a wingspan around six feet.

species.habitat: Almost any wetland or water edge — marshes, ponds, lakes, rivers, coastlines — plus nearby fields and lawns where it hunts small animals.
species.where_to_look: Look along pond banks and shallow water, but also scan lawns and open grassy areas. Great Blue Herons hunt both aquatic and terrestrial prey.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident and an occasional visitor at Palma Sola.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched normally. Do not handle an injured or trapped heron; the long pointed bill can cause serious injury.
danger.pets: Keep dogs from chasing or cornering wildlife.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. If a hunting bird stops feeding, walks away or flies as you approach, give it more room.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Great Egrets are entirely white, slightly smaller and slimmer, with black legs. Ordinary Great Blue Herons are blue-gray and substantially heavier-looking. In southern Florida a white-form Great Blue can resemble a Great Egret but is bulkier, with a much heavier bill and paler legs.

how_it_lives.text: It hunts by either standing still or stalking slowly through shallow water and open ground. When prey comes within reach, the long neck extends in a rapid strike.
Fish are the main food, but the diet is unusually broad for a heron and includes amphibians, reptiles, insects and small mammals.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Stands close to four feet tall and spans more than six feet across the wings — the largest heron in North America.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Blue-gray body with a pale head and a broad black stripe running back from the eye.

how_to_know_it.label: In flight
how_to_know_it.text: Flies with the neck folded back onto the shoulders and the long legs trailing behind. Wood Storks and cranes fly with the neck held straight out.

how_to_know_it.label: White form
how_to_know_it.text: In extreme southern Florida an all-white form occurs, known as the Great White Heron. It keeps the massive size, heavy bill and pale legs.
Look for a very large blue-gray bird standing still or walking slowly at the water's edge.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Check the pond banks and shallow water first, then look at the lawns. A Great Blue Heron standing in dry grass well back from the water is hunting, not resting.
A year-round Florida resident, and an occasional visitor here rather than a bird to expect on every walk.

what_it_does_here.text: This is a hunter that works by patience. It stands motionless for minutes, then drives its head and neck forward in a single stroke. Fish make up most of the diet, but the list runs on through frogs, snakes, large insects, turtles and small mammals — which is why the mown grass is as good a hunting ground as the pond edge.
Away from the nesting colony they feed alone, by day or well after dark.

They nest colonially, usually high in trees and sometimes in mangroves or shrubs. The big stick nests are reused and enlarged season after season, and the cup is lined with whatever is at hand — pine needles, reeds, grass, moss, mangrove leaves, finer twigs.

at_a_glance.text: Great Blue Herons stand close to four feet tall and can span more than six feet from wingtip to wingtip, making them the largest herons in North America.
A hunting bird may stand motionless for minutes before driving its head and neck forward in a sudden strike.
Fish dominate the diet, but Great Blue Herons also hunt frogs, snakes, insects, turtles and small mammals, including prey caught on lawns and open ground.
In extreme southern Florida, Great Blue Herons also occur in an all-white form known as the Great White Heron.

species.teaser: A Great Blue Heron standing in a lawn may be hunting just as seriously as one beside a pond. It takes rodents, snakes and other land prey as well as fish.

quick_hits: Monarch caterpillars can eat only milkweeds. Those plants are therefore not just nectar sources — they are the nursery on which the next generation depends.
Florida is different: some monarchs remain and breed through winter rather than joining the long-distance migration.
Many monarchs from eastern North America migrate thousands of miles to mountain forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter in enormous colonies.

The round trip spans several generations. The late-summer migratory generation lives much longer than summer monarchs and makes the long southbound journey; later generations continue the return north.

Milkweeds contain defensive chemicals called cardenolides. Monarch caterpillars store some of them in their bodies, which can make the caterpillars and adult butterflies distasteful or toxic to some predators.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America and now established in several other parts of the world. Florida supports both migratory monarchs and populations that remain and breed in the state. Not every monarch seen here is on its way to or from Mexico.
more_information: Florida sits outside the simple textbook migration map. Some monarchs reaching the state remain and breed, and researchers are still working out how Florida's resident and migratory populations interact.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Orange wings with heavy black veins and a black border marked with white spots.

blocks.label: Male and female
blocks.text: Males have a small black scent patch on each hindwing and slightly thinner black veins. Females lack the spots and usually have heavier veining.

blocks.label: Caterpillar
blocks.text: Yellow, black and white bands, with pairs of long dark filaments. Look for it on milkweed.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Viceroys are smaller and have an extra black line crossing the hindwing, which Monarchs lack.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a large orange-and-black butterfly feeding at flowers or searching around milkweed. Viceroys have an extra black line crossing the hindwing; Monarchs do not.

species.diet: Caterpillars eat milkweed. Adults drink nectar from many flowering plants.
species.behavior: Adults feed at flowers, while females search for milkweed on which to lay eggs. Migratory monarchs travel during the day and may gather in trees at night during long journeys.
species.ecological_role: Monarch caterpillars are specialist herbivores of milkweed, while adults visit many flowers for nectar and can carry pollen between blooms. Their milkweed-derived chemical defenses also affect which predators can eat them successfully.
species.plant_connections: Milkweed is essential: Monarchs lay their eggs on milkweeds, and the caterpillars eat no other kind of plant. Adults are much less specialized and feed from many nectar flowers. In Florida, native milkweeds are the better conservation choice — Palma Sola grows swamp milkweed, Asclepias incarnata. Tropical milkweed, Asclepias curassavica, stays green through winter, can encourage year-round breeding and increases opportunities for the OE parasite to spread; UF/IFAS now classifies it as invasive in Florida.

size.length: Wingspan about four inches.
size.lifespan: Summer adults usually live only a few weeks. The migratory generation can live for many months.

species.habitat: Open, sunny places with flowers and milkweed — meadows, gardens, roadsides, marsh edges, and parks. Breeding depends entirely on the presence of milkweed.
species.where_to_look: Check flowering beds for adults and native milkweeds for eggs and caterpillars. Milkweed is required for breeding; nectar flowers fuel the adults.
species.when_to_see: Monarchs can occur in Florida through much of the year because the state supports both resident and migratory butterflies. Palma Sola records are still too limited to define a local peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling. Supporting native milkweeds and a succession of nectar flowers is more useful than handling or feeding butterflies.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and North America. Not invasive.

conservation.status: The migratory monarch is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has proposed listing the Monarch as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act, but no final rule has yet been issued, so that proposed federal protection is not currently in effect. Habitat loss, pesticide exposure, climate change and conditions at breeding, migratory and overwintering sites all contribute to concern.

species.internal_notes: Ties to milkweed plantings (host plant) and the park's Monarch Waystation story.

seasonality.note: Florida supports both resident and migratory monarchs. Palma Sola records are too few to define local seasonal peaks.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The viceroy is smaller and has an extra black line arcing across the hindwing that the monarch lacks.
The queen is a darker chestnut with less black veining than the monarch.
The gulf fritillary has narrower wings and brilliant silver spangles underneath; the monarch is broad-winged with heavy black veins and no silver.

how_it_lives.text: Adults feed at flowers, while females search for milkweed on which to lay eggs.

how_it_lives.label: On migration
how_it_lives.text: Migratory monarchs travel during the day and may gather in trees at night during long journeys.

how_to_know_it.label: Wings
how_to_know_it.text: Orange wings with heavy black veins and a black border marked with white spots.

how_to_know_it.label: Male and female
how_to_know_it.text: Males have a small black scent patch on each hindwing and slightly thinner black veins. Females lack the spots and usually have heavier veining.

how_to_know_it.label: Caterpillar
how_to_know_it.text: Yellow, black and white bands, with pairs of long dark filaments. Look for it on milkweed.

how_to_know_it.label: Look-alike
how_to_know_it.text: Viceroys are smaller and have an extra black line crossing the hindwing, which Monarchs lack.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: Wingspan about four inches.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look for a large orange-and-black butterfly feeding at flowers or searching around milkweed. Viceroys have an extra black line crossing the hindwing; Monarchs do not.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Check flowering beds for adults and native milkweeds for eggs and caterpillars. Milkweed is required for breeding; nectar flowers fuel the adults.
Monarchs can occur in Florida through much of the year because the state supports both resident and migratory butterflies. Palma Sola records are still too limited to define a local peak.

where_to_find_it_here.label: When
where_to_find_it_here.text: Florida supports both resident and migratory monarchs. Palma Sola records are too few to define local seasonal peaks.

what_it_does_here.text: The caterpillar's milkweed diet is also its armor. Compounds taken from the plant stay in the body through adulthood and make the butterfly unpalatable, which is why a Monarch can advertise itself in orange and black instead of hiding.

Milkweed is essential: Monarchs lay their eggs on milkweeds, and the caterpillars eat no other kind of plant. Adults are much less specialized and feed from many nectar flowers. In Florida, native milkweeds are the better conservation choice — Palma Sola grows swamp milkweed, Asclepias incarnata. Tropical milkweed, Asclepias curassavica, stays green through winter, can encourage year-round breeding and increases opportunities for the OE parasite to spread; UF/IFAS now classifies it as invasive in Florida.
Florida has Monarchs both ways. Some pass through on migration while others stay and breed here year-round, so a Monarch in the park may be a traveller or a resident.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: The migratory monarch is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has proposed listing the Monarch as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act, but no final rule has yet been issued, so that proposed federal protection is not currently in effect. Habitat loss, pesticide exposure, climate change and conditions at breeding, migratory and overwintering sites all contribute to concern.

at_a_glance.text: Monarch caterpillars can eat only milkweeds. Those plants are therefore not just nectar sources — they are the nursery on which the next generation depends.
Florida is different: some monarchs remain and breed through winter rather than joining the long-distance migration.
Many monarchs from eastern North America migrate thousands of miles to mountain forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter in enormous colonies.

The round trip spans several generations. The late-summer migratory generation lives much longer than summer monarchs and makes the long southbound journey; later generations continue the return north.

Milkweeds contain defensive chemicals called cardenolides. Monarch caterpillars store some of them in their bodies, which can make the caterpillars and adult butterflies distasteful or toxic to some predators.

species.teaser: Not every Florida monarch flies to Mexico. Florida supports both migratory monarchs and butterflies that remain and breed here instead.

quick_hits: A Great Egret is a tall, all-white heron with a long yellow bill and black legs and feet.
It often hunts by doing almost nothing: standing motionless in shallow water until a fish comes within striking distance.

During breeding season, adults grow long ornamental plumes on the back. Demand for those feathers in the hat trade devastated egret populations in the late 1800s and helped spur some of America's earliest bird-protection campaigns.
Great Egrets nest in colonies, building stick nests in trees and shrubs, often over water and alongside other herons and egrets.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas and found across much of the world. In Florida it is a familiar year-round resident of fresh, brackish and coastal wetlands.

blocks.label: Body
blocks.text: Entirely white, with a very long neck and long black legs.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Long, straight and usually yellow.

blocks.label: Feet
blocks.text: Black. This immediately separates an adult Great Egret from a Snowy Egret, which has yellow feet.

blocks.label: Breeding season
blocks.text: Long white plumes grow from the back, and the bare skin between the bill and eye becomes brighter green.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a tall, slender white heron with a yellow bill and black legs. It often stands motionless in shallow water with its neck partly drawn in, then strikes suddenly at prey.

species.diet: Mostly fish, plus frogs, crustaceans, aquatic insects and other small animals.
species.behavior: It hunts in shallow water by standing still or walking slowly, then drives the long bill forward when fish or other prey come within reach.
species.ecological_role: A predator of fish and other small wetland animals. Great Egrets also concentrate in mixed nesting colonies that become important feeding sites for predators and scavengers.
species.plant_connections: Trees and shrubs provide the structure for nesting colonies. Great Egrets build stick nests in woody vegetation, often over water; documented nest plants include live oak, wax myrtle, mangroves and buttonwood. Along the shoreline, aquatic and emergent plants also create cover for the fish and other prey the birds hunt.

size.length: About three feet tall, with a wingspan around four and a half to five and a half feet.

species.habitat: Shallow fresh and salt water — marshes, ponds, lake edges, mudflats, and coastal shorelines — with open water for hunting and trees or reeds for nesting.
species.where_to_look: Look along pond edges and shallow water. Great Egrets often hunt alone, either standing motionless or walking slowly along the shoreline.
species.when_to_see: Present in Florida year-round and an occasional visitor to Palma Sola's ponds.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched at a normal distance. An injured or trapped egret should not be handled; its pointed bill can cause serious injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. If the bird stops feeding, retreats or flies away as you approach, give it more space.

conservation.status: Least Concern today. Great Egrets were nearly eliminated from parts of North America by hunting for the plume trade in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Legal protection allowed populations to recover.

seasonality.note: Year-round Florida resident. Recorded at Palma Sola by several observers, though not on every visit.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much smaller, with a black bill, black legs and bright yellow feet.
Young Little Blue Herons are also white, but smaller, with dull greenish legs and a pale bill tipped with black.
The rare white form is larger and heavier-bodied with paler legs. An ordinary Great Egret has black legs.
Wood Storks are white with broad black flight feathers, a bare dark head and a heavy downcurved bill. A Great Egret is all white with a straight yellow bill and a feathered head.

how_it_lives.text: It hunts by standing still or walking slowly through shallow water, then driving the long bill forward when a fish comes within reach. Frogs, crustaceans, insects and small reptiles go the same way.

how_to_know_it.label: Bill
how_to_know_it.text: Long, straight and usually yellow.

how_to_know_it.label: Feet
how_to_know_it.text: Black. This immediately separates an adult Great Egret from a Snowy Egret, which has yellow feet.

Present in Florida year-round and an occasional visitor to Palma Sola's ponds — recorded by several observers, though not on every visit.

what_it_does_here.text: A nesting colony concentrates food as well as birds. Dozens of nests packed into a few trees draw predators and scavengers that would have no reason to gather there otherwise, so the colony becomes its own small ecosystem for as long as it lasts.

what_it_does_here.label: Trees make the colony
what_it_does_here.text: Trees and shrubs provide the structure for nesting colonies. Great Egrets build stick nests in woody vegetation, often over water; documented nest plants include live oak, wax myrtle, mangroves and buttonwood. Along the shoreline, aquatic and emergent plants also create cover for the fish and other prey the birds hunt.
