It often hunts by doing almost nothing: standing motionless in shallow water until a fish comes within striking distance.

During breeding season, adults grow long ornamental plumes on the back. Demand for those feathers in the hat trade devastated egret populations in the late 1800s and helped spur some of America's earliest bird-protection campaigns.
Great Egrets nest in colonies, building stick nests in trees and shrubs, often over water and alongside other herons and egrets.

species.teaser: The long white plumes grown during breeding season nearly got this bird exterminated. Demand for those feathers helped trigger the early bird-protection movement.

quick_hits: A Common Gallinule is a dark marsh bird with a bright red forehead shield, a red-and-yellow bill and a white stripe along each side.
It swims like a duck but has no webbing on its feet. The Common Gallinule belongs to the rail family.
Very long toes spread its weight across soft mud and floating vegetation, letting the bird walk where a web-footed duck would push through.
Gallinules are often heard before they are seen, giving loud clucks, squawks and whinnying calls from dense pond vegetation.
species.range_and_origin: Native across much of the Americas. In Florida it is a year-round resident of freshwater and brackish ponds, marshes and other quiet water with abundant aquatic vegetation.
more_information: Until 2011, the New World Common Gallinule and the Old World Common Moorhen were treated as one species. They are now classified separately.

blocks.label: Adults
blocks.text: Dark slate-gray with a brownish back, bright red forehead shield, red bill tipped with yellow and a bold white stripe along the side.

blocks.label: Legs and feet
blocks.text: Yellow-green legs with extremely long, unwebbed toes.

blocks.label: Young
blocks.text: Brown and paler below, with a dull greenish bill and forehead shield. The white side stripe remains useful.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look along vegetated pond edges for a dark bird swimming with a head-bobbing motion or walking across floating plants. The red-and-yellow bill and white side stripe identify an adult.

species.diet: Seeds and other parts of aquatic plants, plus insects and snails. Gallinules sometimes flip floating leaves with their feet to expose small animals hiding underneath.
species.behavior: Swims along pond margins, walks across floating vegetation and soft ground, and retreats into dense cover when disturbed. Common Gallinules are often vocal and may feed in pairs, family groups or loose groups.
species.sounds: Listen for loud clucks, squawks and whinnying calls from dense wetland vegetation.
species.ecological_role: An omnivore in marsh food webs, eating aquatic plants, seeds, insects and snails and becoming prey for larger wetland predators.
species.plant_connections: Aquatic plants are feeding surface, food, cover and nest material. Gallinules walk across floating leaves, eat seeds and other plant parts, hide in emergent vegetation and build broad nests from grasses and sedges anchored among wetland plants.

size.length: A medium-sized marsh bird, a little over a foot long.

species.habitat: Freshwater marshes, ponds, lakes, and slow canals with plenty of cattails, reeds, and floating vegetation along the edges.
species.where_to_look: Look where open water meets thick aquatic vegetation. Gallinules swim along the edges and walk across floating leaves and plant mats, often disappearing quickly into cover.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident and regularly recorded at Palma Sola. Listen as well as look; birds hidden in pond-edge vegetation often call.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and do not feed it. Give birds along the pond edge enough room to remain out and feeding rather than retreating into cover.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and the Americas. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

species.internal_notes: Count includes 2 subspecies-level observations folded in.

seasonality.note: Recorded repeatedly at Palma Sola over several years.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Coots have a white bill and forehead shield and lobed toes. Common Gallinules have a bright red-and-yellow bill, a white stripe along the side and long toes without lobes.

how_it_lives.text: Long toes let the bird walk across floating leaves, plant mats and soft mud. It also swims well despite having no webbed feet.

Gallinules eat both plants and small animals, picking seeds and vegetation from the water and taking insects, snails and other invertebrates. They sometimes flip floating leaves with their feet to expose small animals hiding underneath.

how_to_know_it.label: Adults
how_to_know_it.text: Dark slate-gray with a brownish back, bright red forehead shield, red bill tipped with yellow and a bold white stripe along the side.

how_to_know_it.label: Legs and feet
how_to_know_it.text: Yellow-green legs with extremely long, unwebbed toes.

how_to_know_it.label: Young
how_to_know_it.text: Brown and paler below, with a dull greenish bill and forehead shield. The white side stripe remains useful.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: A medium-sized marsh bird, a little over a foot long.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Loud clucks, squawks and whinnying calls from dense wetland vegetation — often the first sign one is there.

how_to_know_it.label: What to look for
how_to_know_it.text: Look along vegetated pond edges for a dark bird swimming with a head-bobbing motion or walking across floating plants. The red-and-yellow bill and white side stripe identify an adult.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look where open water meets thick aquatic vegetation. Gallinules swim along the edges and walk across floating leaves and plant mats, often disappearing quickly into cover.
A year-round Florida resident and regularly recorded at Palma Sola. Listen as well as look; birds hidden in pond-edge vegetation often call.

what_it_does_here.text: Aquatic plants are feeding surface, food, cover and nest material at once. Gallinules walk across floating leaves, eat seeds and other plant parts, hide in emergent vegetation and build broad nests from grasses and sedges anchored among wetland plants.
Until 2011 this bird and the Old World Common Moorhen were treated as a single species. They are now considered separate.

It swims like a duck but has no webbing on its feet. The Common Gallinule belongs to the rail family.
Very long toes spread its weight across soft mud and floating vegetation, letting the bird walk where a web-footed duck would push through.
Gallinules are often heard before they are seen, giving loud clucks, squawks and whinnying calls from dense pond vegetation.

species.teaser: It swims without webbed feet. Long, widely spread toes let the Common Gallinule walk across floating plants and soft mud.

quick_hits: A flock of white birds walking across wet grass with long downcurved reddish bills is usually a flock of White Ibises.
Young White Ibises are brown and white rather than all white. Their adult plumage and bright red-pink bare parts develop gradually.
The curved bill is a sensitive probe. An ibis pushes it into mud or soft ground and closes it when it feels a crayfish, crab, insect or other prey.
White Ibises nest in colonies in trees, shrubs and sometimes dense marsh vegetation, often alongside other wading birds.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, Caribbean, Central America and northern South America. In Florida it is a familiar year-round resident of wetlands, shorelines, parks and wet lawns.
more_information: Florida folklore says the ibis is the last wildlife to seek shelter before a hurricane and the first to return afterward. The University of Miami cites that tradition as part of the reason the ibis became the Hurricanes' mascot.

blocks.label: Adults
blocks.text: White overall with a long downcurved reddish-pink bill, red facial skin and reddish legs. Black wingtips show mainly in flight.

blocks.label: Juveniles
blocks.text: Brown above and white below, with the same long curved bill. They become progressively whiter as they mature.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for medium-sized white birds walking through wet lawns or shallow water with their heads down and curved bills probing the ground. Black wingtips show in flight. Brown-and-white birds with the same bill shape are juveniles.

species.diet: Crayfish, crabs, insects and other aquatic invertebrates, plus small fish, frogs, snails and similar prey.
species.behavior: Highly social. White Ibises often feed in groups on wet ground or in shallow water and roost communally in trees.
species.ecological_role: A predator of crayfish, crabs, insects and other small animals in wet soils and shallow water.
species.plant_connections: White Ibises nest colonially in trees and shrubs near water. Documented nesting plants include black mangrove, red bay, willow, cypress and elderberry; where woody sites are limited, they may nest in dense grasses or sedges. Wet lawns and low marsh vegetation also create the soft feeding ground where they probe for prey.

size.length: About two feet tall, with a wingspan a little over three feet.

species.habitat: Shallow wetlands of all kinds — marshes, mudflats, flooded fields, pond edges, and coastal shorelines — plus well-watered lawns and parks.
species.where_to_look: Check damp lawns, grassy pond edges and shallow water, often for several birds feeding together. Soft wet ground lets the curved bill probe easily for buried prey.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident and one of the more regularly recorded wading birds at Palma Sola.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a comfortable distance and do not feed them. Let the flock continue probing and moving naturally across the lawn or shoreline.

conservation.status: Globally classified as Least Concern. White Ibis was removed from Florida's state threatened-species list in 2017 but remains included in Florida's Imperiled Species Management Plan.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Much larger, with a bare dark head and heavy downcurved bill. White Ibises are smaller, with reddish facial skin and a much narrower curved bill.

how_it_lives.text: White Ibises feed mainly by touch, probing soft mud, shallow water and wet soil with the curved bill for crayfish, crabs, insects and other small animals.
They are highly social, feeding and roosting in groups and often traveling between sites in lines or loose formations.

how_to_know_it.label: Adults
how_to_know_it.text: White overall with a long downcurved reddish-pink bill, red facial skin and reddish legs. The black wingtips show mainly in flight.

how_to_know_it.label: Juveniles
how_to_know_it.text: Brown above and white below, with the same long curved bill. They whiten gradually as they mature.

how_to_know_it.label: Size
how_to_know_it.text: About two feet tall, with a wingspan a little over three feet.
A group of white birds walking across wet grass with long downcurved bills is almost always this species.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Damp lawns and grassy pond edges, usually several birds working the same patch. Soft wet ground is the requirement — the bill has to be able to push into it — so the hours after rain are the best time to look.
Present year-round, and one of the more regularly recorded wading birds at the park.

what_it_does_here.text: The curved bill is a probe worked entirely by feel. An ibis pushes it into mud or soft turf and closes it the instant it touches a crayfish, crab, insect or snail. A flock crossing a lawn after rain is hunting, not grazing.

They nest in colonies in trees and shrubs near water — black mangrove, red bay, willow, cypress and elderberry have all been recorded — and will drop into dense grasses or sedges where woody cover is short.

Florida folklore holds that the ibis is the last bird to take shelter before a hurricane and the first to come back out afterward. The University of Miami cites that tradition as part of the reason the ibis became the Hurricanes' mascot.

at_a_glance.text: A flock of white birds walking across wet grass with long downcurved reddish bills is usually a flock of White Ibises.
Young White Ibises are brown and white rather than all white. Their adult plumage and bright red-pink bare parts develop gradually.
The curved bill is a sensitive probe. An ibis pushes it into mud or soft ground and closes it when it feels a crayfish, crab, insect or other prey.
White Ibises nest in colonies in trees, shrubs and sometimes dense marsh vegetation, often alongside other wading birds.

species.teaser: A flock of White Ibises probing a lawn after rain is hunting, not grazing. Their curved bills feel for prey hidden in soft soil.

quick_hits: An Anhinga often swims with its body submerged and only the long snakelike neck above water, which is why it is called the snakebird.
Its feathers become waterlogged more easily than those of most waterbirds. Combined with dense bones, that reduces buoyancy and helps the bird slip below the surface to hunt.
Underwater, an Anhinga stalks fish and drives its sharp bill through the side of the prey with a rapid thrust.
After fishing, Anhingas often perch with their wings spread, drying waterlogged feathers before flying again.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the warmer Americas. In Florida it is a year-round resident of shallow ponds, lakes, marshes and slow waterways, with occasional use of brackish coastal water.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Long, straight and sharply pointed.

blocks.label: Neck
blocks.text: Very long and slender, often the most visible part of a swimming bird.

blocks.label: Plumage
blocks.text: Adult males are black with silvery-white streaks on the wings and back. Females and young have a pale tan head, neck and breast.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Long and fan-shaped, extending conspicuously behind the body.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a long-necked waterbird swimming extremely low or perched with its wings spread. The straight daggerlike bill and long fan-shaped tail separate it from the Double-crested Cormorant.

species.diet: Mostly small and medium-sized fish, with small amounts of crustaceans and other aquatic animals.
species.behavior: Hunts underwater by slowly stalking fish, then perches in the open to dry its feathers. Anhingas are also strong soaring birds and may circle high overhead on thermals.
species.ecological_role: A specialized predator of small and medium-sized fish in shallow wetlands.
species.plant_connections: Anhingas depend on waterside vegetation in two ways. Submerged plants provide structure around which fish can hide and be stalked, while trees and shrubs over or beside the water provide drying perches and nest sites. Nests are bulky stick platforms that may be lined with fresh leaves and green twigs.

size.length: Wingspan about three and a half feet.

species.habitat: Calm fresh and brackish water — ponds, lakes, slow rivers, marshes, and mangrove edges — with fish to hunt and branches or snags for perching and drying.
species.where_to_look: Scan calm pond water for a swimming bird with its body mostly submerged, then check branches, snags and banks around the water for birds drying their wings.
species.when_to_see: A year-round Florida resident and regularly recorded at Palma Sola. Look whenever the ponds are active; perched birds with spread wings are especially conspicuous.

danger.people: No meaningful danger when watched at a normal distance. Do not handle an injured or trapped Anhinga; the sharp bill can cause injury.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and do not feed it. Give perched birds enough room to remain in place while they dry their feathers.

invasive.notes: Native to Florida and the Americas. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

species.internal_notes: Observed by 9 different people — broadest community appeal in the dataset.

seasonality.note: Recorded repeatedly at Palma Sola over multiple years.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Cormorants are heavier-bodied, with shorter tails and bills that hook at the tip. Anhingas are slimmer, with long fan-shaped tails and straight daggerlike bills.

how_it_lives.text: Underwater, the Anhinga swims slowly around submerged vegetation and stalks fish rather than chasing them at high speed. It usually strikes by thrusting its partly opened bill through the side of a fish.
After fishing, it often climbs onto a branch or bank and spreads its wings while the waterlogged feathers dry. Once airborne, it can soar high on rising warm air.

Submerged plants provide structure around which fish can hide and be stalked, while trees and shrubs over or beside the water provide drying perches and nest sites. Nests are bulky stick platforms that may be lined with fresh leaves and green twigs.

at_a_glance.text: An Anhinga often swims with its body submerged and only the long snakelike neck above water, which is why it is called the snakebird.
Its feathers become waterlogged more easily than those of most waterbirds. Combined with dense bones, that reduces buoyancy and helps the bird slip below the surface to hunt.

quick_hits: A small brown lizard doing push-ups on a fence, wall or tree trunk is often a Brown Anole. Males also flash a reddish-orange throat fan during displays.
Brown Anoles are native to Cuba, the Bahamas and nearby Caribbean islands. They were introduced to Florida and are now widespread across the state.
Where Brown Anoles become abundant, native Green Anoles often shift to higher perches in shrubs and trees, reducing overlap between the two species.
If grabbed by a predator, a Brown Anole can shed part of its tail. A replacement grows later, but it usually looks different from the original.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Cuba, the Bahamas and nearby Caribbean islands. Brown Anoles were introduced to Florida and have since spread widely through the state, especially in disturbed and urban habitats.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Brown, tan or gray, often with darker triangles, diamonds or a pale stripe along the back. Unlike the Green Anole, it cannot turn bright green.

blocks.label: Throat fan (dewlap)
blocks.text: Adult males have a reddish-orange dewlap, usually edged with yellow.

blocks.label: Body
blocks.text: Stockier than a Green Anole, with a shorter snout and rough-looking keeled scales.

blocks.label: Behavior cue
blocks.text: Usually found low on trunks, fences, walls and the ground. Males commonly perform head bobs and push-up displays.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small brown lizard perched low on a post or trunk, bobbing up and down. If it flashes an orange throat fan, it is a displaying male. It cannot turn bright green — that is the native Green Anole, which tends to use higher vegetation.

species.diet: Mostly insects and other small animals, including beetles, ants, flies and spiders. Brown Anoles may also eat smaller lizards and their eggs.
species.behavior: Active by day and usually found close to the ground. Males defend small areas with head bobs, push-up displays and dewlap flashes. When seized by a predator, a Brown Anole can shed part of its tail and later grow a replacement.
species.ecological_role: Brown Anoles are predators of insects and other small animals and are themselves eaten by birds, snakes, larger lizards and other predators. Because they are introduced and abundant in many developed areas, they also interact strongly with native lizards such as the Green Anole.
species.plant_connections: Brown Anoles use plants mainly as structure rather than food. Low trunks, stems, shrubs and groundcover provide basking sites, hunting perches and escape cover. Where Brown and Green Anoles live together, differences in perch height can determine how the two species divide the same garden vertically.

size.length: Usually about five to eight inches from snout to tail tip; males are larger than females.

species.habitat: Sunny, open spots low to the ground — tree trunks, fences, walls, garden edges, leaf litter, and shrubbery. Thrives in yards, parks, and other human-altered landscapes.
species.where_to_look: Look low: fence rails, tree trunks, sidewalk edges, walls and sunny planting beds. On warm days, displaying males are especially easy to notice because of their repeated head bobs and push-ups.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Most active and visible on warm, sunny days; scarce during cold snaps.

danger.people: No meaningful danger to people. Brown Anoles are not venomous and normally flee when approached. Avoid handling them.
danger.pets: No known meaningful danger to pets. Cats and dogs may chase or catch them.

interaction.guidance: Watch without feeding or handling. Brown Anoles are already abundant at the park and do not need supplemental food.

invasive.notes: Introduced and widely established in Florida. Brown Anoles compete with native Green Anoles and can alter how Green Anoles use habitat, often pushing them toward higher perches. They also prey on small lizards, including young anoles.

conservation.status: Abundant and not a species of conservation concern in Florida. Management attention instead focuses on its ecological effects as an introduced species.

species.internal_notes: Most-observed animal in the export (23 obs). Strong 'introduced species' interpretive angle. Framing resolved — treated as invasive (invasive=Red), tied to the documented decline of the native green anole.

seasonality.note: Recorded repeatedly at Palma Sola throughout the year. Activity is highest during warm conditions and drops during cold weather.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Green Anoles are slimmer, can change from green to brown, and generally use higher vegetation where both species occur. Brown Anoles remain brown or gray, are stockier, and often show darker back patterns. Adult males of both species have colorful dewlaps, so use several clues rather than throat color alone.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Brown, tan, or gray, usually patterned with triangles, diamonds, or a pale stripe down the back. The one thing it will never do is turn bright green.

how_to_know_it.caption: A hidden Brown Anole on mottled spurge, one of the odder plants in the succulent garden. A lovely find by one of our high school volunteers.

how_to_know_it.label: Throat fan
how_to_know_it.text: Males flash a reddish-orange dewlap edged with yellow. Male Green Anoles have a pink to reddish dewlap, so the throat fan can be a useful clue — but use it alongside body shape and perch height rather than on its own.

how_to_know_it.label: Body
how_to_know_it.text: Stocky, short-snouted, with ridged scales that give the back a slightly rough look.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Brown Anoles are essentially silent to human observers. Most communication is visual: head bobs, push-ups and dewlap displays.

how_to_know_it.label: Where it sits
how_to_know_it.text: Brown Anoles commonly perch low on fences, walls, trunks and the ground. Where both species occur, Green Anoles often use higher vegetation.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look anywhere the sun reaches low surfaces: fence rails, tree trunks, sidewalk edges and planting beds. Warm, sunny areas are especially productive.
They are present year-round, but cold weather can keep them hidden. Warm, sunny periods bring them out to bask and display.

where_to_find_it_here.label: In this park
where_to_find_it_here.text: The Brown Anole is among the most frequently recorded animals in Palma Sola's wildlife observations, with records going back to 2018. If you are looking for a lizard, this is the one you are most likely to find.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day and usually close to the ground. Males defend small territories and signal with head bobs, push-ups and flashes of the dewlap. These displays communicate with rival males and potential mates.
They eat insects, spiders and other small animals they can overpower. If seized by a predator, an anole can shed part of its tail; a replacement grows gradually afterward.

what_it_does_here.text: Brown Anoles were introduced to Florida from the Caribbean and are now widespread through much of the state.
Brown and Green Anoles overlap in diet and perch use. Where Brown Anoles become abundant, Green Anoles often shift upward into shrubs and trees. Brown Anoles may also prey on young Green Anoles.

what_it_does_here.caption: A Brown Anole on a plant label reading NOT NATIVE. The label means the philodendron — but it is true of the lizard too.

what_it_does_here.label: Evolution you can watch
what_it_does_here.text: In experimental island populations where Brown Anoles were introduced, Green Anoles quickly shifted to higher, narrower perches. Within only a few generations, those populations also evolved larger toepads with more adhesive structures, improving their grip on those perches.

at_a_glance.text: A small brown lizard doing push-ups on a fence or low tree trunk is often a Brown Anole.
It is native to the Caribbean, not Florida, and is now widespread across the state.
Where Brown Anoles become common, native Green Anoles often shift upward into shrubs and trees.
Experiments have shown that Green Anole populations pushed onto higher, narrower perches can evolve larger toepads within only a few generations.

take_care.text: No meaningful danger to people. Brown Anoles are not venomous and normally flee when approached. Avoid handling them, and note that cats and dogs may chase or catch them.
Watch without feeding or handling. Brown Anoles are already abundant at the park and do not need supplemental food.

take_care.label: Conservation
take_care.text: Abundant and not a species of conservation concern in Florida. Management attention instead focuses on its ecological effects as an introduced species.

species.teaser: The push-ups are not exercise. A male Brown Anole uses head bobs and a bright throat fan to advertise territory and communicate with other anoles.
